### Working With a Factoring Company: Setup, Paperwork and Payments
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/working-with-a-factoring-company/
Published: 2026-10-21

Signing up is the easy part. **Working with a factoring company** day to day is where carriers either get fast, steady cash or end up chasing chargebacks and missing payments. This guide covers the routine that keeps funding smooth, from the first notice of assignment to switching companies if you ever need to.

If you are still comparing offers, read [how to choose a factoring company](/blog/how-to-choose-a-factoring-company.html) first.

## Onboarding: what to expect

Typical setup steps include:

- An application with your company details, MC and DOT numbers
- Copies of your operating authority, W-9, insurance certificate and bank details
- A signed factoring agreement
- A UCC-1 filing by the factor on your receivables
- A list of brokers and shippers you work with, so the factor can check their credit

Keep a copy of everything you sign. Note your contract's renewal date and notice period in your calendar now, not when you want to leave.

## The notice of assignment

The notice of assignment (NOA) is a letter from the factoring company telling a broker: "This carrier's invoices are assigned to us. Pay us, not the carrier."

- The NOA is sent to each broker you invoice, usually when you set up with them or on your first factored load.
- Many brokers want the NOA as part of your carrier packet. See the [carrier packet checklist](/blog/carrier-packet-checklist.html).
- If a broker pays you directly by mistake, your contract almost always requires you to forward that payment to the factor. Report it immediately.

## Submitting a clean invoice packet

Every factored load needs a complete packet. Missing or unclear documents are the number one cause of delays.

### Standard packet

1. Your invoice with load number, broker name, rate and any accessorials
2. Signed rate confirmation that matches the invoice amount
3. Signed BOL or proof of delivery, legible, with all pages
4. Lumper receipts or other reimbursable receipts
5. Detention, layover or TONU confirmation from the broker, if billed

### Paperwork tips

- Scan or photograph documents flat, in good light, with all corners visible
- Submit the same day you deliver, before the factor's cutoff
- Make sure the invoice total matches the rate con plus approved accessorials
- Ask drivers to check that receivers signed and dated the BOL before leaving

Our guide to [how to read a rate confirmation](/blog/how-to-read-a-rate-confirmation.html) helps you catch mismatches before they cause funding problems.

## Understand advances, reserves and fees

Read your funding statement for every batch. It should show:

- Gross invoice amount
- Advance paid
- Factoring fee and any other fees
- Reserve held, if any
- Chargebacks or deductions

### Worked example

Hypothetical example: you submit a $3,000 invoice. Your agreement advances 90% with a 3% fee, and releases the reserve when the broker pays.

- Advance today: 90% x $3,000 = $2,700
- Reserve held: $300
- Fee: 3% x $3,000 = $90
- When the broker pays in full, reserve released: $300 - $90 = $210
- Total you receive: $2,700 + $210 = **$2,910**

If the broker short pays $100, that amount usually comes out of your reserve or next funding. Track it so you can dispute the short pay with the broker. Build the factoring fee into your per-mile math when you price loads.

## Avoid chargebacks and short pays

Chargebacks happen when an invoice is not paid in full within the period in your agreement. Common causes and fixes:

| Cause | Prevention |
|---|---|
| Missing or unsigned POD | Check signatures before leaving the receiver |
| Rate con and invoice mismatch | Bill exactly what the rate con says |
| Accessorial not approved | Get accessorials confirmed in writing first |
| Claim or damage dispute | Note exceptions at pickup and delivery |
| Broker credit problem | Run a credit check before every booking |
| Broker paid the carrier directly | Make sure every broker has your NOA |

Detention and TONU are frequent short-pay items. See [how to get detention paid](/blog/how-to-get-detention-paid.html) for documentation that holds up.

## Use the credit check every time

Most factoring companies let you check a broker's credit before you book. Make it a rule: no credit check, no load. If the factor declines a broker, ask why. It may be slow payment, fraud warnings or a lack of history. Pair this with your own checks from [how to vet a freight broker](/blog/how-to-vet-a-freight-broker.html).

## Keep your own records

Do not rely only on the factor's portal. Keep a simple ledger:

- Load number, broker, invoice date and amount
- Date funded and amount advanced
- Date broker paid and reserve released
- Any fees, chargebacks or short pays

Reconcile it weekly with your bank deposits. It also makes tax time and bookkeeping easier. If you would rather hand this off, our [back office services](/trucking-back-office-services.html) can help keep records organized.

## Switching or leaving a factoring company

If you decide to leave:

1. Check your contract for notice period, how notice must be sent and any exit fees.
2. Send written notice on time.
3. Settle open invoices, chargebacks and any balance.
4. Request a release letter for the NOA, to send to each broker.
5. Confirm the UCC filing is terminated or amended.
6. Send the new factor's NOA, or your own payment details, to brokers only after the release.

Brokers will keep paying the old factor until they receive a proper release, so do not skip steps 4 and 5. If the terms are confusing, talk to an attorney.

## How Texas Solutions can help

Texas Solutions is a dispatch service, not a broker, motor carrier or factoring company. Our dispatchers book loads with brokers your factor approves, collect rate cons and paperwork, and help keep invoice packets clean, 24/7, and you approve every load. See our [dispatch services](/dispatch.html) or [talk to a dispatcher](/contact.html).

### Winter Driving and Chain Laws: A Trucker's Survival Guide
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/winter-driving-and-chain-laws/
Published: 2026-10-21

**Winter driving** tests every part of a trucking operation: the driver, the truck and the plan. Snow, ice and closed passes can turn a profitable load into days of delays, and chain laws add rules that change from state to state.

This guide covers how chain laws work, how to prepare your truck, how to drive in winter conditions and how winter affects your hours. Chain laws and traction rules are set by states and can change, so check each state's department of transportation before you run their mountain routes.

## How chain laws work

There is no single national chain law. Each state sets its own rules, and they usually work in two ways:

- **Carry requirements.** Some states require commercial vehicles to carry chains on certain routes during the winter season, even on clear days.
- **Use requirements.** When conditions get bad, the state posts chain controls or traction law levels, and trucks must chain up before continuing.

States with major mountain passes in the West, such as California, Oregon, Washington, Colorado, Idaho, Montana, Utah and Wyoming, are known for active chain and traction rules, but rules can apply elsewhere too. Many states use tiered levels, where higher levels require more vehicles to chain or close the road to trucks.

Penalties for not carrying chains or not chaining when required can be significant, and higher if your truck blocks the road. Check each state's DOT site and the posted signs on approach.

### Chain-up basics

- Use designated **chain-up areas**. Never chain up in a travel lane.
- Wear high-visibility clothing, gloves and a headlamp.
- Lay chains out flat, drape them over the tire, drive forward slightly and fasten them tight.
- Re-tighten after a short distance, and keep your speed low with chains on.
- Remove chains in a chain removal area once conditions allow.

**Practice at home before the season.** Learning to chain in a blizzard at night is how drivers get hurt.

## Prepare your truck before winter

Use this checklist in the fall:

- [ ] **Fuel:** use winter-blend diesel where available, carry an anti-gel additive and add it before the fuel cools
- [ ] **Fuel filters:** replace them and carry a spare, since gelled fuel often shows up as a clogged filter
- [ ] **Air system:** service the air dryer and drain air tanks regularly to keep moisture from freezing in lines and valves
- [ ] **Batteries and charging:** test batteries and clean terminals
- [ ] **Block heater:** confirm it works if your truck has one
- [ ] **Tires:** check tread depth and pressure; cold weather lowers pressure
- [ ] **Wipers and fluid:** winter blades and fluid rated for freezing temperatures
- [ ] **Lights:** clean and working, plus a brush to clear snow and ice
- [ ] **DEF:** know how your system handles freezing and keep fresh DEF on hand
- [ ] **Chains:** the right size for your tires, plus repair links, bungees and tensioners

Our [truck maintenance schedule](/blog/truck-maintenance-schedule.html) and [pre-trip inspection checklist](/blog/pre-trip-inspection-checklist.html) cover the rest. Set money aside for winter repairs before the season starts.

## Winter emergency kit

If you get stuck on a closed highway, you could be there for many hours. Keep these in the cab:

- Warm clothes, boots, gloves, hat and a sleeping bag or heavy blanket
- Several days of water and non-perishable food
- Flashlight or headlamp with spare batteries
- Phone chargers and a backup power bank
- First aid kit and any medications you need
- Ice scraper, snow brush and a small shovel
- Sand or traction mats
- Warning triangles and flares
- Extra fuel filter and anti-gel additive

## Driving in winter conditions

### Slow down and add space

Reduce speed well below the limit on snow and ice, and greatly increase following distance. Federal regulations require extreme caution in hazardous conditions and say a driver should stop when conditions become dangerous enough. A truck needs far more distance to stop on ice than on dry pavement.

### Watch for black ice

Bridges, overpasses, shaded curves and areas near water freeze first. Watch for spray from other vehicles: if it disappears while the road still looks wet, the road may have turned to ice. Check outside temperature readings often.

### Avoid jackknifes

- Brake gently and early; avoid sudden steering inputs.
- Be extra careful with an empty or light trailer, which is more likely to swing out.
- Follow your manufacturer's guidance on the engine brake on slick roads.
- Do not use cruise control on snow or ice.

### Know when to stop

If visibility drops, trucks are sliding off the road or the road is closing, find safe parking and wait. Tell your broker or dispatcher early. A late load is far better than a crash or a cargo claim. Plan stops in advance with our guide to [truck parking and trip planning](/blog/truck-parking-and-trip-planning.html).

## Winter and hours of service

Delays in winter eat into your clock. The federal **adverse driving conditions exception** can allow up to 2 additional hours of driving and can extend the 14-hour window by up to 2 hours. It only applies to conditions like snow, ice or unusual road conditions that you did not know about, and could not reasonably have known about, when you started your trip or shift. Forecast storms you could have planned around may not qualify. Confirm the current wording with FMCSA before you rely on it, and annotate your log when you use it.

## Planning winter freight

- **Check forecasts for the whole route,** not just the pickup.
- **Build buffer time** into appointments and tell the broker about expected weather delays before you book.
- **Price the risk.** Mountain lanes in winter can mean slower miles, chain-up time and closures. Your rate should reflect that. Run the numbers with the [load profitability calculator](/load-profitability-calculator.html).
- **Protect reefer and temperature-sensitive freight** from freezing as carefully as you would from heat.

## How Texas Solutions can help

Texas Solutions is a dispatch service, not a broker or motor carrier. Our dispatchers find and negotiate loads, handle broker packets and paperwork 24/7, and watch weather on your lanes so appointments leave room for safe winter driving. You approve every load. See our [dispatch services](/dispatch.html) or [talk to a dispatcher](/contact.html).

### Weigh Stations and Bypass: Weight Limits, Scales and Tips
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/weigh-stations-and-bypass/
Published: 2026-10-21

**Weigh stations** are a normal part of every trucker's day, but a scale ticket or a surprise inspection can cost you hours and money. Knowing the weight limits, how to load legally and how bypass programs work makes scales a quick stop instead of a problem.

This guide covers the basics as we understand them. Weight and size rules vary by state and change over time, so confirm current limits with FMCSA, the Federal Highway Administration and each state you run.

## What happens at a weigh station

Weigh stations, sometimes called ports of entry or inspection stations, are run by states. Officers check:

- **Weight:** gross vehicle weight and individual axle weights
- **Size:** height, width and length when needed
- **Credentials:** registration, IFTA, operating authority and permits
- **Safety:** obvious defects, and sometimes a full roadside inspection
- **Driver items:** license, medical card and hours of service

Most stations weigh you as you roll slowly across the scale. Signals or signs then tell you to continue, pull around back or park and bring in your paperwork. Read the signs carefully; missing a "report to scale house" signal can turn a quick stop into a citation. For what happens if you are pulled in, see our guide to [DOT roadside inspections](/blog/dot-roadside-inspections.html).

## Federal weight limits

On the Interstate System, the general federal limits are:

| Limit | Federal maximum |
|---|---|
| Gross vehicle weight | 80,000 lb |
| Single axle | 20,000 lb |
| Tandem axle | 34,000 lb |
| Axle groups | Governed by the federal bridge formula |

The **bridge formula** limits how much weight can sit on a group of axles based on how many axles there are and how far apart they are. It is why axle spacing matters, not just total weight.

States can have different limits on non-interstate roads, and some states allow heavier weights through permits or older grandfather rules. Many states also set rules for steer axle weight and kingpin-to-rear-axle distance. If you need to haul heavier or wider freight, see our guide to [oversize and overweight permits](/blog/oversize-overweight-permits.html).

Some states allow a small enforcement tolerance, but do not plan around it. Load to the legal limit.

## Who has to stop

Each state decides which vehicles must enter an open station. The threshold is often based on gross vehicle weight rating or vehicle type, and it can include smaller trucks like hotshots and box trucks. Do not assume you can skip a scale because you drive a pickup with a trailer. Read the signs at the station entrance, which often state who must enter.

## How bypass programs work

Bypass programs let qualified trucks skip some weigh stations without slowing down. They come in two main forms:

- **Transponder-based programs** that use a device mounted on the windshield
- **Smartphone or in-cab app programs** that use GPS and the phone or ELD tablet

As you approach a participating site, the system checks your vehicle, carrier and sometimes weigh-in-motion data. You then get a green signal (bypass) or red signal (pull in). Factors that affect bypass eligibility often include:

- Your carrier's safety record, including inspection and violation history
- Whether your credentials are valid
- Weigh-in-motion readings on approach, where available
- Random selection, so even good carriers get pulled in sometimes

Questions to ask before you sign up for any bypass service:

- [ ] Which states and sites does it cover on my lanes?
- [ ] What does it cost per month, per truck or per bypass?
- [ ] Does it work with my ELD tablet, or do I need separate hardware?
- [ ] How does it handle toll payment, if at all?
- [ ] Can I cancel without long contract fees?

A clean safety record is what earns bypasses over time. Our guide to [CSA scores explained](/blog/csa-scores-explained.html) shows how inspections and violations feed into it.

## Balancing your axle weights

You can be under 80,000 pounds and still be overweight on an axle. The fix is usually adjusting the trailer tandems or the fifth wheel.

**Hypothetical example:** A driver scales at a certified truck scale before heading out:

- Steer: 11,800 lb
- Drives: 32,600 lb
- Trailer tandems: 35,100 lb
- Gross: 79,500 lb

Gross is legal, but the trailer tandem is 1,100 pounds over the 34,000-pound limit. Sliding the trailer tandems toward the rear of the trailer shifts weight forward onto the drive axles. After a slide and a re-weigh:

- Steer: 11,900 lb
- Drives: 33,800 lb
- Trailer tandems: 33,800 lb
- Gross: 79,500 lb

Every axle group is now legal. How much weight moves per hole depends on the trailer, so re-weigh after each adjustment instead of guessing. Sliding the fifth wheel moves weight between the steer and the drive axles in the same way. Also check that your slide does not break a state's kingpin-to-axle rule.

If you cannot balance the load legally, the freight may need to be reworked at the shipper. Raise it before you leave, and note it on the bill of lading if possible.

## Tips to get through scales smoothly

1. **Scale after loading** at a certified scale near the shipper, and keep the ticket.
2. **Know your empty weights** so you can estimate how much freight you can take.
3. **Ask the broker for accurate weight** before booking. Our [how to read a rate confirmation](/blog/how-to-read-a-rate-confirmation.html) guide covers what to check.
4. **Keep paperwork organized:** registration, IFTA license, permits, insurance, medical card and bill of lading.
5. **Do a quick walk-around** at fuel stops; lights and tires are easy reasons to get pulled in.
6. **Follow every sign and signal,** even if you have bypass.

## How Texas Solutions can help

Texas Solutions is a dispatch service, not a broker or motor carrier. Our dispatchers find and negotiate loads, confirm weights with brokers before booking, and handle broker packets and paperwork 24/7. You approve every load. See our [dispatch services](/dispatch.html) or [talk to a dispatcher](/contact.html).

### UCR Registration Guide: Who Needs It, Fees and Deadlines
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/ucr-registration-guide/
Published: 2026-10-21

**UCR registration** is a once-a-year task that is easy to forget until a roadside officer or a broker asks for it. This guide explains who must register for the Unified Carrier Registration program, how the fee is figured, and how to file without overpaying.

## What UCR is

The Unified Carrier Registration program is a federal law program run by a board of state and federal representatives, with fees set through FMCSA rulemaking. Fees collected go to participating states, largely to support motor carrier safety programs and enforcement.

UCR does not replace your USDOT number, operating authority, IRP or IFTA. It is a separate annual registration. Brokers and shippers may check it during carrier setup, and roadside officers in participating states can see whether you are registered for the current year.

## Who needs UCR

UCR generally applies to businesses that operate in interstate or international commerce, including:

- **For-hire motor carriers** with interstate operations,
- **Private motor carriers** of property in interstate commerce,
- **Exempt carriers** that haul exempt commodities interstate,
- **Freight brokers, freight forwarders and leasing companies.**

Interstate commerce can include a trip that stays inside one state if the freight is part of a longer interstate move, such as a port or rail container. If you are not sure, check with the UCR program before assuming you are exempt.

If you lease onto another carrier and run under its authority, the carrier usually registers and counts your truck. If you have your own authority, it is on you.

## How UCR fees work

UCR fees are set in **brackets based on the number of commercial motor vehicles** you operate. Brokers and freight forwarders that do not operate trucks pay the lowest bracket. The fee amounts are adjusted from time to time by FMCSA, so look up the current table on the official UCR website rather than relying on an old invoice.

### Counting your vehicles

The fleet count generally includes power units (trucks and tractors) you operate in interstate commerce. The program gives carriers a choice of counting method, typically based on your vehicle count on your most recent MCS-150 or on the vehicles you operated over a recent 12-month period. Trailers are generally not counted. Check current UCR guidance for the exact rules before you file.

### Worked example: choosing the right bracket

Here is a hypothetical example. Bracket boundaries and fees below are placeholders, not actual UCR figures.

- Your MCS-150 shows **3 power units**.
- You sold one truck mid-year and now run **2**.
- The current UCR table puts 0-2 vehicles in the lowest bracket and 3-5 in the next.
- Depending on the counting method you are allowed to use, you might fall in either bracket. Keep records (titles, bills of sale, MCS-150 update) that support the count you report.

The takeaway: keep your MCS-150 updated, because it is one source the UCR program uses for your fleet size. See how to [keep your MC authority active](/blog/keep-your-mc-authority-active.html) for MCS-150 timing.

## When to register

UCR is registered by **calendar year**. Registration for the next year typically opens in the fall, and states generally begin enforcing the new year's registration early in the new year. Exact opening and enforcement dates are announced by the UCR program each year, so check the official site and register early.

If you get new authority partway through the year, register for the current year before you start hauling interstate. If you plan to stop running interstate or close the business, check with the UCR program before skipping a year, and update your FMCSA records so your status is accurate.

## Base state and participating states

Your **base state** is generally the state where your principal place of business is located. Most states participate in UCR. If your home state does not participate, you register through a nearby participating state as directed by the program.

## Step-by-step: how to register

1. **Have your USDOT number** and business information ready.
2. **Go to the official UCR registration website.** Be careful with search results; look-alike sites charge extra service fees.
3. **Confirm your company details** pulled from FMCSA records.
4. **Choose your classification** (carrier, broker, freight forwarder or leasing company, or a combination).
5. **Enter your vehicle count** using an allowed counting method.
6. **Pay the fee** for your bracket.
7. **Save your receipt** and keep a copy in the cab and in your office files.

### UCR checklist

- [ ] USDOT number active and MCS-150 up to date
- [ ] Classification matches what you actually do
- [ ] Vehicle count supported by records
- [ ] Registered for the correct calendar year
- [ ] Paid on the official site, not a third-party look-alike
- [ ] Receipt saved digitally and on paper
- [ ] Calendar reminder set for next fall

## Where UCR fits with other filings

UCR sits alongside insurance, the [BOC-3 filing](/blog/boc-3-filing-explained.html), the MCS-150 update, [Form 2290](/blog/how-to-file-form-2290.html), IFTA and IRP. Missing any one can stop a broker setup. If you want help with the paperwork side, see our [trucking business services](/trucking-business-services.html).

This guide is general information. UCR fees, brackets, dates and rules are set by the UCR program and FMCSA and can change, so confirm the current details on the official UCR website.

## How Texas Solutions can help

Texas Solutions is a dispatch service, not a broker or motor carrier. Our dispatchers find and negotiate loads, handle broker packets and paperwork, and work 24/7, while you approve every load. We help keep your compliance documents ready so broker setups go smoothly. See our [dispatch services](/dispatch.html) or [talk to a dispatcher](/contact.html).

### TWIC Card and Port Drayage: A Guide for Owner-Operators
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/twic-card-and-port-drayage/
Published: 2026-10-21

The **TWIC card** (Transportation Worker Identification Credential) is the federal ID that lets you into secure areas of ports and maritime terminals without an escort. If you want to haul containers in and out of a port, the TWIC is step one, but it is not the only thing standing between you and your first drayage load.

## What a TWIC card is

TWIC is run by the Transportation Security Administration together with the US Coast Guard. It is a tamper-resistant card tied to a background check, and it is required for unescorted access to secure areas of facilities and vessels regulated under the Maritime Transportation Security Act. That includes container terminals at seaports and many river and inland port facilities.

Key facts:

- The card is generally **valid for five years**.
- It is tied to you, not to a company. It moves with you if you change carriers.
- Holding a TWIC does not by itself grant entry. Each terminal still decides who comes in, and usually requires a business reason, such as a booked container move.

## Who can get one

TSA runs a security threat assessment that checks criminal history, immigration status and certain other records. US citizens and lawful permanent residents are eligible, along with some other immigration categories. Certain serious offenses disqualify applicants permanently or for a set period, and TSA has a waiver and appeal process. Review TSA's current list of disqualifying offenses before you apply.

## How to apply for a TWIC, step by step

1. **Pre-enroll online** through TSA's official enrollment program. Pre-enrolling saves time at the center.
2. **Book an appointment** at an enrollment center. Many are in port cities, and some are inside other TSA enrollment locations.
3. **Bring identity documents.** Usually a passport, or a combination such as a driver's license plus a birth certificate. Check the accepted list before you go.
4. **Give fingerprints and pay the fee.** The fee is set by TSA; check the current amount.
5. **Wait for the background check.** Many applicants are approved within a few weeks; some take longer.
6. **Pick up or receive the card,** depending on the option you chose, and activate it if required.

If you lose the card, report it and order a replacement; there is a separate replacement fee.

## Beyond TWIC: what else drayage requires

The TWIC gets you through the gate. Pulling a container also usually requires:

| Requirement | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| Intermodal interchange agreement | Steamship lines and equipment providers require carriers to sign a standard interchange agreement before you can take their containers and chassis. |
| Terminal or port registration | Many ports keep a registry of trucks and carriers allowed to enter. Some tie it to clean-truck or engine-age rules. |
| Insurance | Interchange agreements usually require specific coverages, often including trailer interchange coverage. Talk to your insurance agent. |
| SCAC code | Many terminals and steamship lines use your Standard Carrier Alpha Code to identify your company. |
| Appointment system access | Most busy terminals require a booked appointment for each pickup or return. |
| Day cab or sleeper | Either works. Many drayage operators run day cabs because they are lighter and easier to maneuver. |

Requirements are set by each port, terminal and equipment provider, and they change. Ask the terminals you plan to serve exactly what they need.

## The chassis check you should never skip

In drayage, you often hook to a chassis you have never seen before. You are responsible for its roadability once you leave the gate. Before you pull out:

- Check tires for tread depth, cuts and proper inflation.
- Test all lights, including brake and turn signals.
- Look at brakes, slack adjusters and air lines for leaks.
- Confirm twist locks are engaged on every corner.
- Check the mudflaps, landing gear and the inspection sticker.
- Note container seal number and compare it to your paperwork.

If something fails, take it to the terminal's repair area before leaving. A defect found at a roadside inspection is your violation, not the chassis owner's. See our [pre-trip inspection checklist](/blog/pre-trip-inspection-checklist.html).

## Watch the weight

Containers are loaded by shippers you never meet, and some leave the port heavy. Federal limits generally cap gross weight at 80,000 lbs on the Interstate system, with axle limits on top of that. Ways to protect yourself:

- Check the declared weight on the paperwork before you accept the move.
- Scale the load at the first certified scale if you have any doubt.
- Know your tractor and chassis tare weight so you can do quick math.

Hypothetical example: tractor 17,500 lbs + chassis 6,500 lbs = 24,000 lbs empty. That leaves about 56,000 lbs for container plus cargo before you hit 80,000 lbs. A 40-foot container itself can weigh around 8,000 lbs, so cargo much above 48,000 lbs is a red flag. Some states allow overweight container permits on certain routes near ports; see [oversize and overweight permits](/blog/oversize-overweight-permits.html).

## Making drayage pay

Drayage is paid per move, not per mile, so time is the real cost. Things that eat into it:

- **Terminal wait times.** Long lines can turn a 40-mile move into a full day.
- **Detention and chassis fees.** Know who pays if the receiver holds your chassis.
- **Per diem and storage charges** on late container returns. Get clear on who is responsible.
- **Dry runs.** If the container is not available when you arrive, ask for dry run pay.

Track your average hours per move and compare it to the rate. The [detention pay calculator](/detention-pay-calculator.html) and [cost per mile calculator](/cost-per-mile-calculator.html) can help you see your true hourly earnings.

## Quick drayage startup checklist

- TWIC card issued and activated
- USDOT and MC active, SCAC code obtained
- Interchange agreement signed
- Port or terminal registration complete
- Insurance meeting interchange requirements
- Appointment system logins set up
- Pre-trip routine for unfamiliar chassis

Fees, eligibility rules and port programs change. Confirm current requirements with TSA, the US Coast Guard, and each port and terminal you plan to serve.

## How Texas Solutions can help

Texas Solutions is a dispatch service, not a broker or a motor carrier. Our dispatchers find and negotiate loads, including inland moves that connect with port freight, handle broker packets and paperwork 24/7, and you approve every load. See our [dispatch services](/dispatch.html) or [talk to a dispatcher](/contact.html).

### Trucking Tax Basics for Owner-Operators
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/trucking-tax-basics/
Published: 2026-10-21

**Trucking tax basics** are not complicated once you see the moving parts, but the penalties for ignoring them can sink a small carrier. This guide explains the main taxes an owner-operator runs into and how to stay organized. It is general education, not tax advice: confirm every decision with a CPA or enrolled agent who works with trucking businesses.

## The taxes most owner-operators deal with

Think of your taxes in two groups: taxes on your profit, and taxes on your truck and fuel.

**Taxes on profit**

- **Federal income tax** on your net business profit (revenue minus deductible expenses).
- **Self-employment tax**, which covers Social Security and Medicare for people who work for themselves. An employer normally pays half of these for employees; as an owner-operator you cover both halves. The combined rate has long been 15.3% on most net self-employment earnings, but confirm current figures with the IRS.
- **State income tax**, depending on where you live. Some states have none, others do.

**Taxes on the truck and fuel**

- **Heavy Vehicle Use Tax (HVUT)**, filed on IRS Form 2290 for heavy highway vehicles. See our guide on [how to file Form 2290](/blog/how-to-file-form-2290.html).
- **Fuel tax through IFTA** if you run interstate with a qualifying vehicle. Our [IFTA filing guide](/blog/ifta-for-owner-operators-how-to-file.html) walks through the quarterly return.
- **Registration fees** through your base state and IRP for apportioned plates.

## Why quarterly estimated taxes matter

A company driver has taxes withheld from every paycheck. You do not. The IRS expects you to pay as you earn, usually through **quarterly estimated tax payments**. Missing them can lead to underpayment penalties and a large bill in April that you are not ready for.

The simplest habit is to treat taxes like a fixed cost:

1. Open a separate bank account just for taxes.
2. Every time a settlement or factoring payment arrives, move a set percentage into it.
3. Pay your estimated taxes from that account on each due date.
4. Review the percentage with your CPA at least once a year, or after a big change in revenue.

Your CPA can tell you the due dates, the safe-harbor rules that may protect you from penalties, and how much to pay each quarter.

## Common deductible expenses

Business expenses that are ordinary and necessary for your trucking work are generally deductible. Typical categories include:

- Fuel and DEF
- Repairs, maintenance, tires and washes
- Truck insurance (liability, cargo, physical damage)
- Dispatch fees, factoring fees and load board subscriptions
- ELD service, phone and data plans used for the business
- Permits, tolls, scale fees and parking
- Licenses, registration and the HVUT
- Accounting, legal and bookkeeping fees
- Interest on business loans

The key is proof. Keep receipts, settlement statements, fuel reports and rate confirmations. Without records, a deduction is hard to defend. Our guide to [trucking LLC setup and bookkeeping](/blog/trucking-llc-and-bookkeeping.html) covers simple systems for this.

## Depreciation: how the truck itself gets deducted

A truck is a long-term asset, so its cost is usually recovered through **depreciation** rather than deducted like a fuel receipt. Tax law has offered accelerated options (such as Section 179 expensing and bonus depreciation) that let some buyers deduct a large share of the cost in the first year. The limits and percentages have changed many times, so do not plan a purchase around a number you read online.

A big first-year deduction can lower your tax bill now but leave fewer deductions for later years, and selling the truck can trigger tax on the depreciation you took. Ask your CPA to model both paths before you buy. If you are weighing a purchase, bring the quote to your CPA before you sign.

## Per diem for drivers on the road

Drivers who are away from home overnight may be able to deduct meal and incidental expenses using the IRS per diem method instead of saving every meal receipt. Transportation workers subject to DOT hours-of-service rules have historically been allowed a higher deductible percentage than other travelers. Rates and rules are set by the IRS and change, and how per diem works depends on whether you are self-employed or an employee. Track your days away from home with the [per diem calculator](/per-diem-calculator.html) and let your CPA apply the current rules.

## A worked example of setting money aside

Here is a **hypothetical** month to show the habit, not a real tax calculation:

| Item | Hypothetical amount |
|---|---|
| Gross revenue | $20,000 |
| Operating expenses (fuel, insurance, repairs, fees) | $14,500 |
| Estimated net profit | $5,500 |
| Tax set-aside at a CPA-chosen 25% of profit | $1,375 |

In this example, $1,375 moves into the tax account the same week the money arrives. The 25% is only a placeholder; your real percentage depends on your situation. Track your cost per mile to keep your expense side accurate, because a wrong cost number leads to a wrong tax estimate.

## Year-end tax checklist

- Reconcile every bank and card account to your books
- Collect 1099 forms from brokers, shippers or carriers you leased to
- Total fuel, IFTA miles and gallons by quarter
- List equipment bought or sold during the year, with dates and prices
- Gather insurance, loan interest and registration statements
- Tally days away from home for per diem
- Send everything to your CPA early, not the week before the deadline

## Mistakes that cost owner-operators money

- **Spending the tax money.** A strong month feels like profit until the quarterly payment is due.
- **Mixing personal and business accounts.** It makes deductions harder to prove and bookkeeping slower.
- **Buying a truck for the write-off.** A deduction only saves a portion of what you spend. Buy equipment because the business needs it.
- **Filing late.** Late HVUT, IFTA or income tax returns can bring penalties and interest, and some can put your registration at risk.

## How Texas Solutions can help

Texas Solutions is a dispatch service, not a tax preparer, broker or motor carrier. Our dispatchers find and negotiate loads, handle broker packets and paperwork, and send you clean rate confirmations and load records that make your CPA's job easier, 24/7, with you approving every load. Learn more about our [dispatch services](/dispatch.html) or [talk to a dispatcher](/contact.html).

### Trucking LLC Setup and Simple Bookkeeping for Owner-Operators
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/trucking-llc-and-bookkeeping/
Published: 2026-10-21

Choosing between a sole proprietorship and a **trucking LLC** is one of the first business decisions a new owner-operator makes, and good bookkeeping is what keeps that business alive afterward. This guide explains the common options in plain English and gives you a simple weekly routine for your books. It is general education; confirm your entity choice with an attorney and your tax setup with a CPA.

## Sole proprietor, LLC or corporation

Here is how the common structures generally compare:

| Structure | How it generally works | Things to weigh |
|---|---|---|
| Sole proprietorship | You and the business are the same for legal and tax purposes | Simplest to start; no separation between business and personal liability |
| Single-member LLC | A separate legal entity under state law; by default the IRS treats it like a sole proprietor for income tax | State filing fees and annual reports; separation only works if you keep money separate |
| LLC taxed as an S corporation | An LLC that elects S corp tax treatment; owner may take a salary plus distributions | Payroll, extra filings and accounting costs; only sensible at certain profit levels |
| Corporation | Separate entity with its own formalities | More paperwork; rarely the first choice for a one-truck operator |

Two points matter most:

1. **An LLC is not insurance.** Your auto liability and cargo coverage are your real protection against claims. An LLC's separation can be lost if you treat business money as personal money.
2. **Tax treatment is a separate choice.** An LLC can be taxed in different ways. Whether an S corp election makes sense depends on your profit and costs, so have a CPA run the numbers.

## Setting up the business the right way

If you choose an LLC, the usual order looks like this:

1. **Form the LLC with your state** and pick a registered agent.
2. **Get an EIN** from the IRS (free).
3. **Open a business checking account** in the LLC's name.
4. **Apply for your USDOT and MC number** under the business name. Use the exact business name you registered.
5. **Get insurance** in the business name, matching your authority.
6. **Set up your books** before your first load, not after tax season starts.

Make sure the legal name is exactly the same on your LLC filing, EIN letter, bank account, FMCSA records and insurance. Mismatches slow down broker setup and factoring approvals. For the full startup path, read [how to start a trucking company](/blog/how-to-start-a-trucking-company.html).

## Keep business and personal money apart

This is the single most useful bookkeeping habit:

- All load payments go into the business account.
- All business expenses come out of the business account or a business card.
- You pay yourself with a transfer to your personal account (an owner's draw or salary, depending on structure).
- Personal expenses never touch the business account.

Clean separation makes your books faster, your deductions easier to prove and your LLC's separation more meaningful.

## A simple chart of accounts for trucking

You do not need hundreds of categories. A one-truck operation can start with these:

**Income**
- Linehaul revenue
- Fuel surcharge
- Accessorials (detention, layover, TONU, lumper reimbursements)

**Expenses**
- Fuel and DEF
- Repairs and maintenance
- Tires
- Insurance
- Truck and trailer payments (split into interest and principal with your CPA's help)
- Dispatch fees
- Factoring fees
- Permits, licenses and registration
- Tolls and scales
- ELD, phone and software
- Office, accounting and legal
- Travel and per diem days (tracked as your CPA advises)

Categories that match how you run the truck make it easy to compare against your [cost per mile calculator](/cost-per-mile-calculator.html) results.

## The 30-minute weekly bookkeeping routine

Pick one day a week and do this every time:

1. **Record each load:** date, broker, origin, destination, loaded miles, empty miles, rate and accessorials.
2. **Match payments:** mark which invoices were paid and which are still open.
3. **Enter expenses:** upload fuel receipts, repair invoices and fees. Photograph paper receipts the same day you get them.
4. **Move tax money:** transfer your set percentage into a separate tax account.
5. **Check the balance:** confirm the bank balance roughly matches what your books say.

Once a month, reconcile every account line by line and review your profit. Once a quarter, pull your miles and gallons for IFTA and send your numbers to your CPA for estimated taxes. Our [trucking tax basics](/blog/trucking-tax-basics.html) guide explains why those quarterly steps matter.

## Worked example: why weekly books catch problems

Imagine a **hypothetical** owner-operator who reviews books weekly. In week three the numbers show:

- Revenue booked: $6,000
- Payments received: $2,400
- Open invoices: $3,600, one of them 40 days old

Without weekly books, that 40-day invoice might go unnoticed until rent is due. With them, the owner calls the broker the same day. Unpaid invoices are a cash flow problem even when the business is profitable on paper. If you factor, check your factoring reports just as closely.

## Records to keep

- Rate confirmations, bills of lading and proof of delivery
- Settlement statements and factoring reports
- Fuel receipts and IFTA mileage records
- Repair and maintenance invoices (also useful for DOT and resale)
- Insurance policies and certificates
- Loan, lease and equipment purchase documents
- Business formation papers, EIN letter and annual state filings

Store digital copies in organized folders by year and month. Ask your CPA how long to keep tax records and check FMCSA rules for safety-related records.

## When to hire help

Doing your own books is fine at one truck if you stay consistent. Consider a bookkeeper when you fall behind more than two weeks, add a second truck, or start paying drivers. Our [trucking back-office services](/trucking-back-office-services.html) page describes paperwork support we offer alongside dispatch.

Texas Solutions is a dispatch service, not a broker, motor carrier, law firm or accounting firm. Our dispatchers find and negotiate loads, handle broker packets and paperwork, and send you organized rate confirmations and load details that drop straight into your books, 24/7, and you approve every load. See our [dispatch services](/dispatch.html) or [talk to a dispatcher](/contact.html).

### Trucking KPIs to Track: 10 Numbers That Run Your Business
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/trucking-kpis-to-track/
Published: 2026-10-21

**Trucking KPIs** (key performance indicators) are the handful of numbers that tell you whether your truck is making money and why. Gross revenue is not enough: a truck can gross a lot and still lose money if deadhead, fuel or slow-paying brokers eat the margin. Here are ten KPIs worth tracking, how to calculate each one, and a hypothetical example that ties them together.

## Why KPIs matter more than gross revenue

Gross is what everyone talks about, but profit decides whether you stay in business. KPIs let you:

- Compare loads and lanes on equal terms
- Spot rising costs before they become a crisis
- Negotiate with confidence because you know your floor
- Decide when you are ready to add a truck

## The 10 KPIs to track

### 1. Revenue per total mile
Total revenue divided by **all** miles driven, loaded and empty. This is your real rate, not the per-loaded-mile figure on the rate confirmation.

### 2. Cost per mile
All costs (fixed and variable) divided by total miles. Calculate it monthly with the [cost per mile calculator](/cost-per-mile-calculator.html). Our guide to the [cost of running a semi truck per mile](/blog/cost-of-running-a-semi-truck-per-mile.html) explains what goes in it.

### 3. Profit per mile
Revenue per total mile minus cost per mile. If this number is thin or negative, more miles will not fix it.

### 4. Deadhead percentage
Empty miles divided by total miles, times 100. Lower is generally better, though a short deadhead into a strong market can pay off. See [what deadhead is and how to reduce it](/blog/what-is-deadhead-in-trucking-how-to-reduce-it.html).

### 5. Miles per truck per week
How much the truck actually works. Low miles may point to long waits, poor load planning or too much home time for your cost structure.

### 6. Revenue per truck per week
A simple utilization check that matters a lot once you have more than one truck.

### 7. Fuel economy (MPG)
Gallons used versus miles driven. Track it per truck and per driver; changes often signal mechanical issues or driving habits.

### 8. Maintenance cost per mile
Repairs, tires and maintenance divided by miles. A steady rise usually means a truck is getting closer to a major repair.

### 9. Average days to pay
How long, on average, from delivery to cash in the bank. Slow payment strains cash flow even when you are profitable.

### 10. Unpaid time
Hours spent in detention, waiting on loads, or broken down. Track detention hours and whether they were paid, so you know which shippers and brokers cost you time.

## Formulas at a glance

| KPI | Formula |
|---|---|
| Revenue per total mile | Total revenue / (loaded miles + empty miles) |
| Cost per mile | Total costs / total miles |
| Profit per mile | Revenue per total mile - cost per mile |
| Deadhead % | Empty miles / total miles x 100 |
| Miles per truck per week | Total miles / trucks / weeks |
| Fuel economy | Total miles / gallons used |
| Maintenance cost per mile | Maintenance and repair costs / total miles |
| Average days to pay | Sum of (payment date - delivery date) / number of loads |

## Worked example: one hypothetical month

Here is a **hypothetical** month for one truck:

- Revenue: $22,000
- Loaded miles: 8,400
- Empty miles: 1,100
- Total costs: $17,575
- Gallons used: 1,520
- Maintenance and repairs: $1,330

Now the KPIs:

- **Total miles:** 8,400 + 1,100 = 9,500
- **Revenue per loaded mile:** $22,000 / 8,400 = about $2.62
- **Revenue per total mile:** $22,000 / 9,500 = about **$2.32**
- **Cost per mile:** $17,575 / 9,500 = **$1.85**
- **Profit per mile:** $2.32 - $1.85 = about **$0.47**
- **Deadhead:** 1,100 / 9,500 = about **11.6%**
- **Fuel economy:** 9,500 / 1,520 = **6.25 mpg**
- **Maintenance per mile:** $1,330 / 9,500 = **$0.14**

The rate confirmations averaged $2.62 per loaded mile, but the business really earned $2.32 per mile driven. That gap is the cost of deadhead. Cutting empty miles from 1,100 to 600 would raise revenue per total mile with no change in rates.

## How to track KPIs without a big system

1. **Keep a load log.** One row per load: date, broker, lane, loaded miles, empty miles, rate, accessorials, delivery date and payment date.
2. **Keep a monthly expense summary** using the same categories every month.
3. **Calculate weekly** the load-level numbers: revenue per total mile, deadhead and miles.
4. **Calculate monthly** the full set, including cost per mile and maintenance per mile.
5. **Compare to last month and the same month last year.** Trends matter more than a single number.
6. **Act on one number at a time.** Pick the weakest KPI and work on it for a month.

## Using KPIs to make decisions

- **Accepting a load:** check revenue per total mile including the deadhead to reach it, against your cost per mile.
- **Dropping a broker:** if their average days to pay keeps climbing, factor that into whether their rates are worth it.
- **Choosing lanes:** compare profit per mile by lane, not by load.
- **Adding a truck:** only when the first truck has steady profit per mile, healthy reserves and you understand what a second truck changes. Read [how to grow from 1 to 5 trucks](/blog/grow-from-1-to-5-trucks.html).

## How Texas Solutions can help

Texas Solutions is a dispatch service, not a broker or motor carrier. Our dispatchers find and negotiate loads against your real cost per mile, plan lanes to keep deadhead down, handle broker packets and paperwork, and work 24/7, while you approve every load. See our [dispatch services](/dispatch.html) or [talk to a dispatcher](/contact.html).

### Trucking Insurance Explained: Coverages Owner-Operators Need
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/trucking-insurance-explained/
Published: 2026-10-21

Insurance is often one of the largest fixed costs for an owner-operator, and one of the most confusing. With **trucking insurance explained** in plain English, you can see what each coverage does, which ones are required, and what to ask before you sign. This guide is general information, not insurance advice. Review your situation with a licensed insurance agent.

## Why insurance matters beyond the law

Without the right coverage you cannot get or keep active authority, most brokers will not set you up, and a single accident can wipe out years of savings. The goal is not to buy everything. It is to cover the risks that could put you out of business, at a price your rates can carry.

## Leased-on or your own authority?

Your needs depend on how you operate:

- **Your own authority (MC number):** you are the motor carrier. You need primary liability filed with FMCSA, plus the coverages your brokers and lender require.
- **Leased onto a carrier:** the carrier usually provides primary liability while you are under dispatch. You may still need non-trucking liability or bobtail, physical damage, and sometimes occupational accident coverage. Read your lease to see exactly what you must buy.

If you are still deciding, our guides on [getting your MC number](/blog/how-to-get-mc-number-authority-owner-operator.html) and [leasing onto an MC](/mc-lease.html) explain both paths.

## The main coverages

### Primary auto liability

Pays for injuries and property damage you cause to others with the truck. For carriers with their own authority, the insurer files proof of this coverage with FMCSA, and your authority cannot become or stay active without it.

FMCSA sets minimum amounts based on what you haul and the vehicle size. For many for-hire general freight carriers in heavier trucks, the minimum has been $750,000, with higher limits for certain hazardous materials. Many brokers and shippers require $1,000,000. Confirm current minimums for your operation with FMCSA.

### Motor truck cargo

Covers the freight you haul if it is damaged or lost. Most brokers require cargo coverage and will tell you the limit they need. Watch for:

- **Excluded commodities:** some policies exclude items such as electronics, alcohol, tobacco or certain high-value goods.
- **Reefer breakdown:** spoilage from a reefer unit failure may need a specific endorsement.
- **Unattended vehicle and theft conditions:** some policies limit theft coverage when the truck is left unattended.

### Physical damage

Covers your own truck and trailer for collision, and often for theft, fire and other losses (comprehensive). If the truck is financed or leased, the lender usually requires it. Choose a stated value that matches what it would cost to replace the truck, and a deductible you could pay tomorrow.

### Non-trucking liability and bobtail

For leased-on drivers. These cover liability when you are not under dispatch for the carrier. The wording varies between policies, so ask exactly when coverage applies and when it does not.

### General liability

Covers claims that are not caused by driving, such as damage at a customer's dock or injuries at your place of business. Some shippers and facilities require it.

### Occupational accident or workers' compensation

Covers you if you are hurt on the job. Owner-operators often buy occupational accident coverage, and some carriers require it in the lease. If you hire employees, workers' compensation rules depend on your state, so check with your agent and state agency.

### Trailer interchange and non-owned trailer

Covers damage to a trailer you do not own but are pulling under an agreement, such as in power-only or drop-and-hook work. Ask about it if you pull customer trailers. See [power-only dispatch](/power-only-dispatch.html) if that is your model.

## What affects your premium

Insurers look at many factors. Common ones include:

- Years of CDL experience and your driving record.
- How long your authority has been active.
- Your safety record and inspection history.
- What you haul and its value.
- Where the truck is garaged and how far you travel.
- The value and age of the truck and trailer.
- Coverage limits and deductibles you choose.
- Claims history.

You cannot change all of these, but a clean record, careful driving and fixing inspection violations quickly help over time.

## Worked example: choosing a deductible (hypothetical)

Your agent quotes physical damage two ways:

| Option | Deductible | Yearly premium |
|---|---|---|
| A | $1,000 | $4,800 |
| B | $2,500 | $4,200 |

Option B saves $600 a year but costs $1,500 more if you have a claim. If you go about two and a half years without a claim, B comes out ahead. If you cannot pay $2,500 in cash tomorrow, A may be safer. These numbers are only an example; real quotes vary widely.

Add your actual premium into the [cost per mile calculator](/cost-per-mile-calculator.html) so every rate you accept covers it.

## Questions to ask your insurance agent

1. Which coverages do I need for how I operate (own authority or leased on)?
2. What limits do my brokers, shippers and lender require?
3. What commodities are excluded from my cargo policy?
4. Does my cargo policy cover reefer breakdown, theft and unattended trucks?
5. Is my truck insured at a stated value that would replace it?
6. Who are the listed drivers, and what happens if someone else drives?
7. What radius or territory limits are in the policy?
8. How fast can you issue certificates of insurance to brokers?
9. How are payments structured, and what happens if one is late?
10. What do I do, step by step, right after an accident or cargo claim?

## Insurance checklist

- [ ] Coverage matches how you operate.
- [ ] Liability filing confirmed active with FMCSA.
- [ ] Limits meet broker and lender requirements.
- [ ] Cargo exclusions reviewed against what you haul.
- [ ] Physical damage value and deductible make sense.
- [ ] Certificates of insurance ready for broker packets.
- [ ] Premium included in your cost per mile.
- [ ] Renewal date on your calendar, with time to shop.

## How Texas Solutions can help

Texas Solutions is a dispatch service, not a broker or motor carrier, and we do not sell insurance. Our dispatchers send your insurance certificates and broker packets, check that loads fit your cargo coverage, negotiate rates and work 24/7, while you approve every load. [Talk to a dispatcher](/contact.html) to get started.

### How to Write a Trucking Business Plan (With a Simple Template)
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/trucking-business-plan/
Published: 2026-10-21

A **trucking business plan** is a short, honest document that answers one question: can this truck (or fleet) make money, and how? You do not need fancy language. You need realistic costs, a clear plan for finding freight and a break-even number you can hit. This guide gives you the sections to include, a simple template and a hypothetical example. Have a CPA review your financial projections, especially if you will show the plan to a lender.

## Why write one at all

- **It tests your numbers before you spend money.** Many new carriers discover on paper that their plan only works at rates they cannot get.
- **Lenders may ask for it** when you apply for a truck loan or line of credit.
- **It keeps you focused** when the first slow month hits.
- **It becomes your yardstick.** Each month you compare reality against the plan.

## The sections to include

### 1. Business summary
One or two paragraphs: who you are, your experience, your legal structure, your authority status and what you will haul. Include your CDL years and any specialty experience.

### 2. Services and equipment
Truck and trailer type, year and condition, and the freight it suits. Explain why you chose it. If you are still deciding, compare rates, freight availability and equipment cost for each trailer type in your area.

### 3. Market and lanes
Where you will run, what kinds of shippers and brokers move that freight, and how seasonal it is. Be specific: home base, typical lanes, how often you plan to be home.

### 4. How you will find loads
Load boards, direct shippers, broker relationships, a dispatcher, or a mix. A new authority often faces broker restrictions at first, so plan for that. Our guide on [how to get loads with a new MC number](/blog/how-to-get-loads-with-new-mc-number.html) covers the early months.

### 5. Operations and compliance
Insurance, ELD, drug and alcohol testing program, maintenance plan, IFTA and IRP, and who handles paperwork. Lenders and partners want to see you understand the rules.

### 6. Startup costs
Everything you must pay before the first load is paid for.

### 7. Monthly operating budget
Fixed costs (truck payment, insurance, permits, ELD) and variable costs (fuel, maintenance, tolls, dispatch and factoring fees).

### 8. Revenue projection and break-even
Expected miles, realistic rate per total mile, and the minimum you must earn to cover costs.

### 9. Cash reserve and risk plan
How many months of fixed costs you can cover with no revenue, and what you will do if the truck is down.

### 10. Growth plan
What has to be true before you add a second truck. See [how to grow from 1 to 5 trucks](/blog/grow-from-1-to-5-trucks.html).

## Worked example: hypothetical startup and break-even

All figures are **hypothetical** to show the method, not real costs.

**Startup costs**

| Item | Hypothetical amount |
|---|---|
| Truck down payment | $15,000 |
| Authority, registrations and filings | $1,500 |
| First insurance down payment | $4,000 |
| ELD, phone and setup | $800 |
| Initial repairs and supplies | $2,500 |
| Cash reserve (fixed costs plus a repair and living buffer) | $18,000 |
| **Total** | **$41,800** |

**Monthly fixed costs (hypothetical):** truck payment $2,000, insurance $1,600, ELD and software $150, permits and other $250. Total: **$4,000 a month**. In this example the $18,000 reserve covers three months of fixed costs ($12,000) plus a $6,000 buffer for repairs and slow weeks. Adjust it to your situation.

**Variable costs (hypothetical):** fuel $0.85 per mile, maintenance $0.15 per mile, other variable $0.20 per mile. Total: **$1.20 per mile**.

**Break-even at 9,000 miles a month:**

- Fixed cost per mile: $4,000 / 9,000 = about $0.44
- Total cost per mile: $0.44 + $1.20 = about **$1.64**
- Revenue needed just to break even: $1.64 x 9,000 = about **$14,800**

Then add the owner's pay and a profit target. If you need $6,000 a month to live and want $1,500 profit, you need about $22,300 a month, or roughly $2.48 per total mile at 9,000 miles. Is that realistic for your freight and lanes? That is the real question the plan answers. Run your own version in the [break-even calculator](/break-even-calculator.html) and [cost per mile calculator](/cost-per-mile-calculator.html).

## A one-page template you can copy

```
BUSINESS SUMMARY: name, structure, owner experience, authority status
EQUIPMENT: truck, trailer, freight type
LANES: home base, main lanes, home time plan
LOAD SOURCES: boards / brokers / direct / dispatcher
COMPLIANCE: insurance, ELD, testing program, IFTA/IRP, maintenance
STARTUP COSTS: itemized total
MONTHLY BUDGET: fixed $____ + variable $____/mile
BREAK-EVEN: $____/mile at ____ miles/month
TARGET: owner pay $____ + profit $____ = $____/month
RESERVE: ____ months of fixed costs
GROWTH TRIGGER: what must be true before truck #2
```

## Common business plan mistakes

- Using your best-ever rate as the average
- Forgetting deadhead miles in the revenue math
- Leaving out the owner's own pay
- Skipping the cash reserve
- Assuming the truck will never break down
- Never updating the plan once real numbers arrive

## How Texas Solutions can help

Texas Solutions is a dispatch service, not a broker, motor carrier or financial advisor. Once your plan is set, our dispatchers find and negotiate loads against your break-even, handle broker packets and paperwork, and work 24/7 while you approve every load. See our [dispatch services](/dispatch.html) or [talk to a dispatcher](/contact.html).

### Trucking Apps for Owner-Operators: What You Actually Need
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/trucking-apps-for-owner-operators/
Published: 2026-10-21

A phone can run much of a one-truck business, but only if the right tools are on it. With so many **trucking apps for owner-operators** competing for your money, it helps to think in categories: what job does each app do, and do you really need it? This guide covers the main types, what to look for, and the questions to ask before you subscribe.

We do not recommend specific brands here. Features and prices change often, so compare current options yourself against the checklists below.

## Core apps most owner-operators need

### 1. Truck-specific GPS and navigation

A truck GPS lets you enter height, weight, length, axle count and hazmat status, then routes around low bridges, weight-restricted roads and truck-prohibited routes.

Look for:

- Vehicle profile settings for every truck and trailer you run.
- Up-to-date truck restrictions and live traffic.
- Offline maps for areas with weak signal.
- Points of interest such as truck stops, scales and rest areas.

Even with a good truck GPS, check posted signs and your company's route plan. No app is perfect.

### 2. ELD and hours of service

If you are required to use an electronic logging device, the system must be on FMCSA's registered ELD list. Most ELDs come with a driver app for logs and inspections.

Look for:

- Clear hours of service clocks and alerts.
- Easy roadside data transfer for inspectors.
- Electronic DVIRs.
- Mileage by state exports for IFTA.
- Good support when the device malfunctions.

Confirm current ELD rules and the registered device list on the FMCSA website. To double-check a trip plan, our [hours of service calculator](/hours-of-service-calculator.html) is a quick reference.

### 3. Load boards

Load board apps let you search and book freight, set lane alerts and check market conditions. Compare features such as search filters, rate data, broker credit and payment information, and how many loads are posted on your lanes. Our [load boards guide](/blog/truck-loads-and-load-boards-guide.html) explains how they work.

### 4. Document scanning

Brokers and factoring companies want clean copies of bills of lading, proof of delivery and receipts, fast. A scanning app turns phone photos into readable PDFs.

Look for:

- Automatic edge detection and contrast cleanup.
- Multi-page documents in one file.
- Easy sending by email or upload.
- Cloud backup so documents are not lost with the phone.

### 5. Expense and mileage tracking

You need records for taxes, IFTA and knowing your real cost per mile. An expense app or simple accounting tool can:

- Photograph and categorize receipts.
- Track fuel gallons and cost by state.
- Track income by load.
- Export reports for your CPA.

Talk to a CPA about which records you need to keep and for how long. Pair your records with the [cost per mile calculator](/cost-per-mile-calculator.html) to see what each mile costs.

## Useful extras

| App type | What it helps with | Worth it if you... |
|---|---|---|
| Fuel price finder | Compares diesel prices along your route | Fuel in many states or buy fuel at many stops |
| Fuel card app | Discounts, spending controls, receipts | Use a fuel card that offers one |
| Truck parking | Shows lots and, in some cases, available spaces | Run nights or busy corridors |
| Weigh station bypass | May let you bypass open scales if eligible | Pass many scales on your regular lanes |
| Weather and road conditions | Storms, wind, chain laws, closures | Run mountains, plains or winter routes |
| Factoring app | Submit invoices and track payments | Factor your receivables |
| Communication | Messaging with dispatch, brokers and shippers | Juggle many contacts each day |

## Questions to ask before you pay for any app

1. **What problem does it solve for me?** If you cannot name one, skip it.
2. **What does it really cost?** Check monthly fees, setup charges, per-truck pricing, hardware and cancellation terms.
3. **Is there a contract?** Avoid long commitments until you know the app works for you.
4. **Does it work with my other tools?** Exports to spreadsheets or accounting software save hours.
5. **Does it work offline?** Many lanes have dead zones.
6. **Who owns my data?** Read how the app uses and shares your location, load and financial data.
7. **What does support look like?** Ask whether help is available nights and weekends when you are actually driving.
8. **Is it secure?** Use strong passwords, two-step login where offered, and never share login details through texts or emails you did not expect.

## Watch out for scams

Fraudsters target carriers through fake apps, phishing links and fake load offers. Download apps only from official app stores, check the publisher, and be careful with any app that asks for broad access to your accounts. Never give your login, FMCSA portal details or bank information to someone who contacts you unexpectedly.

## Example: a lean app setup (hypothetical)

A new one-truck owner-operator might start with:

- One truck GPS with offline maps.
- One registered ELD with IFTA mileage export.
- One load board subscription.
- One scanning app with cloud backup.
- One expense tracker or spreadsheet shared with a CPA.

Extras like a fuel price finder or parking app can wait until you see where you lose time or money on the road. If each paid tool costs a modest monthly fee, add them up and include the total in your fixed costs. Review the list every few months and cancel anything you have not used.
