Our dispatchers search load boards and broker networks for you, negotiate rates, and handle broker packets and paperwork 24/7, so you may need fewer apps and less screen time. You approve every load. See our [owner-operator dispatch](/owner-operator-dispatch.html) or [talk to a dispatcher](/contact.html).

### Truck Parking and Trip Planning: How to Never Get Stuck
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/truck-parking-and-trip-planning/
Published: 2026-10-21

Finding a safe place to park is one of the hardest parts of the job, and poor **truck parking** planning can cost you hours, sleep and even a violation. Drivers who rarely get stuck usually are not lucky. They plan where they will stop before they leave.

This guide gives you a simple trip planning method built around hours of service, a worked example and a checklist you can use on every load.

## Why parking planning matters

When you cannot find a spot, every option is bad:

- You keep driving while tired, looking for space.
- You run out of hours and risk a violation.
- You park somewhere unsafe or illegal, like a ramp or an empty lot with no lighting.
- You use up your 14-hour window circling, which cuts into tomorrow's miles.

Good planning protects your safety, your logbook and your income. It also makes it easier to hit appointments, which keeps brokers calling you back.

## Step-by-step trip planning method

### 1. Start with your clocks

Before you plan miles, know your available time: driving hours left, time left in your 14-hour window, when your 30-minute break is due and how much room you have on your 60/70-hour cycle. The [hours of service calculator](/hours-of-service-calculator.html) helps you map them out.

### 2. Estimate realistic driving speed

Do not plan with the speed limit. Plan with an average that includes traffic, construction, fuel stops, weather and terrain. Many drivers use a conservative average well below the posted limit for planning, then adjust from experience on that lane.

### 3. Find your "must stop" point

Multiply your available driving hours by your realistic average speed. That tells you roughly how far you can go. Then check that you also fit inside your 14-hour window, including loading, fueling and breaks.

### 4. Pick a primary spot before that point

Choose a parking spot about an hour before you run out, not right at the edge. That cushion covers traffic jams and full lots.

### 5. Pick one or two backups

List backups both before and after your primary spot, if hours allow. A backup 30 to 60 minutes earlier is often more useful than one farther ahead.

### 6. Plan truck-legal routes

Use truck-specific routing that accounts for low clearances, weight-restricted bridges, restricted routes and hazmat restrictions if you haul hazmat. Consumer navigation apps can send a truck down roads it should not be on.

### 7. Check fuel and weather

Plan fuel stops so you are not forced to stop at a crowded location at the wrong time. Check weather along the route, especially in winter. See our [winter driving and chain laws](/blog/winter-driving-and-chain-laws.html) guide.

## Worked example

Here is a hypothetical day for a driver hauling a dry van load 640 miles:

- Driver comes on duty at 05:00 after a full 10-hour break.
- Pre-trip and paperwork: 30 minutes. Driving starts at 05:30.
- Planning average: 52 mph including traffic and stops.
- 11 hours of driving x 52 mph = about 572 miles possible today.
- The 14-hour window ends at 19:00.

The load is 640 miles, so the driver will not deliver today. The plan:

| Item | Time |
|---|---|
| Drive 05:30 - 10:30 | about 260 miles |
| 30-minute break and fuel | 10:30 - 11:00 |
| Drive 11:00 - 16:30 | about 285 miles, 545 total |
| Park at primary spot | 16:30, with 30 minutes of driving and 2.5 hours of window left |
| Backup spot | about 40 miles earlier, if the primary is full |

The driver parks around 545 miles in, ahead of the evening rush for spaces, with 95 miles left for the morning. That leaves an easy early-morning delivery and keeps hours in reserve for the next load. Stopping slightly early here cost little, while pushing to the last minute could have meant hunting for parking at dark with no hours left.

## Where to park

Common options, each with tradeoffs:

- **Truck stops and travel centers.** Fuel, food and showers, but popular ones fill up in the evening. Some offer paid reserved spaces you can book ahead.
- **Public rest areas.** Free and convenient, but spaces are limited and time limits vary by state.
- **Shipper and receiver lots.** Some allow overnight parking before an appointment or after unloading. Ask at booking, not at 9 p.m. Get permission in writing if possible.
- **Truck-friendly businesses.** Some retailers and businesses allow trucks, others ban them or tow. Always confirm with the manager and look for posted signs.
- **Secure paid lots.** Fenced, lit lots near big metro areas. Useful for high-value loads or long resets.

Avoid ramps, shoulders and unlit empty lots. Besides the legal risk, they are dangerous for you and other drivers.

## Parking and the 14-hour clock

Delays at shippers are the most common reason drivers end up short on time and parking. Before you accept a load, ask about facility hours, average wait times and whether they allow overnight parking. If a facility holds you past your appointment, document the times so you can request detention. Our guide on [how to get detention paid](/blog/how-to-get-detention-paid.html) explains how. When you get kicked out after unloading with no hours left, personal conveyance may apply. See [personal conveyance and yard moves](/blog/personal-conveyance-and-yard-moves.html) for when it does and does not.

## Daily trip planning checklist

- [ ] Clocks checked: 11, 14, 30-minute break, 60/70 cycle
- [ ] Realistic average speed chosen for this lane
- [ ] Truck-legal route confirmed
- [ ] Fuel stops planned
- [ ] Weather checked along the full route
- [ ] Primary parking spot about an hour before hours run out
- [ ] One or two backup spots identified
- [ ] Shipper/receiver parking rules and hours confirmed
- [ ] Reserved parking booked if arriving late in a busy area

## How Texas Solutions can help

Texas Solutions is a dispatch service, not a broker or motor carrier. Our dispatchers find and negotiate loads, handle broker packets and paperwork 24/7, and plan pickups and deliveries that fit your hours and leave room for safe parking. You approve every load. See our [dispatch services](/dispatch.html) or [talk to a dispatcher](/contact.html).

### Truck Maintenance Schedule for Owner-Operators
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/truck-maintenance-schedule/
Published: 2026-10-21

Breakdowns cost far more than the repair bill. A truck in the shop earns nothing, can miss appointments, and may leave you paying for a hotel and a tow. A written **truck maintenance schedule** turns surprise repairs into planned, cheaper ones and helps keep you clear of roadside violations.

## Why a schedule beats fixing things when they break

Preventive maintenance is about catching small problems early. A worn belt, a slow air leak or a weeping hub seal is cheap to fix in your own time. The same problem on the side of the highway can cost a load, a tow and a day or more of revenue.

A schedule also helps with:

- **Roadside inspections:** fewer defects mean fewer violations and out-of-service orders.
- **Safety scores:** vehicle maintenance violations can affect your carrier's safety record.
- **Resale value:** a truck with full service records is easier to sell.
- **Budgeting:** you know roughly what is due and when.

## Federal rules to know

FMCSA's rules on inspection, repair and maintenance are in 49 CFR Part 396. In plain terms, as generally understood:

- Every commercial motor vehicle must be systematically inspected, repaired and maintained.
- Drivers must be satisfied the vehicle is in safe operating condition before driving it (the pre-trip inspection).
- Drivers must complete a written post-trip inspection report (DVIR) when required, and defects that affect safety must be repaired before the vehicle runs again.
- Each vehicle needs a periodic inspection at least once every 12 months, done by a qualified inspector, with proof kept in the vehicle or available.
- Maintenance records must be kept for a set period.

Details, exceptions and record retention periods matter, so confirm current requirements in 49 CFR Part 396 on the FMCSA website or with a compliance professional.

## The schedule, interval by interval

### Daily checks

Every day you drive:

- Pre-trip inspection: tires, wheels and lugs, brakes and air system, lights and reflectors, coupling devices, steering, mirrors, horn, wipers, fluid leaks.
- Check engine oil, coolant and DEF levels.
- Drain air tanks if your system does not have automatic drains.
- Post-trip inspection and DVIR, noting any defects.

### Weekly and monthly checks

| Interval | What to check |
|---|---|
| Weekly | Tire pressure with a gauge, tread depth, battery terminals, belts and hoses, fifth wheel lubrication and wear, trailer lights and seals |
| Monthly | Brake adjustment and lining wear, suspension and air bags, exhaust and aftertreatment for leaks, wiper blades, cab and sleeper HVAC, fire extinguisher and warning triangles |

These are good habits, not a substitute for your manufacturers' recommendations.

### Preventive maintenance (PM) services

PM services happen at mileage or engine-hour intervals set by your engine, transmission and component manufacturers. Intervals depend on the make, model, oil type and how hard the truck works, so use your owner's manuals as the source.

A typical PM service may include:

1. Engine oil and filter change.
2. Fuel filters and water separator.
3. Air filter check or replacement.
4. Chassis lubrication (grease all fittings).
5. Coolant condition and level check.
6. Brake, steering and suspension inspection.
7. Driveline, U-joints and wheel-end inspection.
8. Battery and charging system test.
9. Review of fault codes and aftertreatment health.

Less frequent items, such as transmission and differential fluids, valve adjustments, coolant replacement and aftertreatment cleaning, come up at longer intervals. Track them on the same schedule so they do not slip.

**Consider oil analysis.**

Sending an oil sample to a lab can reveal coolant leaks, fuel dilution or unusual wear before they become failures. It can also help you decide whether an extended drain interval is safe for your engine.

### Annual and seasonal items

- **Annual periodic inspection:** schedule it before it is due, not on the last day.
- **Before winter:** batteries, coolant protection, block heater, wipers, fuel water separator, chains.
- **Before summer:** cooling system, A/C, belts and hoses; for reefers, the reefer unit service.
- **Trailer:** brakes, lights, tires, doors and seals, landing gear. Reefer units have their own service schedule.

## Keep records

Good records help with compliance, roadside questions and resale. For each service, write down:

- Date, mileage and engine hours.
- Work done and parts used.
- Who did the work.
- Cost.

A simple spreadsheet or maintenance app works, as long as you use it every time.

## Budget for maintenance

Repairs come in lumps, but you can save for them in small, steady amounts. A common approach is to put a set amount per mile into a separate maintenance account.

### Worked example (hypothetical)

Say you choose to set aside $0.18 per mile and drive 9,000 miles a month:

- 9,000 x $0.18 = **$1,620 per month**
- Over 12 months: about **$19,440** for tires, PM services and repairs

An older truck may need more; a newer truck under warranty may need less. Use the [maintenance budget calculator](/maintenance-budget-calculator.html) to set your number, and include it in your [cost per mile](/cost-per-mile-calculator.html) so your rates cover it.

## Maintenance checklist summary

- [ ] Pre-trip and post-trip inspections every driving day.
- [ ] Weekly tire, belt, battery and fifth wheel checks.
- [ ] Monthly brake, suspension and exhaust checks.
- [ ] PM services at manufacturer intervals.
- [ ] Annual periodic inspection scheduled ahead of time.
- [ ] Seasonal prep before winter and summer.
- [ ] Every service recorded with date, mileage and cost.
- [ ] Money set aside per mile in a maintenance account.

## How Texas Solutions can help

Texas Solutions is a dispatch service, not a broker or motor carrier. Our dispatchers can plan loads around your scheduled shop time, so maintenance does not cost you a good week of freight. We find and negotiate loads, handle broker packets and paperwork 24/7, and you approve every load. See our [dispatch services](/dispatch.html) or [talk to a dispatcher](/contact.html).

### TONU, Layover and Lumper Pay: How Truckers Get Paid for Each
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/tonu-layover-and-lumper-pay/
Published: 2026-10-21

Not every dollar in trucking comes from linehaul. **TONU, layover and lumper pay** are accessorials: charges for situations where a load does not go as planned. They are easy to lose if you do not set terms up front and keep proof, and they can turn a bad day into a break-even one if you handle them right.

## Why accessorials need terms before the load

Accessorials are negotiated, not automatic. A broker is far more likely to pay a charge that appears on the signed rate confirmation than one you raise after the fact. Before you sign any rate con, confirm the TONU amount, layover rate and lumper process are written in. Our guide on [how to read a rate confirmation](/blog/how-to-read-a-rate-confirmation.html) walks through the full list.

## TONU: truck ordered not used

TONU applies when a broker cancels a load after you have committed the truck, usually after dispatch or arrival at the shipper. Common causes include freight not ready, an order cancelled by the shipper or a broker double-booking a load.

### What TONU covers

TONU is meant to offset the lost day: deadhead miles to the shipper, fuel, hours of service used and the other loads you turned down. It rarely replaces the full load rate, so it is a cushion, not a win.

### How to get TONU paid

1. **Have the amount on the rate con.** Ask for it before booking, especially for loads with long deadhead.
2. **Get the cancellation in writing.** Ask the broker to confirm by email that the load is cancelled and TONU applies.
3. **Document your position.** ELD records, GPS history or a timestamped photo at the gate show you were there or en route.
4. **Ask for a TONU rate con.** Many brokers issue a revised confirmation showing the TONU amount. That becomes your billing document.
5. **Invoice right away.**

### Worked example

Hypothetical example: you deadhead 90 miles to a shipper and the load is cancelled. Your all-in operating cost is about $1.90 per mile. Deadhead cost is 90 x $1.90 = $171. If the rate con lists a $250 TONU, you recover your direct cost plus a bit for lost time. Without it on paper, you might get offered much less, or nothing. Use the [deadhead miles calculator](/deadhead-miles-calculator.html) and your own cost per mile to know your own numbers before you negotiate.

## Layover pay

Layover is a flat payment when you are held over to another day because a load could not be picked up or delivered as scheduled, through no fault of yours. Examples: the receiver pushes your appointment to the next morning, or the shipper's freight is not ready until tomorrow.

### How to get layover paid

- Confirm the layover rate and when it applies on the rate con. Some brokers define layover as a delay past a certain number of hours or past midnight.
- Notify the broker as soon as you learn of the delay, and get the new appointment in writing.
- Keep the original appointment confirmation and the reschedule message.
- Note whether the broker will pay both detention and layover for the same delay. Policies differ.

Layover also affects the next load. Being stuck a day can push you off a lane, so planning around it matters. See [how to plan a profitable round trip](/blog/plan-a-profitable-round-trip.html) for ideas on rebuilding the week.

## Lumper fees

A lumper is a third-party worker or crew that unloads trucks at some warehouses, especially grocery and food distribution centers. The facility charges a fee for the service, and the question is who pays.

### How lumper fees are usually handled

- **Broker pays directly.** The broker issues an electronic payment code or check number the driver gives to the lumper service. This is the cleanest option.
- **Carrier pays and gets reimbursed.** The driver pays by card or cash, then submits the receipt with the invoice for reimbursement.
- **Rate includes it.** Rarely, the linehaul is set high enough to cover the lumper. Avoid this unless the amount is known in advance.

### Lumper checklist

- Ask before booking: "Is there a lumper at delivery, and how is it paid?"
- Get the reimbursement method on the rate con
- Call the broker for an electronic payment code before you reach the dock
- Always get an itemized receipt showing facility, date, amount and load or PO number
- Include the receipt in your invoice packet, and send a photo to the broker the same day

Federal law prohibits coercing a carrier to load or unload freight, or to hire someone to do it, as a condition of the load. If a facility demands unexpected fees or labor, contact the broker and document it. Confirm the current rules with FMCSA if a dispute escalates.

## Detention, layover, TONU and lumper compared

| Accessorial | When it applies | Typical structure | Key proof |
|---|---|---|---|
| Detention | Waiting past free time | Hourly after free time | Signed in and out times |
| Layover | Held over to another day | Flat per day | Reschedule notice in writing |
| TONU | Load cancelled after dispatch | Flat amount | Cancellation email, location records |
| Lumper | Third-party unloading | Reimbursed at cost | Itemized receipt |

For detention specifically, see our full guide on [how to get detention paid](/blog/how-to-get-detention-paid.html).

## Bill accessorials fast and clean

Accessorials get denied most often for paperwork reasons. Build a habit:

- Send accessorial requests with the original invoice, not separately weeks later
- Include the load number, the term from the rate con and the supporting proof
- Keep copies in one load folder
- Follow up on unpaid accessorials within the broker's payment terms

If you factor, ask how your factoring company handles accessorials and lumper reimbursements. Some fund them with the load, others only after the broker approves. Our guide on [working with a factoring company](/blog/working-with-a-factoring-company.html) covers the details.

## How Texas Solutions can help

Texas Solutions is a dispatch service, not a broker or motor carrier. Our dispatchers negotiate TONU, layover and lumper terms onto the rate con, handle broker communication and paperwork 24/7, and you approve every load. See our [dispatch services](/dispatch.html) or [talk to a dispatcher](/contact.html).

### Team Driving in Trucking: Pay, Hours and How to Make It Work
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/team-driving-guide/
Published: 2026-10-21

**Team driving** puts two drivers in one truck so the wheels keep turning while one of them sleeps. It can roughly double the miles a truck covers in a week, which is why expedited and long-haul shippers like teams. It also means living in a small space with another person for weeks at a time. Here is how it works, how the money splits and what makes teams last.

## How team driving works

One driver drives while the other rests in the sleeper berth or rides as a passenger. When the driver nears their limit, they swap. A well-run team can keep a truck moving most of the day, stopping mainly for fuel, inspections, loading and unloading.

Each driver:

- Holds their own license, medical card and qualifications
- Logs their own hours on the ELD under their own login
- Must follow their own driving, on-duty and weekly limits

## Hours of service for teams

The same basic limits apply to each team driver as to a solo driver: the 11-hour driving limit, the 14-hour window, the 30-minute break requirement and the 60/70-hour weekly limit. Our [hours of service rules guide](/blog/hours-of-service-rules-explained-11-14-70-hour.html) explains each one.

What makes teams different is how rest happens:

- **Sleeper berth splits.** Drivers can split their required off-duty time between the sleeper berth and another rest period in certain combinations. See [the sleeper berth split explained](/blog/sleeper-berth-split-explained.html).
- **Passenger seat time.** The rules include a team-specific provision that lets a limited amount of time in the passenger seat, right before or after a long sleeper period, count toward rest. Confirm how it works today before relying on it.
- **Swap timing.** The team has to plan swaps so neither driver runs out of hours at a bad place, such as in the middle of a city at rush hour or far from parking.

Rules can change, so confirm current details with FMCSA before building a schedule around them.

## A sample team schedule

Here is a simple schedule pattern many teams start with and then adjust:

| Time block | Driver A | Driver B |
|---|---|---|
| 6:00 am to 6:00 pm | On duty: up to 11 hours driving, plus break, fuel and inspection | Sleeper berth |
| 6:00 pm to 6:00 am | Sleeper berth | On duty: up to 11 hours driving, plus break, fuel and inspection |

Each driver works inside a 12-hour block, which fits within the 14-hour window, then gets 12 hours off, which covers the 10-hour reset. Watch the weekly 60/70-hour limit: 12-hour on-duty days use up 70 hours in under a week, so plan shorter shifts or a restart.

Real schedules shift with appointments, traffic and how well each driver sleeps in a moving truck. Some drivers sleep better at night, some do not mind day sleep. Match the shift to the person.

## What freight suits teams

Teams earn their premium on freight that values speed or long distances:

- **Expedited and time-critical loads**, where a solo driver legally cannot make the delivery time. See the [expedited freight guide](/blog/expedited-freight-guide.html).
- **Long cross-country lanes**, where non-stop driving saves a day or more.
- **High-value or security-sensitive loads**, where the shipper prefers the truck to stay attended.
- **Dedicated runs** with tight transit windows.

If your loads are short regional trips with long waits at docks, a team adds cost without adding much revenue.

## How team pay works

### Company teams

Many carriers pay a team rate per mile on all miles the truck runs, split between the two drivers, often 50/50. Others pay each driver only for the miles they personally drive. Ask which method applies and how detention, layovers and breakdowns are paid.

### Owner-operator teams

If you own the truck and run with a partner, you set the split. Common setups:

- **Spouses or partners** often treat it as one household income.
- **Owner plus hired co-driver**: the owner pays the co-driver per mile, a percentage, or a weekly amount. Treat this as hiring a driver, with full qualification and payroll or contractor decisions made with a CPA.
- **Two partners sharing ownership**: put it in a written agreement covering pay, expenses, who decides on loads and what happens if one person leaves.

## Hypothetical revenue example

These numbers are made up to show the math, not market rates.

- Solo truck: 2,500 miles per week at $2.30 per mile = **$5,750 gross**
- Team truck: 4,800 miles per week at $2.30 per mile = **$11,040 gross**

The team truck burns roughly twice the fuel and wears tires, brakes and the engine faster, and you are paying two people. Per-mile fixed costs (truck payment, insurance) drop because they are spread over more miles, but insurance often costs more with two drivers. Check the real result with the [cost per mile calculator](/cost-per-mile-calculator.html) before deciding.

## Choosing a team partner

Most teams fail because of the people, not the money. Before you commit:

- [ ] Run a short trial trip before a long contract
- [ ] Agree on driving style, speed and following distance
- [ ] Agree on cleanliness, food, smoking, music, phone calls and pets
- [ ] Set rules for who handles fuel, paperwork and broker calls
- [ ] Agree on home time and how long you stay out
- [ ] Plan how to resolve disagreements before they happen
- [ ] Confirm both drivers are approved by the insurer
- [ ] Put pay and expense splits in writing

Sleep is the biggest health issue. Invest in a good mattress, blackout curtains and earplugs, and make the cab quiet when one person is sleeping. A tired team is not safer than a solo driver.

## How Texas Solutions can help

Texas Solutions is a dispatch service, not a broker or motor carrier. For teams, our dispatchers look for freight that uses the extra hours, negotiate rates, handle broker packets and paperwork, and work 24/7, and you approve every load. Learn about [owner-operator dispatch](/owner-operator-dispatch.html) or [talk to a dispatcher](/contact.html).

### How to Start a Cargo Van Business: A Practical Guide
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/start-a-cargo-van-business/
Published: 2026-10-21

A **cargo van business** is one of the lowest-cost ways to get into freight. You can start with one van, a regular driver's license and a modest budget, and haul small, time-sensitive loads that bigger trucks cannot do economically. The catch is that margins are thin, so the business only works if you plan it like a real carrier from day one.

## Choose your freight model first

Before you shop for a van, decide what kind of work you want. Each model needs different equipment, hours and customers.

- **Local courier and same-day delivery.** Short runs for medical labs, parts suppliers, print shops and offices. Steady if you build relationships, but many small jobs.
- **Contract routes.** Recurring routes for a logistics company or retailer. Predictable income, less freedom on rates.
- **Long-distance expedite.** One shipment, one van, driven straight through to the receiver. Higher pay per load, more time on the road and more empty miles coming back. See our [expedited freight guide](/blog/expedited-freight-guide.html).
- **Final mile.** Delivering goods to homes and businesses, sometimes with assembly or inside delivery. A growing niche with its own customers and equipment needs.

Pick one to start. Trying to do everything at once usually means you are good at nothing.

## Pick the right van

The van should match the freight, not the other way around. Questions to ask before you buy:

- **Cargo length and height.** Can it take a standard pallet or two? A high-roof extended van gives more room than a standard roof.
- **Payload.** Check the manufacturer's payload rating, not just the cargo space. Overloading hurts brakes, tires and your insurance claim.
- **Fuel economy and engine.** You will put a lot of miles on it. Compare real fuel use and maintenance costs, not just purchase price.
- **Doors and floor.** Side and rear doors, a good floor and tie-down points (E-track or D-rings) make loading faster and safer.
- **Condition and history** if buying used. Get a pre-purchase inspection.

Keep the purchase price realistic. A van with a big payment can sink the business before you build a customer base.
## Set up the business and paperwork

Here is a typical sequence. Requirements change, so confirm current rules with FMCSA, the IRS and your state.

1. **Form a business entity** (many owners choose an LLC) and get an EIN from the IRS. Talk to a CPA or attorney about which structure fits you.
2. **Open a separate business bank account.** Keep every dollar of van income and expense in it.
3. **Get the right registrations.** If you haul for-hire across state lines, you generally need a USDOT number and FMCSA operating authority (MC number), plus a process agent filing (BOC-3) and UCR registration. In-state-only work follows your state's rules.
4. **Buy commercial insurance.** Brokers and shippers commonly ask for auto liability and cargo coverage. A personal auto policy usually will not cover commercial hauling. Ask your insurance agent exactly what limits your customers require.
5. **Set up bookkeeping** from the first day so you can track cost per mile and taxes.

If you want help with the filings, our [trucking authority setup](/trucking-authority-setup.html) service walks through the steps with you.

### What about hours of service and medical cards?

Many federal rules for commercial vehicles are tied to vehicle weight, and most cargo vans fall under the main weight thresholds. That can mean fewer federal requirements than a heavier truck. But state rules, hazmat loads and customer contracts can add requirements, so confirm with FMCSA and your state rather than assuming you are exempt.

## Know your cost per mile before you quote

Van rates per mile are lower than for semis, so small cost mistakes matter a lot. Here is a simple hypothetical example for one month.

| Cost item (hypothetical) | Monthly |
|---|---|
| Van payment | $900 |
| Insurance | $600 |
| Fuel (8,000 miles at 16 mpg, $3.50/gal) | $1,750 |
| Maintenance and tires reserve | $480 |
| Phone, software, load board, misc. | $250 |
| **Total** | **$3,980** |

That works out to about **$0.50 per mile** on 8,000 miles, before paying yourself. If a load pays $1.20 per loaded mile but you drive back empty the same distance, you only earn $0.60 per total mile. That is barely above cost. Run your own numbers with the [cost per mile calculator](/cost-per-mile-calculator.html), and always count the empty miles home.

## Find freight and customers

Cargo van freight comes from several places:

- **Expedite and van-specific load boards** used by brokers for small shipments.
- **Direct local customers** such as labs, print shops, parts stores and contractors. Walk in, call, and follow up.
- **Contract routes** with delivery and logistics companies.
- **Brokers who specialize in expedite** and need reliable vans on short notice.

Reliability is your product. Answer the phone fast, show up on time, send pictures of signed paperwork right away, and your best customers will call you before they post the load anywhere.

## Common mistakes to avoid

- Buying a van before you know what freight you will haul.
- Using personal insurance for commercial work.
- Accepting long one-way runs without a plan to get home loaded.
- Mixing personal and business money.
- Ignoring maintenance until something breaks on the road.

## When to move up to a box truck

Many cargo van owners grow into a box truck once they keep turning down freight that will not fit. A box truck can carry more pallets, often has a liftgate, and opens up different loads and customers. It also brings more rules: depending on weight, you may need a DOT medical card, hours-of-service compliance and an ELD. Read [box truck vs cargo van](/blog/box-truck-vs-cargo-van.html) before you make the jump.

## How Texas Solutions can help

Texas Solutions is a dispatch service, not a broker or motor carrier, and we do not currently dispatch cargo vans. We can still help you set up your authority and handle back-office work such as broker setup paperwork and invoicing. When you move up to a box truck, our [box truck dispatch](/box-truck-dispatch.html) team finds and negotiates loads, handles broker packets and paperwork 24/7, and you approve every load. Questions? [Talk to a dispatcher](/contact.html).

### Sleeper Berth Split Explained: 7/3 and 8/2 With Examples
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/sleeper-berth-split-explained/
Published: 2026-10-21

The **sleeper berth split** lets a property-carrying driver break the required 10 hours off duty into two pieces instead of one long block. Used well, it helps you wait out a late appointment, dodge rush hour or nap through the hottest part of the day without wasting your 14-hour window.

It is also the hours of service rule drivers most often get wrong. This guide walks through how the split works under the federal rules as we understand them, with a worked example. Rules can change, so confirm the current version with FMCSA before you rely on it.

## The basic rule

Under the federal hours of service rules for property-carrying drivers, you normally need 10 consecutive hours off duty before you can drive again. The sleeper berth provision gives you an alternative:

- **One period of at least 7 consecutive hours in the sleeper berth**, and
- **One period of at least 2 consecutive hours** off duty, in the sleeper berth, or a combination of both, and
- **The two periods together must total at least 10 hours.**

That gives you two practical combinations: **7/3** and **8/2**. (A longer long period, such as 7.5/2.5, also works as long as the long period is in the sleeper and the total reaches 10.)

When two qualifying periods are paired, **neither period counts against your 14-hour window**. That is the real value of the split. The periods can be taken in either order.

Passenger-carrying drivers have different sleeper berth rules, so this guide only covers property carriers.

## How to recalculate your hours

This is the part that confuses people. After you complete the second period of a qualifying pair, you recalculate your available hours **starting from the end of the first period of the pair**.

In plain terms:

1. Find the end of the first qualifying rest period.
2. Count the **driving time** since then. Subtract it from 11 to get the driving time you have left.
3. Count the **elapsed time** since then, but leave out the second rest period. Subtract it from 14 to get what is left of your window.

Each new qualifying period can then pair with the one before it, so a driver can keep "leapfrogging" through the week. Your 60/70-hour limit still applies the whole time.

## Worked example: a 7/3 split

Here is a hypothetical day. Times are on a 24-hour clock.

| Time | Status | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 06:00 - 12:00 | Driving | 6 hours driving |
| 12:00 - 15:00 | Off duty | 3 hours, the short period (also covers the 30-minute break) |
| 15:00 - 19:00 | Driving | 4 more hours; total driving 10, elapsed 13 since 06:00 |
| 19:00 - 02:00 | Sleeper berth | 7 hours, the long period |

At 02:00 the 3-hour and 7-hour periods pair up (3 + 7 = 10). Now recalculate from the end of the first period, which was 15:00:

- **Driving since 15:00:** 4 hours. 11 - 4 = **7 hours of driving left**.
- **Window since 15:00, leaving out the 7-hour sleeper period:** 15:00 to 19:00 = 4 hours. 14 - 4 = **10 hours of window left**.

So at 02:00 the driver can drive up to 7 hours, all within a window that runs until 12:00.

Say the driver drives 02:00 to 09:00 (7 hours), then takes 3 hours off duty from 09:00 to 12:00. That 3-hour period pairs with the previous 7-hour sleeper period. Recalculate from the end of the 7-hour period (02:00): 7 hours driven, so 4 hours of driving left, and the window used is 7 hours, so 7 hours of window left. The leapfrog continues.

Notice what made the example work: on the first day, the driver stayed inside the original 14-hour window (06:00 to 20:00) while driving. Do not plan to drive past your 14th hour on the assumption that a future break will fix it. If the second period never happens, the time is a violation.

## The 30-minute break and the split

The federal 30-minute break applies after 8 cumulative hours of driving without at least a 30-minute interruption. Under current rules the interruption can be on duty not driving, off duty or sleeper berth time. Both periods of a split are long enough to count as that break. Short-haul drivers using certain exceptions may not need the 30-minute break at all. Check FMCSA for the current wording.

## When the split helps, and when it hurts

The split is a planning tool. It helps when:

- **A receiver will not take you until a set time.** Spend the wait in the sleeper as part of a qualifying period instead of burning your window in a parking lot.
- **You want to avoid city traffic.** Park for 2 or 3 hours during rush hour and come back with your window preserved.
- **Detention eats your day.** If you know you will sit for hours, logging part of it as a qualifying period can protect your window. Be honest: if you are on duty, such as being required to stay with the truck and move it, log it that way.

It can hurt when:

- You end up short on sleep because the long period was broken up or noisy.
- Your ELD and your own math disagree. Most ELDs calculate splits automatically, but double-check the clocks before you roll.
- You stack splits all week and lose track of your 70-hour total.

## Quick checklist before you use a split

- [ ] Long period is at least 7 consecutive hours, logged as sleeper berth
- [ ] Short period is at least 2 consecutive hours, off duty or sleeper
- [ ] Both periods total at least 10 hours
- [ ] You stay within your current 11 and 14 hours until the pair is complete
- [ ] Your 60/70-hour cycle has room
- [ ] Your ELD shows the recalculated clocks you expect

For the bigger picture, read our [hours of service rules explained](/blog/hours-of-service-rules-explained-11-14-70-hour.html) guide, and try your own schedule in the [hours of service calculator](/hours-of-service-calculator.html). Team drivers have their own planning challenges, covered in our [team driving guide](/blog/team-driving-guide.html).

## How Texas Solutions can help

Texas Solutions is a dispatch service, not a broker or motor carrier. Our dispatchers find and negotiate loads, handle broker packets and paperwork 24/7, and plan pickups and deliveries around your real available hours, including split breaks, while you approve every load. Learn more about our [dispatch services](/dispatch.html) or [talk to a dispatcher](/contact.html).

### Reefer Loads and Refrigerated Load Dispatch: Rates per Mile, Seasons and Tips
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/reefer-loads-refrigerated-dispatch-guide/
Published: 2026-10-21

Reefer freight pays more than dry van for a reason: it is harder to haul. A missed appointment or a wrong temperature can mean a rejected load and a claim. Good **refrigerated load dispatch** is about the details. This guide covers **reefer rates per mile**, the seasons that drive reefer freight, and what to check before you book.

## Reefer rates per mile in 2026

Our dispatchers plan reefer freight at roughly **$4 to $6 a mile** (October 2026). That is a planning range, not a market index or a quote. Real **reefer rates per mile today** depend on:

- **Lane and direction.** Loads out of produce and food markets in season pay better than loads into them.
- **Distance.** Short loads often pay more per mile; long runs pay more per load.
- **Season.** Produce season and the holiday peak lift reefer demand.
- **Appointment pressure.** Short-notice or hard-to-cover loads leave more room to negotiate.

Always compare loads by rate per total mile, including the empty miles to pick up. The [load profitability calculator](/load-profitability-calculator.html) lets you count reefer fuel too.

## The reefer calendar

| Months | Where reefer freight builds |
|---|---|
| March to May | Florida, South Texas and Mexico border crossings (produce) |
| May to August | California, Arizona, the Northwest |
| August to October | Midwest and Northeast harvests, Michigan, Wisconsin, upstate New York |
| November to December | Holiday peak season: grocery, meat, dairy and frozen food distribution nationwide |

Planning lanes around this calendar keeps a reefer loaded both ways. See [peak season trucking loads](/blog/peak-season-trucking-loads-holiday-freight.html) for the Q4 picture.

## What to check before you accept a reefer load

1. **Temperature setting** and whether the unit must run continuous or cycle.
2. **Pre-cool** requirements before arrival at the shipper.
3. **Appointments:** pickup and delivery times, and what happens if you are late.
4. **Pulp temperature** rules for produce, and who checks it.
5. **Weight**, so you stay legal with fuel in both tanks.
6. **Temperature download** or seal requirements at delivery.
7. **Lumper fees** at grocery warehouses, and how they are paid back. The [detention pay calculator](/detention-pay-calculator.html) helps you claim waiting time.

## Reefer fuel: the hidden cost

A reefer unit burns diesel even when the truck is parked, often somewhere around a gallon an hour depending on the unit, setting and outside temperature. On a long load with waiting time, that is real money. Add it to your [truck fuel cost](/truck-fuel-cost-calculator.html) when you price a load.

## How to find better reefer loads

- **Book the reload before you deliver.** Grocery distribution centers often sit in markets with weak outbound freight.
- **Follow the season.** Position your truck where produce is moving next.
- **Build broker relationships.** Reefer brokers rebook carriers who hit appointments and keep temperatures right.
- **Negotiate.** Ask for more on short-notice loads and loads with long waits.

## When a reefer dispatch service helps

A **reefer dispatch service** handles the search, the broker calls and the appointment details while you drive. At Texas Solutions we confirm temperature and appointment rules before a load reaches you, plan lanes around produce and holiday markets, and are available 24/7 for early appointments and overnight reloads. The fee is 5% of weekly gross for OTR reefer semis, no setup fee, no long-term contract, and your first load is dispatched free. Rates and earnings are not guaranteed. See [reefer dispatch](/reefer-dispatch.html) or compare trailer types in [dry van vs reefer vs flatbed](/blog/dry-van-vs-reefer-vs-flatbed-which-trailer.html).

### Reefer Loads in Summer Heat: How to Protect the Load
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/reefer-loads-in-summer-heat/
Published: 2026-10-21

Summer is when **reefer loads** get tested. High outside temperatures, produce season volume and long waits at hot docks all push the unit and the product to their limits. Most temperature claims trace back to a few avoidable mistakes, and this guide walks through how to prevent them.

## Why summer is harder on reefer freight

Heat works against you from every direction:

- **Heat soaks into the trailer** walls, floor and doors while it sits in the sun.
- **Product may load warm,** especially fresh produce picked in the field.
- **Door openings** at hot docks let in a lot of warm air quickly.
- **The unit runs harder,** burning more fuel and putting more strain on belts, compressors and alternators.
- **Delays cost more,** because every hour of waiting is an hour of heat load.

Summer is also busy season for produce in many regions, which means more freight and often better rates. See our guide on the [freight market calendar](/blog/freight-market-calendar.html) for when produce seasons tend to peak.

## Before you arrive: pre-cool and pre-trip

1. **Read the instructions.** Confirm set point, mode (continuous or cycle), and whether the reading is in Fahrenheit or Celsius. A wrong unit setting is an expensive mistake.
2. **Pre-cool the empty trailer** to the set point before arrival, unless the shipper says otherwise. Give it enough time; on a hot day this can take a while.
3. **Check the unit:** fuel level, belts, coolant, alarms and any active fault codes.
4. **Check the trailer:** door seals, air chute, floor drains, and that the trailer is clean and odor-free. Food shippers can reject a dirty trailer.
5. **Check tires** while cool. Heat raises tire pressure, so cold checks give the honest reading.

## At the shipper: pulp temps and paperwork

The temperature that matters is the product, not the air. Use a calibrated probe thermometer to check **pulp temperature** on a few pallets from different parts of the load, following the shipper's rules on how and whether you can probe.

If the product is warmer than the required temperature:

- Tell the shipping office before you leave.
- Ask them to cool it further, or to note the actual temperature on the bill of lading.
- Write the temperatures you measured and the time on your copy of the BOL.
- Notify your dispatcher and the broker.

A reefer unit is designed to **hold** temperature, not to pull heat out of a trailer full of warm product. If warm product is not documented at pickup, the receiver's rejection may become your claim. Our [cargo claims guide](/blog/cargo-claims-guide.html) explains how claims are decided.

## Loading for airflow

Cold air has to circulate around the product and back to the unit. Watch for:

- **Gap at the front:** do not let pallets block the return air bulkhead.
- **Gap at the top:** leave space between the top of the load and the air chute so air can travel to the rear.
- **Gap at the rear:** a small space at the doors helps air return along the floor.
- **No plastic sheets or loose cardboard** over pallets unless the shipper requires them.
- **Floor channels clear,** so air can move under the load.

If the load is shipper load and count, you may not control the pattern, but you can note poor airflow conditions on the BOL.

## Continuous vs cycle mode

| Mode | How it works | Common use |
|---|---|---|
| Continuous | Unit runs all the time with steady airflow | Many fresh produce and sensitive loads |
| Cycle (start/stop) | Unit shuts down when set point is reached and restarts as needed | Many frozen loads; saves fuel |

**Run the mode the shipper or broker specifies.** If it is not on the paperwork, ask and get the answer in writing. Do not switch modes to save fuel without permission.

## Fuel and the unit on hot days

Summer heat makes the reefer burn more fuel. A hypothetical example: if your unit burns about 0.8 gallons per hour in continuous mode on a hot day, a 30-hour trip uses about 24 gallons. At a hypothetical $4.50 per gallon, that is about $108 of reefer fuel for one load. Price it into your rate, and use the [truck fuel cost calculator](/truck-fuel-cost-calculator.html) for the tractor side.

Practical tips:

- Fill the reefer tank before every load. Running out of reefer fuel is one of the most common causes of temperature failures.
- In many states, reefer units can run on dyed diesel from a separate tank. It must never go into the truck's fuel tank. Check the rules where you fuel, and keep reefer fuel separate on your IFTA records.
- Park in shade when you can, and keep the unit's condenser clear of dirt and debris so it can shed heat.

## On the road and at the receiver

- **Check temperatures** at every stop, and photograph the unit display with a timestamp if possible.
- **Keep doors closed.** If an officer or the receiver needs to open the trailer, note the time.
- **Move promptly at the receiver.** Long waits in heat add risk. Request detention per your rate confirmation.
- **Download or save the temperature record** after delivery. Many units keep a log; some brokers require the download with your paperwork.

### Food safety rules

The FDA's Sanitary Transportation of Human and Animal Food rule sets duties for shippers, carriers and receivers moving food. For carriers this generally means following the shipper's temperature requirements, providing temperature records when asked, keeping equipment clean, and training staff. Check the current requirements with the FDA.

## Summer reefer checklist

- Set point, unit of measure and mode confirmed in writing
- Trailer pre-cooled, clean, and seals checked
- Reefer tank full; unit with no active alarms
- Pulp temps checked and any warm product documented
- Airflow gaps at front, top and rear
- Temperature checked and recorded at each stop
- Temperature log saved after delivery

## How Texas Solutions can help

Texas Solutions is a dispatch service, not a broker or a motor carrier. Our [reefer dispatch](/reefer-dispatch.html) team finds and negotiates produce and temperature-controlled loads, confirms set points and instructions with brokers, handles broker packets and paperwork 24/7, and you approve every load. You can also [talk to a dispatcher](/contact.html).

### Pre-Trip Inspection Checklist for Truck Drivers
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/pre-trip-inspection-checklist/
Published: 2026-10-21

A good **pre-trip inspection checklist** is the cheapest safety program you will ever run. It catches problems in the yard instead of on the shoulder or at a weigh station, and it protects your CSA scores and your schedule. Use the checklist below as a daily routine, and adjust it for your truck, trailer and state CDL manual.

## Why the pre-trip matters

Federal rules (49 CFR 396.13) require a driver to be satisfied that the vehicle is in safe operating condition before driving. If the last driver vehicle inspection report listed defects, you must review it and confirm repairs were certified before you drive.

The practical reasons are just as strong:

- Roadside inspections often find lights, tires and brakes, which a walkaround catches.
- Out-of-service orders cost you the load, the appointment and sometimes the customer. See [DOT roadside inspections](/blog/dot-roadside-inspections.html) and [out-of-service criteria](/blog/out-of-service-criteria.html).
- A breakdown on the road costs more than the same repair in a shop.

## Work in the same order every time

The order matters less than doing it the same way daily so nothing gets skipped. A common flow:

1. Approach the vehicle: look for leaks, leaning and damage
2. Engine compartment
3. Start engine and inside the cab
4. Lights check
5. Walkaround: front, driver side, rear, passenger side
6. Coupling and trailer
7. Air brake checks
8. Documents and emergency equipment

## The checklist

### 1. Approaching the vehicle
- [ ] Puddles or fresh drips of oil, coolant, fuel or other fluid under the truck
- [ ] Truck or trailer leaning, which can point to suspension or tire problems
- [ ] New damage since you last drove it

### 2. Engine compartment (engine off)
- [ ] Engine oil level
- [ ] Coolant level and condition of radiator and hoses
- [ ] Power steering fluid and hoses
- [ ] Belts: tension, cracks, fraying
- [ ] Air compressor, mounted securely, no leaks
- [ ] Wiring: no chafed or loose wires
- [ ] Windshield washer fluid

### 3. Cab and engine start
- [ ] Gauges read normal: oil pressure, coolant temperature, voltage
- [ ] Air pressure builds within normal range and time, governor cuts out where it should
- [ ] Low air warning works
- [ ] Horn(s), wipers, defroster and heater
- [ ] Mirrors clean, adjusted and secure
- [ ] Windshield free of cracks in the driver's view
- [ ] Seat belt works
- [ ] Steering wheel play within limits
- [ ] Parking brake holds

### 4. Lights and reflectors
- [ ] Headlights (high and low)
- [ ] Turn signals and four-way flashers
- [ ] Clearance, marker and identification lights
- [ ] Brake lights and tail lights
- [ ] Reflectors and reflective tape clean and in place
- [ ] Trailer ABS warning lamp works as designed

### 5. Tires, wheels and hubs
- [ ] Tread depth meets at least the out-of-service minimums (generally 4/32 inch steer, 2/32 inch others)
- [ ] Inflation with a gauge, not a thump
- [ ] No cuts, bulges, exposed cords or mismatched sizes on duals
- [ ] Nothing stuck between duals
- [ ] Rims not cracked or bent
- [ ] Lug nuts present, tight, no rust streaks
- [ ] Hub oil level and no leaks at seals

### 6. Brakes and suspension (each axle)
- [ ] Slack adjusters and pushrods: not out of adjustment
- [ ] Brake chambers secure, no air leaks
- [ ] Air hoses not cracked, chafed or kinked
- [ ] Drums or rotors free of cracks, linings not too thin
- [ ] Springs, hangers and U-bolts: nothing broken, cracked or missing
- [ ] Air bags (if equipped) holding air, no leaks
- [ ] Shocks secure, not leaking

### 7. Coupling and trailer
- [ ] Fifth wheel securely mounted, no cracks, properly greased
- [ ] Locking jaws closed around the kingpin, release arm locked
- [ ] No gap between the fifth wheel and the trailer apron
- [ ] Glad hands and air lines connected, no leaks
- [ ] Electrical cord plugged in and secure
- [ ] Landing gear fully raised, crank handle secured
- [ ] Trailer doors, hinges and seals secure
- [ ] Mud flaps, frame and crossmembers not damaged
- [ ] Load secured (for flatbed, see [flatbed cargo securement](/blog/flatbed-cargo-securement.html))

### 8. Air brake checks
These are general steps. Your state CDL manual lists the exact procedure and pass limits for your vehicle, so follow it.
- [ ] Static leak test: with brakes released and engine off, air loss stays within the allowed limit for one minute
- [ ] Applied leak test: holding full brake application, loss stays within the allowed limit
- [ ] Low air warning activates at or before the required pressure as you fan down
- [ ] Spring brakes apply automatically as pressure drops into the required range
- [ ] Air pressure builds back up within the expected time
- [ ] Tug test with parking brakes and trailer brakes
- [ ] Service brake test at low speed

### 9. Documents and emergency equipment
- [ ] Driver's license and medical card (see [medical card and DOT physical](/blog/medical-card-and-dot-physical.html))
- [ ] Registration and cab card, proof of insurance
- [ ] Permits and IFTA documents as needed
- [ ] ELD user guide, malfunction instruction sheet and blank paper logs
- [ ] Bill of lading and any hazmat shipping papers
- [ ] Fire extinguisher charged and secured
- [ ] Three warning triangles
- [ ] Spare fuses if your vehicle requires them

## Post-trip inspection and DVIR

At the end of the day, walk the truck again. Property-carrying drivers generally must complete a written or electronic driver vehicle inspection report (DVIR) when they find or are told about a defect that would affect safety or cause a breakdown. The carrier must repair or certify that repair is not needed before the vehicle is driven again, and the next driver reviews and signs. Many carriers require a DVIR every day regardless. Keep DVIRs as long as the rules require (generally three months). Confirm current requirements with FMCSA.

## Hypothetical example: what a missed light costs

Say a marker light is out. Fixing it in the yard: a bulb and five minutes. Caught at a weigh station: a violation on your record and maybe an inspection that runs 45 minutes. If that pushes you past a delivery appointment, you could lose the load, pay a late fee, or burn hours you needed for the next pickup. On a hypothetical $1,800 load, missing the appointment can cost far more than the bulb.

## How Texas Solutions can help

Texas Solutions is a dispatch service, not a broker or motor carrier. Our dispatchers build realistic schedules that leave time for a proper pre-trip, find and negotiate loads, handle broker packets and paperwork, and work 24/7, and you approve every load. See our [dispatch services](/dispatch.html) or [talk to a dispatcher](/contact.html).

### Power Only Trucking Explained: How It Works and Who It Fits
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/power-only-trucking-explained/
Published: 2026-10-21

**Power only trucking** is a simple idea: you bring the tractor and the driver, someone else brings the trailer. You hook to a loaded trailer, haul it to the receiver, drop it, and often pick up another trailer for the next run. For owner-operators who want to avoid buying and maintaining a trailer, it can be a smart way to get on the road.

## How power only works

In a typical power only move:

1. A shipper, broker or trailer owner has a loaded trailer waiting at a yard or dock.
2. You book the load and get the trailer number, seal number and pickup details.
3. You arrive, inspect the trailer, hook up and leave, often without waiting for a live load.
4. You deliver and drop the trailer at the receiver or a designated yard.
5. You may pick up an empty or loaded trailer to return or reposition.

Trailers can be dry vans, reefers, flatbeds or specialized units, depending on who owns them.

## Who supplies the trailers

- **Large carriers and leasing companies** that have more trailers than trucks and need extra power.
- **Brokers with trailer pools** who offer power only loads to approved carriers.
- **Shippers with their own trailers** who keep trailers at their docks and hire outside tractors to move them.
- **Rental and leasing trailers being repositioned** from one location to another.

Each source has its own approval process, and some require a certain time in business, safety record or insurance limits.

## Equipment you need

Power only does not mean no equipment. You still need a well-maintained tractor that can pull the trailers you plan to haul. Check:

- **Fifth wheel** in good shape and set at the right height
- **Glad hands and air lines** in working order
- **Electrical connection** (the 7-way plug) and working trailer lights
- **Reefer fuel** if you haul refrigerated trailers (find out who pays for it)
- **Load locks or straps** in case the trailer needs them
- **A good flashlight and a checklist** for trailer inspections at night

## Insurance for power only

This is the area new power only carriers most often get wrong. Your standard policies cover your truck, your liability and the cargo. But if a trailer you do not own is damaged, you may be responsible for it.

Common coverage types to ask your agent about:

- **Trailer interchange.** Covers physical damage to a non-owned trailer when you have a written interchange agreement with the owner.
- **Non-owned trailer physical damage.** Covers damage to trailers you pull without a formal interchange agreement.
- **Primary auto liability and cargo**, at the limits the broker or trailer owner requires.

Which one you need depends on your contracts. Talk to your insurance agent and give them a copy of the agreements before you haul. For the basics, see [trucking insurance explained](/blog/trucking-insurance-explained.html).

## Inspect every trailer before you leave

Since the trailer is not yours, document its condition every time:

- Walk around and photograph all sides, tires, doors and the seal
- Check tires, lights, brakes and the landing gear
- Confirm the seal number matches the paperwork
- Note any damage on the bill of lading or with the shipper before leaving
- Make sure the trailer registration and annual inspection are current

If you skip this, you may end up paying for damage that was there before you hooked up. Report problems before you roll, not after.

## Rates and the money side

Power only rates are often somewhat lower than equivalent loads where you supply the trailer, because you are not providing the trailer. But your costs are lower too. Here is a hypothetical comparison for one month:

| Item (hypothetical) | With own trailer | Power only |
|---|---|---|
| Trailer payment | $800 | $0 |
| Trailer insurance and maintenance | $450 | $0 |
| Non-owned trailer coverage | $0 | $150 |
| Average rate per mile | $2.30 | $2.15 |
| Revenue on 9,000 miles | $20,700 | $19,350 |
| Revenue minus trailer-related costs | $19,450 | $19,200 |

In this example, the gap is small. The bigger advantages of power only are lower startup cash, no trailer repairs and quick drop-and-hook turns. Run your own figures in the [cost per mile calculator](/cost-per-mile-calculator.html).

### Pros and cons

**Pros**

- Lower startup cost, since you do not buy a trailer
- No trailer maintenance, tires or registration
- Drop-and-hook freight can mean less time waiting at docks
- Flexibility to pull different trailer types if your insurance allows

**Cons**

- Approval with trailer pools can take time
- You depend on trailer availability in your area
- Extra insurance requirements
- Responsibility for damage to trailers you do not own
- Rates can be lower on some lanes

## How to get started

1. Make sure your authority is active and your insurance includes trailer coverage your partners accept.
2. Prepare a complete carrier packet: authority, W-9, certificate of insurance and any interchange agreements.
3. Apply with brokers and companies that offer power only freight, and ask about their requirements up front.
4. Vet every broker before you haul. Our guide on [how to vet a freight broker](/blog/how-to-vet-a-freight-broker.html) explains what to check.
5. Track your profit per mile closely for the first few months.

## How Texas Solutions can help

Texas Solutions is a dispatch service, not a broker or motor carrier. Our [power only dispatch](/power-only-dispatch.html) team finds and negotiates power only loads, handles broker setup packets and paperwork 24/7, and you approve every load. [Talk to a dispatcher](/contact.html) to get started.

### How to Plan a Profitable Round Trip in Trucking
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/plan-a-profitable-round-trip/
Published: 2026-10-21

A single high-paying load can look great on a load board and still lose money once you count the trip home. The fix is to **plan a profitable round trip**: price the full loop, not just the first leg. This guide walks through how owner-operators and small fleets do that in practice.

## Think in loops, not loads

Every load you take puts your truck in a new market. That market decides what your next load pays and how far you drive empty to get it. So the real question is never "Is this load good?" It is "Is this load good, plus whatever it takes to get the truck loaded again?"

Two terms help here:

- **Headhaul:** the strong direction of a lane, with lots of freight and higher rates.
- **Backhaul:** the return direction, with fewer loads and lower rates.

Most profitable loops pair a well-paid headhaul with a backhaul that at least covers its own costs.

## Six steps to plan the loop

### Step 1: Know your cost per mile

You cannot judge a loop without knowing what a mile costs you. Add fixed costs (truck payment, insurance, permits) and variable costs (fuel, tires, maintenance) and divide by miles driven. Use the [cost per mile calculator](/cost-per-mile-calculator.html).

This number is your floor. Any loop that averages below it loses money, no matter how good one leg looks.

### Step 2: Check the delivery market before you book

Before accepting a load, look at the city where it delivers:

- How many loads are posted outbound from that area for your trailer type?
- What do those loads pay compared to the inbound rate?
- How far would you likely deadhead to reach a decent pickup?

If the delivery area has few outbound loads, the inbound load needs to pay enough to cover the weak return. That is a strong point when you [negotiate freight rates](/blog/how-to-negotiate-freight-rates.html).

### Step 3: Price the whole loop

Add every mile and every dollar in the trip:

1. Deadhead to the first pickup.
2. Loaded miles on the first leg.
3. Deadhead to the second pickup.
4. Loaded miles on the return leg.
5. Any deadhead to get home or to the next pickup.

Then divide total revenue by total miles. That is your round-trip rate per mile.

**Worked example (hypothetical)**

| Leg | Miles | Revenue |
|---|---|---|
| Deadhead to pickup A | 50 | $0 |
| Load A (headhaul) | 900 | $2,700 |
| Deadhead to pickup B | 120 | $0 |
| Load B (backhaul) | 850 | $1,700 |
| Total | 1,920 | $4,400 |

Load A pays $3.00 per loaded mile and load B only $2.00. But the round trip earns $4,400 over 1,920 miles, or about $2.29 per total mile. If your cost is $1.85 per mile, the loop clears roughly $0.44 per mile, about $850 before your own pay and taxes.

Now compare: if load B were not available and you deadheaded 600 miles home empty, the loop would be $2,700 over 1,550 miles, about $1.74 per mile. That is below cost. The cheaper backhaul made the trip profitable.

Run your own loops with the [load profitability calculator](/load-profitability-calculator.html).

### Step 4: Use triangle routes when the return lane is weak

When the direct return lane is weak, a triangle route can keep the truck loaded. Instead of going A to B and back to A, you go A to B, B to C, and C back to A, where C is a market with better freight.

Triangle routes work best when:

- The middle market is a strong freight area for your equipment.
- The extra loaded miles pay more than the deadhead you avoid.
- You still have enough hours to run it legally under hours of service rules.

### Step 5: Fit the loop into your hours and home time

A loop is only as good as your ability to run it legally and on time. Check:

- **Hours of service:** daily driving limits and the weekly cycle can turn a two-day loop into three.
- **Appointment times:** tight delivery windows can leave you waiting for a reload.
- **Home time:** a loop that strands you far from home on a Friday may cost you a weekend or an expensive deadhead.

The [hours of service calculator](/hours-of-service-calculator.html) helps you check whether a plan fits before you book.

### Step 6: Line up reloads with brokers you trust

The easiest reload is one a broker offers you before it hits the board. After a smooth delivery, tell the broker where you will be empty and when. Brokers who move freight both ways on a lane may have a return load, and repeat business often comes with better communication and faster payment.

Keep a short list of brokers and shippers by market. Over time, that list becomes your own round-trip map, and you spend less time searching every time the truck empties.

## Common round-trip mistakes

- **Chasing the top rate into a dead market.** The inbound load pays well because few trucks want to go there.
- **Ignoring deadhead.** Empty miles still burn fuel, tires and hours.
- **Booking the next load too late.** The best time to find a reload is while you are still loaded on the way in.
- **Forgetting accessorials.** Detention, lumper fees and layovers can change a loop's math. Make sure they are on the rate confirmation.
- **Not tracking results.** Without records, you cannot tell which lanes really pay.

## Round-trip planning checklist

- [ ] I know my current all-in cost per mile.
- [ ] I checked outbound loads from the delivery city before booking.
- [ ] I priced the full loop, including all deadhead.
- [ ] The loop fits my hours of service and appointment times.
- [ ] I have a backup option if the planned reload falls through.
- [ ] Accessorial terms are on the rate confirmation.

## How Texas Solutions can help

Texas Solutions is a dispatch service, not a broker or motor carrier. Our dispatchers plan the next load before the current one delivers, negotiate rates with the whole loop in mind, and handle broker packets and paperwork 24/7. You approve every load. See our [owner-operator dispatch](/owner-operator-dispatch.html) or [talk to a dispatcher](/contact.html).

### PHMSA Hazmat Registration: Who Needs It and How to File
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/phmsa-hazmat-registration/
Published: 2026-10-21

**PHMSA hazmat registration** is a yearly filing with the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration, part of the US Department of Transportation. If your truck hauls placarded hazardous materials, you almost certainly need it, and brokers and shippers will often ask for your certificate before tendering hazmat freight.

## What PHMSA registration is (and is not)

The registration program lives in 49 CFR Part 107, Subpart G. It applies to people and companies who **offer for transport or transport** certain hazardous materials in commerce. The fees fund emergency response planning and training grants.

It is easy to confuse with other hazmat credentials:

| Credential | Who holds it | Issued by |
|---|---|---|
| Hazmat endorsement (H) | The driver | State licensing agency, after a TSA threat assessment |
| PHMSA registration | The company (carrier or shipper) | PHMSA |
| Hazmat safety permit | The carrier, for certain high-hazard materials | FMCSA |
| USDOT number with hazmat marked | The carrier | FMCSA, via the MCS-150 |

You can need all four. Our [hazmat endorsement guide](/blog/hazmat-endorsement-guide.html) covers the driver side.

## Which loads trigger registration

As we understand the current rule, you must register if you transport or offer any of the following during the registration year:

- Any quantity of hazardous material that **requires placards**
- A highway route-controlled quantity of a Class 7 (radioactive) material
- More than a set weight of Division 1.1, 1.2 or 1.3 explosives in a motor vehicle
- More than a set volume per package of a material that is extremely toxic by inhalation (hazard zone A)
- Hazmat in a bulk packaging above a set capacity (large tanks and bulk bins)
- A non-bulk shipment of a single placarded class above a set gross weight

For most owner-operators the first line settles it: **if the load is placarded, plan on registering.** The exact weights and capacities for the other items are in the regulation; check them on the PHMSA website if you haul bulk or specialty hazmat.

There are a few exceptions, for example for certain agricultural operations and government agencies. Do not assume one applies to you without reading it.

## The registration year and fees

- The registration year runs **July 1 through June 30**.
- You can register for one, two or three years at once.
- The fee depends on whether you qualify as a small business under the Small Business Administration size standard for your industry, plus a processing fee. Not-for-profit organizations have their own rate.
- Fees have changed over time, so check the current amount on PHMSA's site before you file.

Because the year does not line up with the calendar year, it is easy to forget. Put a reminder in your compliance calendar for early June. Our guide on [keeping your MC authority active](/blog/keep-your-mc-authority-active.html) has a full list of yearly deadlines worth tracking alongside it, including [UCR registration](/blog/ucr-registration-guide.html).

## How to file, step by step

1. **Confirm you need it.** List the hazmat you expect to haul this year and check each against the thresholds above.
2. **Gather your information.** Legal business name, address, USDOT number, the hazard classes you will transport, and your business size information.
3. **Decide small business or not.** Use the SBA size standard for your industry code. Most single-truck owner-operators qualify as small businesses, but confirm it.
4. **File online with PHMSA.** Use the hazmat registration system on PHMSA's official website and pay by card or another accepted method. Avoid third-party sites that charge extra to "process" the filing unless you deliberately want that service.
5. **Download and save your certificate.** You get a registration number and a certificate of registration.
6. **Put proof in every truck.** A copy of the certificate, or another document showing the registration number, must be on each vehicle hauling regulated hazmat, and you must be able to show it to enforcement on request.
7. **Keep your records.** Keep a copy at your principal place of business for the period the rule requires.

## What to keep in the truck

When you run placarded freight, a simple hazmat folder in the cab saves a lot of trouble at inspections:

- PHMSA registration certificate (current year)
- Shipping papers, within reach and on top or tabbed
- Emergency response information for each material
- Your hazmat training certificate or record
- Hazmat safety permit, if the material requires one
- Placard set for the classes you haul

Officers check hazmat loads more closely. Read our guide on [DOT roadside inspections](/blog/dot-roadside-inspections.html) to know what they look at.

## Common mistakes

- **Letting it lapse on July 1.** A load you haul on July 2 under last year's certificate is not covered.
- **Registering under the wrong name.** Use the same legal name as your USDOT and MC records.
- **Thinking the shipper's registration covers you.** Shippers and carriers each register for their own activity.
- **Paying the large-business fee by mistake, or the small-business fee when you do not qualify.** Check the size standard each time you renew, especially as you add trucks.
- **Not updating the MCS-150.** If you start hauling hazmat, your USDOT record should reflect it.

## A simple example

Hypothetical: a one-truck carrier hauls dry van freight and starts accepting the occasional load of placarded paint. That first placarded load makes the carrier a hazmat transporter for that registration year. Before booking it, the owner checks insurance with the agent, files PHMSA registration as a small business, updates the MCS-150, completes hazmat employee training, and puts the certificate in the truck. The paperwork takes a few hours spread over a week, which is why it is better done before a broker offers the load, not after.

Thresholds, fees and filing methods can change. Always confirm current requirements directly with PHMSA and FMCSA, and talk to your insurance agent before hauling a new hazard class.

## How Texas Solutions can help

Texas Solutions is a dispatch service, not a broker or a motor carrier. Once your hazmat credentials are in place, our dispatchers can search and negotiate hazmat-eligible loads, send your certificates with broker packets, and handle paperwork 24/7, and you approve every load. See our [dispatch services](/dispatch.html) or [talk to a dispatcher](/contact.html).

### Personal Conveyance and Yard Moves: When You Can Use Them
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/personal-conveyance-and-yard-moves/
Published: 2026-10-21

**Personal conveyance** and yard moves are two ELD statuses that let you move your truck without the time counting as regular driving. Both are legal and useful, and both are a common source of violations when drivers stretch them too far.

This guide explains each status, gives examples based on FMCSA's guidance as we understand it, and shows how to log them so they hold up at an inspection or audit. FMCSA guidance can be updated, so check the current version on the FMCSA website, and always follow your carrier's policy, which can be stricter.

## What personal conveyance is

Personal conveyance (PC) is the movement of a commercial motor vehicle for **personal use while off duty**. When you log PC correctly, the time is off duty and does not count toward your 11 hours of driving or your 14-hour window.

The key test is **purpose**. FMCSA looks at why you moved the truck, not how far you went or whether a trailer was attached. If the move advances the load or the business, it is not personal conveyance, even if it is short.

Two more conditions:

- **Your carrier must allow it.** A motor carrier can limit or ban PC. If you are leased on, the carrier's written policy controls.
- **You must be fit to drive.** PC does not exempt you from fatigue rules. Driving tired on PC is still unsafe and can still be cited.

## Examples that usually qualify

Based on FMCSA's published guidance, these are examples of moves that can be personal conveyance:

- Driving from en route lodging (a motel or truck stop) to a restaurant or entertainment and back
- Commuting between your home and your normal work reporting location, or a trailer-drop lot
- Moving the truck a short way at the request of a safety official during off-duty time
- Driving from a shipper or receiver to the **nearest reasonable, safe location** to get required rest after loading or unloading, when you cannot stay at the facility
- Transporting personal property while off duty

Laden or empty does not change the answer. A loaded truck can be on PC if the move is truly personal.

## Examples that do not qualify

These are examples FMCSA guidance treats as **not** personal conveyance:

- Continuing a trip toward the delivery to make up time or reach a better spot when you are out of hours
- Bobtailing or pulling an empty trailer to pick up your next load or reposition the truck for the business
- Driving to a shop for maintenance or repairs
- Driving past a reasonable, safe location to reach a preferred truck stop or home
- Moving the truck after loading to get closer to the receiver

Here is a simple way to check yourself: if the trip would happen even if you had no load and no business plans, it may be personal. If the trip helps the freight, the customer or the next load, it is work.

## What yard moves are

A yard move is moving the truck within a yard, terminal, shipper or receiver lot, intermodal yard or a similar area. On an ELD, yard moves are a special category of **on duty, not driving**. That means:

- The time **counts** toward your 14-hour window and your 60/70-hour cycle.
- The time **does not count** toward your 11 hours of driving.

Typical yard moves include hooking and dropping trailers, moving to a dock door, moving to the scale inside a facility, and shifting the truck while it is being loaded. FMCSA guidance has indicated that a yard move can include a public road only where public access is restricted, such as a road through a port or facility controlled by gates or traffic control. Driving on an open public road between two facilities is driving, not a yard move. Check the current guidance and your carrier's policy before you rely on that.

Your carrier must enable yard moves in the ELD. Some devices end the yard move status automatically if the truck goes faster than a set speed, depending on how the system is configured.

## How to log PC and yard moves correctly

1. **Select the right status before you move.** Switch to PC or yard move first, then drive. If you forget, the ELD records driving time and you will need an annotated edit.
2. **Add an annotation.** Write a short, honest note: "PC from receiver to nearest truck stop, facility does not allow overnight parking" or "Yard move to door 14."
3. **End the status when you stop.** Go back to off duty, sleeper berth or on duty as appropriate.
4. **Keep supporting records.** Receipts, gate times and lumper slips help show the purpose of a move.
5. **Know your carrier's rules.** Some carriers cap PC by distance or time. Follow the stricter rule.

## A quick decision table

| Situation | Likely status |
|---|---|
| Hotel to diner and back, off duty | Personal conveyance |
| Receiver kicks you out, nearest safe parking 6 miles away | Personal conveyance (if allowed by carrier) |
| Out of hours, 40 miles from the receiver, drive there to be first in line | Driving, not PC |
| Moving from the yard to a dock door | Yard move (on duty) |
| Driving down a public highway between two warehouses | Driving |
| Bobtail to the shop for a tire | Driving |

## Why getting this right matters

Misused PC is easy to spot in ELD data: long PC segments that end at a shipper, or PC driving right before a pickup. During an inspection or an audit, that can lead to hours of service violations, which affect your CSA scores. Read our guide to [CSA scores explained](/blog/csa-scores-explained.html). If you believe a violation was written in error, you can challenge it through FMCSA's DataQs system.

For the core limits behind all of this, read [hours of service rules explained](/blog/hours-of-service-rules-explained-11-14-70-hour.html), and plan your stops with the [hours of service calculator](/hours-of-service-calculator.html). Good [truck parking and trip planning](/blog/truck-parking-and-trip-planning.html) also reduces how often you need PC in the first place.
