Texas Solutions is a dispatch service, not a broker or motor carrier. Our dispatchers find and negotiate loads, handle broker packets and paperwork 24/7, and plan appointments around your available hours and safe parking so you are not forced into a bad choice at the end of the day. You approve every load. See our [dispatch services](/dispatch.html) or [talk to a dispatcher](/contact.html).

### Peak Season Trucking Loads: How Owner-Operators Can Plan Q4 Holiday Freight
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/peak-season-trucking-loads-holiday-freight/
Published: 2026-10-21

The last three months of the year are the busiest stretch for many carriers. **Peak season trucking loads** come from retail restocking, holiday food and grocery, and e-commerce. For an owner-operator, Q4 can be the best quarter of the year or a frustrating one stuck in the wrong market. This guide shows how to plan **holiday freight loads**, which regions to watch, and how to keep deadhead down when everyone is busy.

## What drives Q4 freight

- **Retail restocking.** Stores and warehouses fill shelves from late summer through November.
- **Holiday food.** Turkey, meat, dairy, baking goods and frozen food move hard before Thanksgiving and Christmas. Reefer demand climbs.
- **E-commerce.** Parcel and fulfillment networks need extra capacity, which pulls dry van, power only and box truck freight.
- **Year-end shipping.** Some shippers move freight before the year closes.

Then, in the last week or so of December, freight drops off as receivers close. Plan for both.

## Reefer rates per mile in peak season

Reefer is usually the first trailer to feel the holiday rush. Our dispatchers plan reefer freight around roughly $4 to $6 a mile (October 2026 planning range, not a market index or quote). **Reefer rates per mile today** on your lane can sit above or below that. Check the board daily, and read our [reefer loads guide](/blog/reefer-loads-refrigerated-dispatch-guide.html) for what to confirm before booking.

## Regional picture: Texas, Midwest and California loads

### Texas loads

Dallas-Fort Worth and Houston are national distribution hubs, and Laredo is the busiest cross-border crossing. Q4 brings retail, grocery and cross-border freight. Houston also stays busy with energy and construction freight for hotshots and flatbeds. See [Texas truck dispatch](/texas-truck-dispatch.html).

### Midwest loads

Chicago, Indianapolis, Columbus and Kansas City host large warehouse and rail networks. Midwest loads in Q4 include retail, food processing and the end of the harvest. Winter weather can slow everything, so build in time. See [Illinois truck dispatch](/truck-dispatch/illinois.html), [Ohio](/truck-dispatch/ohio.html) and [Indiana](/truck-dispatch/indiana.html).

### California loads

The Southern California ports and Inland Empire warehouses push import freight inland for the holidays. California loads often pay well outbound; the challenge is getting back in without a long empty run. See [California truck dispatch](/truck-dispatch/california.html).

For other states, use our [truck dispatch by state](/truck-dispatch-by-state.html) list.

## Seven ways to make the most of peak season

1. **Position early.** Be near a strong outbound market before the rush, not after.
2. **Book the reload first.** Before you accept a load, check freight out of the delivery city.
3. **Negotiate harder on short-notice loads.** Brokers with uncovered holiday freight have more room.
4. **Watch deadhead.** A high rate with 200 empty miles may pay less than a normal load next door. Use the [deadhead miles calculator](/deadhead-miles-calculator.html).
5. **Plan for waiting.** Warehouses are busy; log check-in times and claim detention. Try the [detention pay calculator](/detention-pay-calculator.html).
6. **Keep the truck ready.** A breakdown in December costs more than any rate gain. Budget with the [maintenance calculator](/maintenance-budget-calculator.html).
7. **Set home time now.** Pick your dates and plan the last loads so you end near home.

## Watch your hours

Peak season tempts long days. The hours-of-service limits do not change for the holidays. Plan loads you can run legally with the [hours of service calculator](/hours-of-service-calculator.html).

## How a dispatcher helps in Q4

A dispatcher who works the boards all day sees holiday freight move first and can line up the next load while you are still loaded. At Texas Solutions, dispatchers are available 24/7 for the night and weekend reloads Q4 brings, negotiate every load, and plan your last runs around your home-time dates. The fee is 5% of weekly gross for OTR semis, 7% for hotshots and 8% for box trucks, with no setup fee and no long-term contract, and your first load is dispatched free. Freight and rates are not guaranteed. [Talk to a dispatcher](/contact.html) before the rush starts.

### Owner-Operator vs Company Driver: Which Path Is Right for You?
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/owner-operator-vs-company-driver/
Published: 2026-10-21

The choice between **owner-operator vs company driver** is one of the biggest decisions a truck driver makes. Running your own truck promises more money and more control, but it also turns you into a business owner with real costs and real risk. This guide compares both paths honestly so you can pick the one that fits your finances, skills and goals.

## The basic difference

- **Company driver:** you drive the carrier's truck, the carrier pays all operating costs, and you get a paycheck, usually per mile, per hour, per load or a percentage. You are typically a W-2 employee.
- **Owner-operator:** you own or lease the truck and pay for fuel, insurance, maintenance, tolls and more. You earn the revenue from loads, and what is left after costs is your income. You are self-employed.

Owner-operators either **lease on** to a carrier and run under its authority, or run under **their own authority** (their own MC number) and work directly with brokers and shippers.

## Side-by-side comparison

| Factor | Company driver | Owner-operator |
|---|---|---|
| Truck cost | None | Payment or lease, plus down payment |
| Operating costs | Paid by carrier | Paid by you |
| Income | Predictable paycheck | Varies with rates, miles and costs |
| Benefits | Often health, retirement, paid time off | You buy your own |
| Taxes | Withheld by employer | Estimated taxes and self-employment tax |
| Choice of loads | Usually assigned | You choose (or approve) loads |
| Home time | Set by carrier policy | You decide, but it affects income |
| Risk | Low financial risk | Breakdowns and slow markets hit you directly |
| Paperwork | Minimal | Bookkeeping, IFTA, permits and more |

## What owner-operators really earn

The big gross numbers can be misleading. Here is a hypothetical week to show the difference between revenue and income.

- Revenue: 2,500 miles x $2.40 = **$6,000**
- Fuel (2,500 miles / 6.5 mpg x $3.90): about $1,500
- Truck payment: $600
- Insurance: $350
- Maintenance and tire reserve: $400
- Dispatch, ELD, permits and other costs: $500
- **Total costs: about $3,350**
- **Left before taxes: about $2,650**

From that, the owner-operator still pays income and self-employment taxes, health insurance and saves for slow weeks. A company driver earning, say, $1,500 to $1,800 a week in this hypothetical has fewer worries, but less upside. Learn more in [how much owner-operators make](/blog/how-much-do-owner-operators-make.html) and run your own numbers with the [cost per mile calculator](/cost-per-mile-calculator.html).

## Advantages of each path

### Company driver

- Steady, predictable pay
- No truck payment or repair bills
- Benefits may be included
- Less paperwork and fewer business decisions
- Easier to change jobs if a company is a bad fit
- Time to learn the industry before taking on risk

### Owner-operator

- Higher earning potential when rates and costs are managed well
- Control over which loads you take and where you run
- Ability to build equity in a truck and a business
- Business expenses may be deductible (ask a CPA)
- Option to grow into a small fleet

## The risks of going independent

Owner-operators fail most often for reasons they could have planned for:

- **Not knowing cost per mile** and taking loads that lose money
- **Too little cash reserve** for a major repair or a slow month
- **Overpriced trucks** with payments the business cannot support
- **Waiting to get paid** for 30 days or more without a plan for cash flow
- **Underestimating paperwork** like IFTA, 2290 and compliance

None of these are reasons not to do it. They are reasons to prepare.

## Signs you are ready to become an owner-operator

Use this checklist before you make the move:

- [ ] At least a couple of years of safe driving experience
- [ ] A clean driving record and inspection history
- [ ] Savings for a down payment and several months of costs
- [ ] A written budget with your expected cost per mile
- [ ] A plan for freight: lease on, own authority with a dispatcher, or direct customers
- [ ] Basic bookkeeping skills or a bookkeeper lined up
- [ ] A clear understanding of the insurance you will need

If several boxes are unchecked, staying a company driver for another year while you save and learn can be the smarter business decision. Our guide on [how to become an owner-operator](/blog/how-to-become-an-owner-operator.html) covers the steps in detail.

## Lease on or get your own authority?

Leasing on to a carrier is a middle step: you own the truck, but the carrier provides authority, insurance options and often freight. It is simpler but you give up some control and pay the carrier a share. Getting your own authority gives you full control but means more setup and compliance. Some new carriers also explore [MC lease options](/mc-lease.html) as they build their own track record. Talk to an attorney about any lease agreement before you sign.

## How Texas Solutions can help

Texas Solutions is a dispatch service, not a broker or motor carrier. For owner-operators with their own authority, our [owner-operator dispatch](/owner-operator-dispatch.html) team finds and negotiates loads, handles broker packets and paperwork 24/7, and you approve every load. [Talk to a dispatcher](/contact.html) if you are weighing the move.

### Oversize and Overweight Permits: A Practical Guide
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/oversize-overweight-permits/
Published: 2026-10-21

**Oversize and overweight permits** let you legally move a load that is wider, taller, longer or heavier than normal limits. Every state on your route issues its own permit with its own conditions, which is why OS/OW freight pays more and demands more planning. Here is how it works for an owner-operator.

## Know the legal limits first

Before you can tell if a load needs a permit, you need the baseline. Commonly cited limits:

| Dimension | Typical legal limit | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Width | 8 ft 6 in (102 in) | Federal standard on the National Network. |
| Height | Often 13 ft 6 in, some states 14 ft or more | Set by each state; no single federal height limit. |
| Length | Varies | States set trailer and overall length rules; overhang rules vary. |
| Gross weight | 80,000 lbs on the Interstate system | Without a permit or state exception. |
| Single axle | 20,000 lbs | Federal Interstate limit. |
| Tandem axle | 34,000 lbs | Federal Interstate limit. |

The federal bridge formula also limits weight based on the number of axles and the distance between them. That is why a truck can be under 80,000 lbs and still be overweight on an axle group.

These numbers are a starting point. Confirm the current limits in every state you will drive through, because state roads and local roads can be stricter.

### Quick height math

On a standard flatbed with a deck height around 5 ft, a 13 ft 6 in limit leaves about 8 ft 6 in for freight. A step deck with a lower deck around 3 ft 6 in leaves about 10 ft. Measure your own equipment; deck heights vary.

## Divisible vs non-divisible loads

States generally issue OS/OW permits only for **non-divisible** loads: items that cannot be broken down without ruining them or taking unreasonable effort. A bulldozer or a 14-ft-wide tank qualifies. Fifty pallets that add up to 95,000 lbs do not; the answer there is a lighter load, not a permit.

Some states have exceptions for specific divisible commodities on specific routes (for example certain agricultural products or sealed containers near ports). These are state-specific; check before you count on them.

## How state permits work

Each state has a permit office, usually in its department of transportation or motor vehicles. In Texas, for example, the Texas Department of Motor Vehicles issues OS/OW permits. Common types:

- **Single-trip permits** for one move on a set route, valid for a few days.
- **Annual or period permits** for repeated loads within set dimensions.
- **Superload permits** for very large or heavy moves, often requiring an engineering review of bridges and a route survey.

What a permit application usually asks for:

1. Carrier name, USDOT number and insurance information
2. Truck and trailer details: plate, VIN, axle count and axle spacing
3. Load description and whether it is non-divisible
4. Overall dimensions: width, height, length, front and rear overhang
5. Gross weight and weight per axle or axle group
6. Origin, destination and requested route
7. Travel dates

The state may change your route to avoid low bridges or weight-restricted structures. **Follow the permitted route exactly.** A detour can void the permit.

## Conditions that come with the permit

Every permit has conditions printed on it. Common ones:

- **Travel time:** many states allow oversize movement only from sunrise to sunset, and some restrict weekends, holidays and rush hours in big cities.
- **Signs, flags and lights:** "OVERSIZE LOAD" banners on the front and rear, red or orange flags at the corners and extremities, and lights for night or limited-visibility rules where allowed.
- **Escorts (pilot cars):** required above certain widths, heights or lengths, which differ by state. Some states require a height pole on the lead car for tall loads, or police escorts for very large moves.
- **Weather:** many states prohibit movement in poor visibility, high winds or icy roads.- **Carry the permit:** keep it in the cab, paper or electronic depending on the state.

## Equipment for OS/OW work

The right trailer often decides whether a load needs a permit at all:

- **Step deck** for taller freight that would be over height on a flatbed.
- **Removable gooseneck (RGN) or lowboy** for heavy machinery and very tall items.
- **Stretch or extendable trailers** for long items like beams.
- **Extra axles** to spread weight and stay within axle limits.

Plus the gear: banners, flags, lights, and chains and binders rated for the load. Securement for heavy machinery has its own rules; see our [flatbed cargo securement guide](/blog/flatbed-cargo-securement.html).

## How to price an OS/OW load

Oversize loads take more time, more cost and more risk. Price all of it in. A hypothetical example for a 700-mile move through three states:

| Cost item | Hypothetical amount |
|---|---|
| Permits (three states) | $300 |
| Escort for part of the route | $600 |
| Extra time from daylight-only travel (one extra day) | $400 |
| Fuel at lower speeds and on the permitted route | $650 |
| Total extra cost vs a legal load | $1,950 |

If a legal flatbed load on the same lane paid $2,800, the oversize load would need to pay at least $4,750 just to match it, before you count the extra risk. Run your own figures in the [load profitability calculator](/load-profitability-calculator.html) and check your [cost per mile](/cost-per-mile-calculator.html).

Also ask the broker before you accept: who orders and pays for permits and escorts? Who pays if the route survey forces a longer route? Get it written on the rate confirmation. Our guide on [how to read a rate confirmation](/blog/how-to-read-a-rate-confirmation.html) shows what to look for.

## Pre-move checklist

- Measure the loaded height, width and length yourself
- Scale the loaded truck and check each axle group
- Permits for every state on the route, with correct dates
- Route reviewed for bridges, construction and curfews
- Escorts booked and briefed
- Banners, flags and lights installed and working
- Securement checked again within the first miles

Permit rules, legal limits and fees are set by each state and change often. Confirm with every state's permit office, FMCSA and your insurance agent before you move an oversize or overweight load.

## How Texas Solutions can help

Texas Solutions is a dispatch service, not a broker or a motor carrier. Our dispatchers find and negotiate loads that fit your equipment, handle broker packets and paperwork 24/7, and you approve every load. See our [dispatch services](/dispatch.html) or [talk to a dispatcher](/contact.html).

### Out-of-Service Criteria: What Puts a Truck or Driver Out of Service
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/out-of-service-criteria/
Published: 2026-10-21

An **out-of-service** (OOS) order is the most expensive result a roadside inspection can bring. The driver or truck is stopped until the problem is fixed, the load runs late, and your safety record takes a heavier hit than for an ordinary violation. Knowing the out-of-service criteria helps you catch these problems first.

## What the out-of-service criteria are

The **North American Standard Out-of-Service Criteria** are published by the Commercial Vehicle Safety Alliance (CVSA). They list the conditions that make a driver or vehicle an imminent hazard, so inspectors in the US, Canada and Mexico apply the same standard.

Two things to understand:

- **Not every violation is OOS.** Many violations are recorded and must be fixed, but you can keep driving. OOS conditions are the serious ones.
- **The criteria change.** CVSA reviews and updates them on a regular basis, usually yearly. The examples below are general; for exact measurements and current wording, check the current CVSA criteria or ask your shop.

## Common driver out-of-service conditions

| Area | Examples that can lead to driver OOS |
|---|---|
| Hours of service | Driving past the 11-hour, 14-hour or 60/70-hour limits; no record of duty status when required |
| Records | Falsified logs in certain situations; ELD problems without required backup records |
| License | No valid CDL, wrong class, suspended or revoked license, missing required endorsement |
| Medical | Not medically qualified in certain cases where required |
| Alcohol and drugs | Any detected alcohol or possession or use of drugs while on duty |
| Fitness | Driver too ill or fatigued to drive safely |

Hours-of-service OOS orders typically last until the driver has taken enough off-duty time to be legal. Our guide to [hours of service rules](/blog/hours-of-service-rules-explained-11-14-70-hour.html) helps you plan legal days.

## Common vehicle out-of-service conditions

| System | What can trigger OOS |
|---|---|
| Brakes | A certain percentage of brakes defective or out of adjustment; inoperative brakes on steering axle; major air leaks |
| Tires | Tread worn below the OOS limit (stricter on steer tires); flat or audibly leaking tires; exposed cords or bulges |
| Lights | Required lamps not working when lights are needed, such as at night |
| Coupling | Fifth wheel not locked or with serious defects; missing or damaged safety devices |
| Steering | Excessive steering wheel lash or loose components |
| Suspension | Broken leaf springs beyond limits; cracked or missing parts |
| Frame | Cracked or broken frame members beyond limits |
| Cargo securement | Not enough tiedowns, damaged tiedowns, or loads that can shift |
| Fuel and exhaust | Fuel leaks; exhaust leaks into the cab in certain cases |

Brakes are usually near the top of the list for vehicle OOS violations, so a good brake check on every pre-trip is one of the best habits you can build.

## What happens when you are placed out of service

1. **The officer completes a report** that lists the OOS violations.
2. **The driver or vehicle may not move** until the condition is corrected. For many vehicle defects that means an on-site repair by a mobile mechanic or a tow.
3. **The repair is documented.** Keep invoices and parts receipts.
4. **The report goes into FMCSA's data** and is weighted more heavily in your [CSA scores](/blog/csa-scores-explained.html).
5. **The carrier must certify repairs** and return the report as instructed, usually within a set number of days.

Operating a vehicle or driving in violation of an OOS order is a serious federal violation with large civil penalties and possible disqualification for drivers. Never move a truck under an OOS order unless an officer has cleared it.

## Worked example: the real cost of one OOS

Here is a hypothetical example to show why prevention pays. All figures are for illustration only.

- Load pays: $2,400
- Truck is placed OOS for a brake problem at 9 a.m.
- Mobile repair: $650, truck back on the road at 3 p.m.
- Six hours lost means a missed appointment; the receiver reschedules for next morning and you lose the reload you had planned. Say that costs $500 in lost margin.
- Total hit: about **$1,150**, plus a heavier violation on your record for the next two years.

A pre-trip check that found the problem the night before may have cost a fraction of that at a regular shop.

## How to avoid out-of-service violations

### Daily

- Walk around with lights on. Check every lamp.
- Look at tires: tread, sidewalls, inflation.
- Check brakes: listen for leaks, look at slack adjusters and chambers, test the low-air warning.
- Confirm the fifth wheel is locked and the kingpin is engaged.
- Check tiedowns and load after the first miles and at every stop as required for your freight. Open-deck loads need extra attention to tiedown count and condition.

### Weekly and monthly

- Keep a preventive maintenance schedule and stick to it. Our [maintenance budget calculator](/maintenance-budget-calculator.html) helps you set money aside.
- Replace tires before they reach the limit, not at it.
- Have brakes inspected and adjusted by a qualified technician.

### Paperwork and hours

- Keep your license, medical certificate and endorsements current.
- Make sure the ELD works and you know the malfunction procedure.
- Plan trips so you are not running out of hours far from parking.

## If you believe the OOS was wrong

Take photos, keep the report and get a written opinion from a mechanic if relevant. You can request a review of inaccurate records through FMCSA's DataQs system. Our guide on [how to dispute a violation with DataQs](/blog/how-to-dispute-a-violation-dataqs.html) walks through the process.

This guide is general information. Out-of-service criteria and penalties change, so confirm current rules with CVSA and FMCSA.

## How Texas Solutions can help

Texas Solutions is a dispatch service, not a broker or motor carrier. Our dispatchers find and negotiate loads, handle broker packets and paperwork, and work 24/7, while you approve every load. If you are placed out of service, we contact the broker, update the appointment and help re-plan your week. See our [dispatch services](/dispatch.html) or [talk to a dispatcher](/contact.html).

### New Entrant Safety Audit: How to Prepare and Pass
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/new-entrant-safety-audit-guide/
Published: 2026-10-21

The **new entrant safety audit** is FMCSA's first close look at how a new carrier runs safety. It is not a test of your driving. It is a records review, and most carriers who fail do so because a program was never set up, not because they drove unsafely. If you just got your authority, start preparing now.

## What the new entrant program is

When you get a USDOT number and begin interstate operations, you enter an 18-month monitoring period called the New Entrant Safety Assurance Program. During that window FMCSA watches your roadside inspections and crash record, and conducts a safety audit. If you pass the audit and stay out of trouble, you move to permanent status at the end of the period.

FMCSA generally aims to audit property carriers within the first 12 months. Some carriers hear nothing for months, then get a notice with a short deadline. FMCSA has also discussed changes to the new entrant process over the years, so check the current requirements on the FMCSA website.

If you are still setting up, our guide to [getting your MC number](/blog/how-to-get-mc-number-authority-owner-operator.html) covers the steps before this one.

## The areas the auditor reviews

The audit usually covers six areas:

1. **Driver qualification:** a complete DQ file for every driver, including you.
2. **Drug and alcohol testing:** for CDL drivers, a working testing program, random pool enrollment, and Clearinghouse use.
3. **Hours of service:** records of duty status, ELD data and supporting documents.
4. **Vehicle maintenance:** inspection, repair and maintenance records, annual inspections and driver vehicle inspection reports.
5. **Insurance:** proof of the required minimum financial responsibility.
6. **Accident register:** a record of DOT-recordable crashes, even if you have had none.

Hazmat carriers get additional review of hazmat registration, training and shipping papers.

## Violations that cause an automatic fail

FMCSA lists certain violations that, if found, fail the audit by themselves. The list appears in the safety audit evaluation criteria in 49 CFR Part 385 (confirm the current version with FMCSA), but in plain terms they cover:

- **No drug and alcohol testing program**, no random testing, or no pre-employment test before a driver performed safety-sensitive work.
- **Using a driver who tested positive or refused a test** without completing the return-to-duty process.
- **Using a driver without a valid CDL**, or with a suspended, revoked or disqualified license.
- **Using a driver without a current medical certificate.**
- **Operating without the required insurance.**
- **Not requiring drivers to keep hours of service records** or having no system for them.
- **Operating a vehicle placed out of service** before it was repaired.
- **No periodic (annual) inspection** of vehicles.
- Certain **hazmat** failures for hazmat carriers.

Notice the theme. Each of these is a missing system rather than a single bad day. One owner-operator who never enrolled in a random testing consortium can fail on that item alone, even with perfect logs.

## Safety audit checklist: documents to have ready

Gather these in one place, labelled by section, before any notice arrives.

**Company**
- [ ] USDOT and MC numbers, current MCS-150 information
- [ ] Proof of insurance and any required filings
- [ ] Accident register covering the past three years (or since you started)
- [ ] Hazmat registration and training records, if applicable

**Each driver**
- [ ] Complete DQ file (use the [driver qualification file checklist](/blog/driver-qualification-file-checklist.html))
- [ ] Current medical certificate and National Registry verification
- [ ] Valid CDL or license copy

**Drug and alcohol program (CDL drivers)**
- [ ] Written testing policy and proof each driver received it
- [ ] Consortium or third-party administrator enrollment for owner-operators
- [ ] Pre-employment negative results
- [ ] Random selection and testing records
- [ ] Clearinghouse registration, pre-employment and annual queries
- [ ] Supervisor reasonable suspicion training records, if you have supervisors

**Hours of service**
- [ ] ELD records for each driver, typically for the past six months
- [ ] Supporting documents such as fuel receipts, bills of lading and toll records
- [ ] ELD user manual, malfunction instruction sheet and blank paper logs in each truck

**Each vehicle**
- [ ] Maintenance file with vehicle identification, inspection and repair records
- [ ] Current annual inspection report
- [ ] Driver vehicle inspection reports and repair certifications for defects

For the testing setup, see the [drug and alcohol testing program](/blog/drug-and-alcohol-testing-program.html) guide. For daily inspection habits that feed your maintenance file, see the [pre-trip inspection checklist](/blog/pre-trip-inspection-checklist.html).
## How the audit goes, step by step

1. **Notice arrives** by mail or email with a date or document request. Read it closely for deadlines and the format they want.
2. **Organize and send documents** in the order requested. Label files clearly. Send what is asked, not your entire filing cabinet.
3. **Interview.** The auditor may ask how you dispatch, how you track hours, how you schedule maintenance and who handles testing. Answer honestly and briefly.
4. **Findings.** You will be told whether you passed and which violations, if any, were found. Even a pass can include violations you should fix.
5. **Follow-up.** If you failed, a written notice explains the corrective action plan deadline.

## If you fail: the corrective action plan

A failed audit is serious but usually fixable. You will get a deadline to submit a corrective action plan (the exact window depends on carrier type, so check your notice). A good plan:

- Names each violation found.
- Explains the cause in one or two sentences.
- Describes what you changed, with proof: an enrollment certificate, a new policy, an updated file, a maintenance schedule.
- Explains how you will prevent it from happening again, and who is responsible.

Submit it early, keep copies, and follow up to confirm it was accepted. Missing the deadline can lead to revocation of your new entrant registration. If the stakes are high, consider getting help from a compliance consultant or transportation attorney.

## How Texas Solutions can help

Texas Solutions is a dispatch service, not a broker or motor carrier. While you build your safety program, our dispatchers find and negotiate loads, handle broker packets and paperwork, and work 24/7, and you approve every load. New carriers can read about [dispatch for new authority](/dispatch-for-new-authority.html) or [talk to a dispatcher](/contact.html).

### DOT Physical and Medical Card: What Truck Drivers Should Know
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/medical-card-and-dot-physical/
Published: 2026-10-21

The **DOT physical** is a short exam with big consequences. Pass it and you get a medical examiner's certificate, the "medical card," that keeps you legal to drive. Let it lapse and your truck sits, no matter how good the load is. Here is what to expect and how to avoid surprises.

## Who needs a medical card

Federal medical standards (49 CFR 391.41 through 391.49) apply to drivers of commercial motor vehicles in interstate commerce. That generally includes:

- All CDL drivers in non-excepted interstate operations
- Non-CDL drivers of vehicles with a gross weight or rating over 10,001 pounds, which covers many [hotshot](/hotshot-dispatch.html) and [box truck](/box-truck-dispatch.html) operations
- Drivers of placarded hazmat vehicles and certain passenger vehicles

Intrastate drivers follow state rules, which are often similar but not identical.

## Who can do the exam

Only a medical examiner listed on the **National Registry of Certified Medical Examiners** (NRCME) can perform a DOT physical. That might be a physician, nurse practitioner, physician assistant, chiropractor or other licensed provider who completed FMCSA training and testing. Before you book, search the registry or ask the clinic to confirm.

Carriers must verify that the examiner is on the registry and keep proof in the [driver qualification file](/blog/driver-qualification-file-checklist.html).

## What happens at the exam

The visit usually takes under an hour. Expect:

1. **Health history form.** You complete the driver section of the exam report. Answer honestly. Leaving out a condition or medication can create bigger problems later.
2. **Vision test.** The federal standard requires at least 20/40 in each eye and with both eyes, with or without correction, a horizontal field of vision of at least 70 degrees in each eye, and the ability to recognize red, green and amber.
3. **Hearing test.** Usually a forced whisper test at about five feet, or an audiometer test. Hearing aids are allowed if you wear them while driving.
4. **Blood pressure and pulse.**
5. **Urinalysis.** This checks for signs of conditions such as diabetes or kidney problems. It is **not** a drug test. The DOT drug test is separate.
6. **Physical exam.** Eyes, ears, heart, lungs, abdomen, spine, extremities and neurological checks.

The examiner then decides: qualified for up to 24 months, qualified for a shorter period, determination pending, or not qualified.

## Conditions that commonly shorten a card

### High blood pressure

Blood pressure is the most common reason drivers get a shorter card. Under FMCSA's guidance, examiners generally issue a one-year card for mildly elevated readings, a short temporary card for higher readings while you get treatment, and do not certify at very high readings until they come down. Exact ranges are in FMCSA guidance, so check with your examiner.

Tips: take your medication as prescribed on exam day, avoid caffeine and nicotine beforehand, and arrive early so you are not rushing.

### Diabetes

Diabetes controlled by diet or oral medication is generally handled by examiner judgment. Insulin-treated diabetes is allowed under a 2018 rule, but the driver needs a completed assessment form from the treating clinician before the exam, and the card is limited to a maximum of 12 months. Confirm current forms and timing with FMCSA.

### Vision in one eye

FMCSA created an alternative vision standard that lets some drivers who do not meet the vision standard in one eye be certified, with an evaluation by an eye specialist first. Ask your examiner and check FMCSA for current details.

### Sleep apnea, heart conditions, medications

These are judgment calls. Bring records: a CPAP compliance report, a cardiologist's clearance letter, a medication list with doses. Missing paperwork is a leading cause of a "determination pending" result and a return visit.

## Medical card checklist

Before the exam:
- [ ] Confirm the examiner is on the National Registry
- [ ] Bring your driver's license and glasses, contacts or hearing aids
- [ ] Bring a list of all medications and dosages
- [ ] Bring specialist records for any ongoing condition (CPAP report, cardiology letter, insulin assessment form)
- [ ] Take regular medications as prescribed

After the exam:
- [ ] Get a copy of your medical examiner's certificate
- [ ] Give a copy to your carrier for the DQ file (or file it yourself if you are the carrier)
- [ ] Confirm your state licensing agency has your updated medical status if you hold a CDL
- [ ] Put the expiration date in your calendar with a 30- and 60-day reminder

## How the card reaches your state

CDL holders must also self-certify their type of operation with their state and keep their medical status current. FMCSA has been moving to electronic transmission of exam results from examiners to FMCSA and then to state licensing agencies. That changes how drivers submit proof and whether a paper card is the primary record. Rules on whether you must still carry the paper card or submit it yourself have been changing, so confirm the current process with your state licensing agency and FMCSA. Keeping a copy in the truck costs nothing.

## Worked example: plan around the expiration

Say your card expires on March 15 and you are an owner-operator running 2,500 miles a week.

- Book the exam in mid-January, about 60 days out.
- If the exam goes smoothly, you are done with weeks to spare.
- If the examiner needs a specialist letter, you still have about eight weeks to get it.

Compare that to booking on March 10. A pending result could leave you unable to drive. At a hypothetical $1,500 of net profit per week, a two-week gap costs about $3,000 plus any loads you had to cancel. Plan home time and routes around the appointment, and use the [hours of service calculator](/hours-of-service-calculator.html) to fit it into your schedule.

Our dispatchers find and negotiate loads, handle broker packets and paperwork, and work 24/7, and you approve every load. ### Load-to-Truck Ratio Explained for Owner-Operators
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/load-to-truck-ratio-explained/
Published: 2026-10-21

Spot rates go up and down for a simple reason: supply and demand. The **load-to-truck ratio** is one of the quickest ways to see that balance. It tells you whether a market has more freight than trucks, or more trucks than freight, and that helps you decide where to go and how hard to negotiate.

## What the load-to-truck ratio means

The ratio compares two counts from load board postings:

- **Loads:** freight posted by brokers and shippers looking for a truck.
- **Trucks:** capacity posted by carriers looking for a load.

The basic formula is:

**Load-to-truck ratio = posted loads / posted trucks**

The ratio is usually split by equipment type (dry van, reefer, flatbed and so on) and by area (region, state or metro market).

| Ratio | What it suggests |
|---|---|
| Well above the market's normal | Tight capacity; carriers have more leverage |
| Around the market's normal | Balanced market |
| Well below the market's normal | Loose capacity; brokers have more leverage |

## Why it moves spot rates

When a broker has a load and few trucks are available, they have to raise the offer to get it covered. When many trucks are posted and waiting, the broker can hold the rate down because someone will take it.

That is why the ratio and spot rates tend to move in the same direction over time. The ratio is not a price, but it is a strong hint about which way prices are leaning.

## How to read it the right way

The ratio is useful, but only if you know its limits.

### Compare like with like

Each load board counts postings in its own way, and its users are not the whole market. A ratio from one source cannot be compared directly with a ratio from another. Stick to one source and compare:

- the same market over time (this week vs. last month), and
- different markets in the same week, for the same trailer type.

### Each trailer type has its own normal

Van, reefer and flatbed ratios sit at very different levels because carriers in each segment post trucks differently. A flatbed ratio that looks huge next to a van ratio may be perfectly normal for flatbed. Compare each type only with itself.

### It only sees the spot market

Contract freight, dedicated lanes and direct shipper loads are not posted on boards. The ratio shows spot market pressure, not the entire freight economy.

### Postings are not perfect

The same load can be posted by several brokers, and some posted loads are already covered. Trucks may stay posted after they book. Small markets can swing wildly from one day to the next. Look for trends over several days, not a single snapshot.

## How owner-operators use it

### 1. Pick where to deliver

Before you accept a load, check the ratio in the delivery market. A strong outbound ratio means a reload is more likely, often at a better rate. A weak one means you should ask more on the inbound load, or plan a longer reposition. Our guide on how to [plan a profitable round trip](/blog/plan-a-profitable-round-trip.html) walks through pricing the full loop.

### 2. Negotiate with confidence

If the ratio in the pickup market is high and climbing, the broker likely has fewer trucks to choose from. That is a good time to counter-offer. If the ratio is low, expect less room. See [how to negotiate freight rates](/blog/how-to-negotiate-freight-rates.html).

### 3. Time your home time

When ratios are low across your lanes, the truck earns less per day. That can be a sensible time for home time or maintenance. Our [freight market calendar](/blog/freight-market-calendar.html) shows the months when markets usually loosen.

### 4. Spot regional shifts

Seasonal freight, such as produce or holiday retail, shows up as rising ratios in certain regions before rates fully catch up. Watching those shifts can help you get the truck in position early.

## Worked example (hypothetical)

You are delivering a dry van load and choosing between two cities for your next pickup. You use one load board for both checks.

| Market | Van loads posted | Vans posted | Ratio | Its usual ratio |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| City A | 1,200 | 300 | 4.0 | about 3.0 |
| City B | 900 | 450 | 2.0 | about 2.5 |

City A has a ratio above its normal level, so capacity looks tight. City B is below its normal level, so trucks are competing harder. All else being equal, City A is the better place to look for a reload, and the inbound load to City B should pay extra to make up for a weaker outbound market.

Before deciding, also check the deadhead from your delivery to each city and the rates actually being paid, then run the numbers in the [load profitability calculator](/load-profitability-calculator.html).

## Watch rates alongside the ratio

The ratio tells you which way the market is leaning. Posted and paid rates tell you where it actually is. Use both together:

- **Ratio rising, rates flat:** rates may follow soon, so hold firm on your counter-offers.
- **Ratio falling, rates still high:** the window may be closing, so book good loads while you can.
- **Ratio and rates both low:** focus on covering costs, shorter trips toward stronger markets, and steady broker relationships.

Neither number matters without your own cost per mile. A busy market only helps if the load pays more than it costs you to run it.

## Quick checklist before you trust the ratio

- [ ] Same data source for every comparison.
- [ ] Same equipment type.
- [ ] Compared to that market's recent history, not a fixed number.
- [ ] Looked at a trend over several days.
- [ ] Checked actual posted rates and deadhead, not just the ratio.

## How Texas Solutions can help
