Our dispatchers watch market conditions every day, find and negotiate loads, and handle broker packets and paperwork 24/7, while you approve every load. If you want market-aware load planning, see our [dispatch services](/dispatch.html).

### Lease vs Buy a Truck: Which Is Better for Owner-Operators?
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/lease-vs-buy-a-truck/
Published: 2026-10-21

The **lease vs buy a truck** decision shapes your cash flow, your repair risk and how much your business is worth in five years. Neither choice is always right. This guide explains the main options, what each one costs in practice, and how to compare them with a simple hypothetical example. It is general education, so have a CPA and, for contracts, an attorney review your specific offers.

## The main ways to get a truck

- **Buy with cash.** You own it outright. No payment, but your cash is tied up in the truck.
- **Buy with a loan.** You own it, the lender holds a lien until it is paid off. See [how to finance a semi truck](/blog/how-to-finance-a-semi-truck.html).
- **Lease from a leasing company.** You pay to use the truck for a set term. Some leases include maintenance (often called full-service), others do not. Some are structured with a set end value you may need to cover.
- **Lease-purchase through a carrier.** You lease a truck from or through a carrier, usually while hauling under that carrier, with a path to ownership at the end.

Each version has many variations, so always ask for the full contract, not a summary.

## Buying: pros and cons

**Pros**
- Usually the lowest total cost if you keep the truck for years
- You build equity and can sell or trade the truck later
- Freedom to choose your shop, your specs and how you run
- Once paid off, your cost per mile drops sharply

**Cons**
- Bigger upfront cash: down payment, taxes, registration
- You pay for every repair, including major engine and aftertreatment work
- Resale value is uncertain
- Credit requirements can be tough for new businesses

## Leasing: pros and cons

**Pros**
- Lower upfront cash in many cases
- Full-service leases can bundle maintenance and sometimes a replacement truck during repairs
- Predictable monthly costs
- Easier to move into newer equipment at the end of the term

**Cons**
- Usually a higher total cost over time
- Little or no equity at the end, depending on the lease type
- Mileage limits, condition rules and early termination fees
- With some carrier lease-purchase deals, the same company controls your freight and your truck, which can limit your choices

## Questions to ask before signing any lease

1. What is the total amount I will pay over the full term?
2. Is there a mileage cap, and what does each extra mile cost?
3. What maintenance is included, and what is excluded (tires, aftertreatment, accidents)?
4. Who pays for repairs when the truck is down, and is there a replacement unit?
5. What happens if I end the lease early, or if I am injured or sick?
6. What do I owe at the end, and can I buy the truck? At what price?
7. For carrier lease-purchase: am I required to haul only for this carrier, how is my pay calculated, and what deductions come out of settlements?
8. Can I have an attorney review the contract before I sign?

If a company will not give you time to review the contract, treat that as a warning sign.

## Worked example: three-year cost comparison

All numbers below are **hypothetical** and simplified to show how to compare. Real offers will differ.

| Item (36 months) | Buy with loan | Full-service lease |
|---|---|---|
| Upfront cash | $20,000 down payment | $5,000 deposit |
| Monthly payment | $2,100 | $3,000 |
| Payments over 36 months | $75,600 | $108,000 |
| Repairs and maintenance (estimated) | $27,000 | $6,000 (items not covered) |
| Total cash out | $122,600 | $119,000 |
| Equity at month 36 (estimated truck value minus loan balance) | $30,000 | $0 |
| Net cost after equity | about $92,600 | about $119,000 |

In this example, leasing uses less cash up front and has steadier costs, but buying ends up about $26,000 cheaper once you count equity. Change any input, such as a big unexpected engine repair or a weak resale market, and the answer can flip. Use the [truck loan calculator](/truck-loan-calculator.html) and [maintenance budget calculator](/maintenance-budget-calculator.html) to plug in your own numbers.

## Convert both options to cost per mile

Whatever you choose, the payment has to fit your freight. Divide the monthly payment plus expected repairs by your realistic monthly miles. At a hypothetical 9,000 miles a month:

- Buy: ($2,100 + $750 repairs) / 9,000 = about $0.32 per mile
- Lease: ($3,000 + about $167 uncovered items) / 9,000 = about $0.35 per mile

Then add that figure to fuel, insurance and your other costs in the [cost per mile calculator](/cost-per-mile-calculator.html). If your rates do not cover it with room for profit, neither option works yet.

## Which one fits you

**Buying often fits when you:**
- Have a cash reserve for repairs, not just a down payment
- Plan to keep the truck for several years
- Have mechanical knowledge or a trusted shop
- Want full control over where and how you run

**Leasing often fits when you:**
- Have limited cash but steady freight
- Want predictable costs and less repair risk
- Prefer to cycle into newer equipment
- Have read and understood every term of the contract

## How Texas Solutions can help

Texas Solutions is a dispatch service, not a lessor, lender, broker or motor carrier. Whether you own or lease, our dispatchers find and negotiate loads that cover your real cost per mile, handle broker packets and paperwork, and work 24/7 while you approve every load. See our [dispatch services](/dispatch.html) or [talk to a dispatcher](/contact.html).

### How to Keep Your MC Authority Active and in Good Standing
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/keep-your-mc-authority-active/
Published: 2026-10-21

Getting your authority is the first hurdle. Learning how to **keep your MC authority active** is what lets you keep hauling. Most revocations and deactivations come from missed filings, not bad driving, and every one of them is avoidable with a simple calendar.

## Authority status vs. USDOT status

Two records matter, and they can fail separately:

- **USDOT number:** your carrier registration. It can be **deactivated**, for example if you miss your biennial MCS-150 update.
- **Operating authority (MC number):** permission to haul regulated freight for hire across state lines. It can be **revoked**, most often for insurance or process agent problems.

Brokers check both. A truck with an active USDOT number but revoked authority cannot legally haul most interstate brokered freight.

## The filings that keep you active

### 1. Liability insurance on file

Your insurer files proof of coverage with FMCSA (commonly a BMC-91 or BMC-91X form for liability). If the policy is cancelled, the insurer notifies FMCSA, and if no new filing arrives before the cancellation date, your authority can be revoked.

- Pay premiums on time and set up auto-pay if you can.
- When switching insurers, make sure the new filing is in place **before** the old one cancels.
- Keep cargo coverage too. It is not always required by FMCSA for general freight, but most brokers require it. Ask your insurance agent what limits brokers in your freight usually expect.

### 2. BOC-3 process agent filing

A BOC-3 names a process agent in each state where you operate. Without it, new authority will not be granted, and a missing or cancelled BOC-3 can put existing authority at risk. Read [BOC-3 filing explained](/blog/boc-3-filing-explained.html).

### 3. MCS-150 biennial update

Every carrier with a USDOT number must update its MCS-150 every two years, even if nothing changed. The filing month and year are based on the last two digits of your USDOT number:

- The **last digit** sets the month (1 = January, 2 = February ... 9 = September, 0 = October).
- The **next-to-last digit** sets the year: odd digit, file in odd-numbered years; even digit, file in even-numbered years.

Missing it can lead to deactivation of your USDOT number and civil penalties. Also update the MCS-150 whenever your address, phone, email, number of trucks or mileage changes. Confirm the current schedule on FMCSA's website.

### 4. UCR registration

Most interstate carriers, brokers and freight forwarders must register for the Unified Carrier Registration program every year. Many states enforce it at roadside. See our [UCR registration guide](/blog/ucr-registration-guide.html).

### 5. Drug and alcohol program and Clearinghouse

CDL drivers in safety-sensitive jobs need a DOT drug and alcohol testing program. An owner-operator with their own authority usually joins a consortium. You also need to be registered in the FMCSA Drug and Alcohol Clearinghouse and run the required queries.

### 6. Taxes and registration

These do not keep the MC itself active, but you cannot run legally without them:

- **Form 2290 (HVUT)** each tax year. See [how to file Form 2290](/blog/how-to-file-form-2290.html).
- **IRP** apportioned plates and **IFTA** quarterly fuel tax returns.

## A simple compliance calendar

| When | Task |
|---|---|
| Every quarter | IFTA return; review insurance billing; check FMCSA status page |
| Every month | Review new roadside inspections and DataQs status |
| Each year (by your state's IRP date) | IRP renewal |
| Each year (by IRS deadline) | Form 2290 and stamped Schedule 1 |
| Each year (before enforcement starts) | UCR registration |
| Each year | Annual vehicle inspections; driver MVR review and Clearinghouse query |
| Every 2 years (your USDOT month) | MCS-150 biennial update |
| As needed | MCS-150 update for any change; new BOC-3 if your agent changes |

Put each date in your phone calendar with a two-week reminder.

## The first 18 months of a new authority

New carriers are in the **New Entrant Safety Assurance Program** for their first 18 months. FMCSA conducts a safety audit, usually within the first 12 months, to check records like driver qualification files, hours of service, maintenance, drug and alcohol testing and insurance. Certain violations are treated as automatic failures. Our guide to the [new entrant safety audit](/blog/new-entrant-safety-audit-guide.html) explains how to prepare.

## Warning signs your authority is at risk

- A letter or email from FMCSA about a missing filing or upcoming revocation.
- An insurance cancellation notice for non-payment.
- Your process agent company closing or cancelling service.
- A broker setup rejected for "authority inactive" or "insurance not on file."
- Your USDOT status showing "inactive" on the public lookup.

Act on any of these the same day. Most problems are much easier to fix before the revocation date than after.

## If your authority was revoked

Reinstatement usually means fixing the cause (new insurance filing, new BOC-3, updated MCS-150), filing the reinstatement request and paying FMCSA's fee. Brokers often see the gap and may ask questions. If your authority has been revoked for a long time, or other problems exist, talk to FMCSA directly or to a compliance professional about your options.

Also protect your FMCSA login. Keep your portal access, email and phone on file current, because FMCSA notices go there. Watch for scam emails and calls claiming to be FMCSA and asking for payment.

This is general information, not legal advice. Fees, forms and procedures change, so confirm current requirements with FMCSA.

## How Texas Solutions can help

Texas Solutions is a dispatch service, not a broker or motor carrier. Our dispatchers find and negotiate loads, handle broker packets and paperwork, and work 24/7, while you approve every load. Starting out? See our [new MC guide](/new-mc.html) or [talk to a dispatcher](/contact.html).

### How to Vet a Freight Broker Before You Haul Their Load
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/how-to-vet-a-freight-broker/
Published: 2026-10-21

Every load you haul is a bet that the broker will pay. Learning **how to vet a freight broker** turns that bet into an informed decision. A few minutes of checks before booking can save you from slow payers, unfair contracts and outright fraud.

## Why vetting matters

When you haul for a broker, you usually extend credit: you deliver now and get paid later. If the broker is slow, disputes everything or goes out of business, you carry the loss. Fraudsters also impersonate real brokers, so a familiar name is not proof. Vetting has two goals: confirm the broker is real and legitimate, and confirm they are likely to pay on time.

## Step 1: Check authority with FMCSA

Search the broker's MC or USDOT number in FMCSA's public records and confirm:

- **Broker authority is active.** Make sure it is broker authority, not only carrier authority. A company with only carrier authority should not be brokering your load.
- **Financial security is on file.** Property brokers must keep a surety bond (BMC-84) or trust fund (BMC-85). The required amount is currently $75,000. Confirm the current figure and status with FMCSA.
- **Legal name and address** match the rate con and setup documents.
- **How long the authority has been active,** and whether it has been revoked or reinstated.

Pending revocation, a cancelled bond or a mismatch in name or address is a reason to stop and ask questions.

## Step 2: Check credit and days to pay

Authority tells you a broker is licensed. Credit tells you whether they pay.

- Run a credit check through your factoring company or a credit service before each load
- Look at average days to pay, not only an approval
- Ask your factor whether the broker has payment complaints or fraud warnings
- Talk to other carriers you trust about their experience

If your factoring company will not approve a broker, take that seriously. Our guide on [working with a factoring company](/blog/working-with-a-factoring-company.html) explains how credit checks fit into your routine.

## Step 3: Verify contact details

Impersonation is common, so verify the people, not just the company.

- Compare the phone number and email domain to the broker's official records and known website
- Watch for free email accounts or domains with a small spelling change
- Call the broker's main number from official records to confirm the agent and load are real
- Be careful when a broker contacts you first with an urgent, high-paying load

See [double brokering and freight fraud](/blog/double-brokering-and-freight-fraud.html) for the common scams that rely on fake contact details.

## Step 4: Read the broker-carrier agreement

The setup agreement governs every load you haul for that broker. Read it before signing, and look closely at:

- **Payment terms:** standard days to pay, quick-pay fees, required documents
- **Fines and deductions:** late fees, tracking failures, missing paperwork
- **Claims:** can they hold payment or deduct claims from unrelated loads?
- **Cargo liability limits** and insurance requirements
- **Non-solicitation:** restrictions on working directly with their shippers
- **Indemnity and dispute terms**

You can ask for changes. Have an attorney review agreements you sign often or that feel one-sided. Our guide on [broker setup and rate confirmations](/blog/broker-setup-rate-confirmation-spot-vs-contract.html) covers the packet process, and [cargo claims](/blog/cargo-claims-guide.html) explains why claim terms matter.

## Step 5: Watch behavior on the first loads

How a broker acts tells you a lot:

- Do they send a complete rate con promptly, matching what you agreed?
- Do they answer the phone after hours when a problem comes up?
- Do they pay detention and TONU when terms are met?
- Do they pay on time without repeated follow-up?

Keep notes. Over a few loads you will know who is worth repeat business.

## Broker vetting scorecard

Use a simple scorecard to make the decision consistent. Hypothetical example scoring a new broker, 1 point per item:

| Check | Result | Point |
|---|---|---|
| Active broker authority | Yes | 1 |
| Bond or trust on file | Yes | 1 |
| Name and address match rate con | Yes | 1 |
| Credit approved by factor | Yes | 1 |
| Days to pay within your limit | Slow | 0 |
| Contacts verified via official records | Yes | 1 |
| Agreement terms acceptable | Yes | 1 |
| Rate in line with market | Yes | 1 |

Score: 7 of 8. A sensible rule might be: 8 means book, 6-7 means book with caution and a smaller exposure, under 6 means pass. Set your own thresholds, but any failure on authority, bond or verification should be an automatic no.

## Red flags that should stop a booking

- Broker authority inactive, pending revocation or missing bond
- Contact details that do not match official records
- Rate far above market with pressure to commit fast
- Refusal to send a written rate con before dispatch
- Request for an upfront fee from you
- BOL at pickup showing a different broker
- Agreement letting them withhold payment on all loads for any dispute

## Balance risk and opportunity

Vetting is not about avoiding every new broker. It is about knowing your exposure. Diversify across several reliable brokers so one slow payer does not stall your cash flow, and use market rate data so you are not tempted by bait offers. Our guide on [how to negotiate freight rates](/blog/how-to-negotiate-freight-rates.html) helps you recognize a fair rate on a lane.

## How Texas Solutions can help

Texas Solutions is a dispatch service, not a broker or motor carrier. Our dispatchers check broker authority, credit and contact details before booking, negotiate rates and terms, and handle broker packets and paperwork 24/7, and you approve every load. See our [dispatch services](/dispatch.html) or [talk to a dispatcher](/contact.html).

### How to Read a Rate Confirmation Before You Sign It
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/how-to-read-a-rate-confirmation/
Published: 2026-10-21

A **rate confirmation** (often called a rate con) is the document a broker sends after you agree on a load. It spells out what you will haul, where, when and for how much, and once you sign it, it is the paper you will rely on to get paid. Reading it carefully takes five minutes and can save you hundreds of dollars in disputes.

## What a rate confirmation is and why it matters

When you set up with a broker, you sign a broker-carrier agreement that covers the general relationship. The rate con is the load-level agreement on top of that. It is what your factoring company, your bookkeeper and the broker's accounts payable team will look at when your invoice comes in.

That means anything not written on the rate con is at risk. If the broker said "we pay detention after two hours" on the phone but the rate con says nothing, you may end up arguing for money you earned. For a broader look at how broker setup and spot versus contract freight fit together, see our guide on [broker setup and rate confirmations](/blog/broker-setup-rate-confirmation-spot-vs-contract.html).

## The header: who you are dealing with

Start at the top and confirm:

- **Broker legal name and MC number.** It should match the company you negotiated with. Look the MC up with FMCSA to confirm the broker authority is active.
- **Contact details.** The phone number and email domain should match what the broker uses elsewhere, not a free email account or a lookalike domain.
- **Your carrier name, MC and DOT number.** A wrong carrier name can delay payment, especially if you factor.
- **Load or reference number.** You will need this on your invoice and for every call about the load.

If any of these look off, stop. A mismatch is one of the most common warning signs of fraud, covered in our guide to [double brokering and freight fraud](/blog/double-brokering-and-freight-fraud.html).

## Pickup and delivery details

Check each stop:

- Facility name and full address
- Appointment date and time, or the FCFS (first come, first served) window
- Pickup number, PO number or other reference the shipper will ask for
- Number of stops, and whether extra stops are paid

Compare this to what you were told. A "live load" that turns out to be a drop, or one stop that turns into three, changes your day and should change the rate.

## Commodity, weight and equipment

Make sure the rate con lists:

- **Commodity.** Know what you are hauling. High-value or theft-target freight may need extra security steps, and some commodities need special permits or endorsements.
- **Weight.** Confirm it is legal for your truck and leaves room for fuel. An overweight surprise at the scale is your problem, not the broker's.
- **Equipment and requirements.** Trailer type and length, temperature setting for reefer, tarps or straps for flatbed, load locks, team requirement, and any special instructions.

## The money section

This is the part most carriers read first, but read it fully:

| Item | What to check |
|---|---|
| Linehaul | Matches the agreed amount |
| Fuel surcharge | Included in the total or listed separately |
| Total rate | Equals what you accepted |
| Extra stops | Rate per stop, if any |
| Detention | Free time and hourly rate |
| Layover | Amount per day |
| TONU | Amount if the load is cancelled after dispatch |
| Lumper | Who pays and how you get reimbursed |

### A quick worked example

Hypothetical example: you agree to $2,400 all-in for a 750-mile load, plus detention at $50 per hour after 2 hours free. The rate con shows $2,400 but no detention line. If the driver waits 5 hours at the receiver, that is 3 billable hours, or $150. Without the detention terms on the rate con, you may only collect if the broker agrees to amend it. The fix takes one email before you sign. You can model wait-time pay with our [detention pay calculator](/detention-pay-calculator.html), and see [how to get detention paid](/blog/how-to-get-detention-paid.html) for the full process.

## The fine print: payment terms, fines and rules

The bottom of the rate con, or an attached page, often carries terms that cost money.

- **Payment terms.** Standard days to pay, quick-pay options and their fees, and the documents required with your invoice.
- **Fines and deductions.** Late fees for missed appointments, charges for failure to check in, deductions for missing tracking updates or late paperwork.
- **Tracking requirements.** Many brokers require an app or ELD tracking link. Know what happens if tracking drops.
- **No re-brokering clause.** Standard and fair. You are agreeing to haul it on your own authority with your own truck.
- **Claims and liability language.** Note any cargo value limits or claims terms. Questions about liability are worth running past your insurance agent or attorney.
- **Paperwork deadlines.** Some brokers require the BOL or POD within a set number of days to avoid a fee.

## A 10-point rate con checklist

Before you sign, confirm:

1. Broker name and MC match the company you negotiated with
2. Your company name, MC and DOT are correct
3. Pickup and delivery addresses, dates and times are right
4. All reference numbers are present
5. Commodity and weight are listed and legal for your setup
6. Equipment and special requirements are clear
7. Total rate matches the agreement
8. Detention, layover, TONU and lumper terms are written in
9. Payment terms and any quick-pay fees are understood
10. Fines, tracking and paperwork rules are acceptable

If any item is wrong or missing, email the broker and ask for a revised rate con. Do not sign one version and rely on a promise to fix it later.

## What to do after you sign

- Send the signed copy back from your business email and keep it with the load file.
- Give the driver the pickup number, appointment times and special instructions.
- Note detention start and stop times and get in-and-out times on the BOL.
- Build your invoice packet: signed rate con, signed BOL or POD, and receipts for any lumper or accessorial.

Clean paperwork is the fastest route to getting paid, whether you bill brokers yourself or work with a factoring company. Our guide on [freight factoring for owner-operators](/blog/freight-factoring-for-owner-operators-explained.html) explains how that packet moves through funding.

## How Texas Solutions can help

Texas Solutions is a dispatch service, not a broker or motor carrier. Our dispatchers find and negotiate loads, read every rate con against what was agreed, handle broker packets and paperwork 24/7, and you approve every load before it is booked. Learn more about our [dispatch services](/dispatch.html) or [talk to a dispatcher](/contact.html).

### How to Get Loads With a New MC Number: A Guide for New Authority Carriers
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/how-to-get-loads-with-new-mc-number/
Published: 2026-10-21

You have the truck, the insurance and an active MC. Now the hard part: **how to get loads with a new MC number**. Many brokers will not book a carrier until the authority is a few months old, and every broker has its own setup process. This guide is the step-by-step plan we use for **loads for new authority carriers**, whether you run a semi, a hotshot or a box truck.

## Step 1: build one complete broker setup packet

Do this once, before you need a load. Keep it as a single PDF and as separate files.

- MC authority letter (or a screenshot of active authority on FMCSA).
- W-9 in the exact legal name on your authority.
- Certificate of insurance from your agent, with auto liability and cargo limits listed. Ask your agent how fast they can issue certificates naming each broker.
- Notice of assignment and letter of release, if you use a factoring company.
- Bank details for payment, if you do not factor.
- A short carrier profile: equipment, trailer length, lanes, contact phone and email.

A packet that is complete the first time is the quickest way through broker onboarding. Missing documents are the most common reason a new carrier waits days for setup. That is why **broker setup packet help** is the first thing we do for a new client.

## Step 2: find brokers that accept new authority

Brokers fall into three groups:

1. **Will not book new MCs** until the authority reaches a set age.
2. **Will book new MCs** if the packet is complete and insurance is verified.
3. **Will book new MCs on certain freight** (often less time-sensitive or lower value loads) while you build history.

Your job is to find groups 2 and 3 and get set up with them before you need a load. Ask directly when you call: "Do you work with new authority?" You save more time asking that up front than you spend on setups that go nowhere.

## Step 3: use load boards the right way

Load boards are where most new carriers find their first loads. Filter for brokers that show they accept new authority, and call fast: good loads go in minutes. Read our [load board guide](/blog/truck-loads-and-load-boards-guide.html) and [best load boards for owner-operators](/blog/best-load-boards-for-owner-operators.html).

## Step 4: pick first lanes that set up the next load

Do not chase the single highest rate. Pick lanes that deliver into markets with plenty of outbound freight, so the reload is easy. Use the [deadhead miles calculator](/deadhead-miles-calculator.html) to see what an empty leg really costs.

## Step 5: negotiate, even with a new MC

A new MC does not have to mean the lowest rate. Know your [cost per mile](/cost-per-mile-calculator.html), ask for more on short-notice loads, and walk away from freight that does not cover your costs. See [how to negotiate freight rates](/blog/how-to-negotiate-freight-rates.html).

## Step 6: deliver perfectly and get rebooked

For the first months, every load is an audition. Be on time, answer check calls, send clear photos of the bill of lading and paperwork the same day. Brokers rebook carriers who make their job easy, and repeat freight is how a new authority stops depending on load boards.

## Common mistakes new authority carriers make

- Waiting until the authority is active to start broker setups.
- Taking every cheap load to "build history" and running at a loss.
- Hauling under someone else's MC: it is risky and does not build your own record.
- Paying a large upfront fee to anyone who promises guaranteed loads. Read [how to avoid truck dispatch scams](/blog/how-to-choose-a-truck-dispatcher-avoid-scams.html).

## When new authority truck dispatch helps

If you would rather drive than spend the day calling brokers, a dispatcher who works with new MC numbers can take over steps 1 to 5. At Texas Solutions we:

- Prepare your packet and handle broker setups.
- Target brokers that accept new authority for your equipment.
- Negotiate every load and plan lanes to keep deadhead down.
- Handle rate confirmations, invoicing and factoring paperwork.
- Answer 24/7 by call, text or WhatsApp.

Your first load is dispatched free. After that, the fee is 5% of weekly gross for OTR semis, 7% for hotshots and 8% for box trucks, with no setup fee and no long-term contract. No one can guarantee loads or rates. See [dispatch for new authority](/dispatch-for-new-authority.html), or if you have not filed yet, [MC number and authority setup](/trucking-authority-setup.html).

### How to Get Detention Paid: A Step-by-Step Guide for Carriers
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/how-to-get-detention-paid/
Published: 2026-10-21

Long waits at shippers and receivers burn hours you could be driving and money you could be earning. **Detention pay** is the compensation for that wait, but it rarely pays itself. Getting it requires terms agreed in advance, clean documentation and fast follow-up.

## What detention pay is

Detention is a charge for time spent at a pickup or delivery beyond the free time allowed. A typical arrangement says something like: "two hours free, then a set hourly rate." The hourly rate, free-time window and any daily cap are negotiated and should appear on the rate confirmation.

Detention matters because your hours of service keep running while you sit at a dock. Under the federal 14-hour rule, on-duty waiting time eats into your driving window, so a long wait can push your next load back by a day. Our guide to [hours of service rules](/blog/hours-of-service-rules-explained-11-14-70-hour.html) explains how that clock works.

## Step 1: Get the terms in writing before pickup

Most denied detention claims fail here. Before you sign the rate con, confirm:

- **Free time** at each stop (for example, 2 hours)
- **Hourly rate** after free time
- **Billing increments** (full hour, half hour or by the minute)
- **Daily cap** if any
- **Notification rule**, such as "notify within 30 minutes of free time expiring"
- **Proof required**, such as signed in-and-out times on the BOL

If detention is missing from the rate con, ask the broker to add it. Our guide on [how to read a rate confirmation](/blog/how-to-read-a-rate-confirmation.html) covers the other lines to check at the same time.

## Step 2: Arrive on time and check in properly

Detention policies usually require that you arrive on time for your appointment. An early arrival does not normally start the clock early, and a late arrival can void detention entirely.

- Check in with security or the shipping office as soon as you arrive.
- Get a check-in time recorded: a gate ticket, a sign-in sheet entry or a timestamp on paperwork.
- Take a photo of the sign-in sheet or gate ticket if allowed.
- Make sure your ELD shows you on duty at the facility.

## Step 3: Notify the broker before free time runs out

Do not wait until you leave to mention detention. When you are getting close to the end of free time, send the broker a short message by email or their load app:

"Load #12345: checked in at 08:00 for an 08:00 appointment, still not loaded. Free time expires at 10:00. Please note detention will start then."

This does two things. It meets the notification requirement many brokers have, and it gives the broker a chance to push the facility. Send updates if the wait drags on, and save every message.

## Step 4: Get out-time documented

When you are released, get the facility to write or stamp the out time on the BOL, with a signature if possible. Combined with your in time, this is your primary proof. Supporting evidence includes:

- ELD logs showing your location and duty status
- GPS or tracking app history
- Timestamped photos
- Your written notifications to the broker

If the facility refuses to note times, write them on your copy, note the refusal and tell the broker right away.

## Step 5: Invoice detention promptly with proof

Bill detention with the load, not weeks later. Your detention request should include:

- Load number and stop
- Appointment time, check-in time and check-out time
- Free time and billable time
- Rate and total amount
- Copies of the BOL with times, and your notification messages

### Worked example

Hypothetical example: your rate con says 2 hours free, then $50 per hour, billed in full hours. Appointment is 08:00. You check in at 07:50, are loaded and released at 13:10.

- Clock starts at the appointment: 08:00
- Time on site counted: 08:00 to 13:10 = 5 hours 10 minutes
- Minus free time: 5:10 - 2:00 = 3 hours 10 minutes
- Billed in full hours: 3 hours
- Detention: 3 x $50 = **$150**

Run your own numbers with the [detention pay calculator](/detention-pay-calculator.html).

## Common reasons detention gets denied

- No detention terms on the rate con
- Late arrival or missed appointment
- No signed in-and-out times
- Broker not notified during the wait
- Detention requested long after delivery
- Delay caused by the carrier, such as a paperwork problem or missing equipment

Each of these is avoidable with a simple routine. Make it a habit for every load, not just the ones where you expect a wait.

## Use detention history when you book

Detention is also information. If a shipper keeps you for hours every time, that lane is worth less than its rate per mile suggests. Track your average wait by facility and use it when you negotiate. Ask for a higher rate or guaranteed detention on known slow docks, and be ready to pass on loads where the wait wipes out the profit. Our guide on [how to negotiate freight rates](/blog/how-to-negotiate-freight-rates.html) covers how to bring that data to the conversation, and the [load profitability calculator](/load-profitability-calculator.html) lets you add expected wait time into your numbers.

If a long wait turns into an overnight stay, that becomes layover, which has its own terms. See our guide to [TONU, layover and lumper pay](/blog/tonu-layover-and-lumper-pay.html).

## How Texas Solutions can help

Texas Solutions is a dispatch service, not a broker or motor carrier. Our dispatchers negotiate detention terms onto the rate con, send notifications during the wait and handle the paperwork that supports your claim, 24/7, and you approve every load. See our [dispatch services](/dispatch.html) or [talk to a dispatcher](/contact.html).

### How to Finance a Semi Truck: A Step-by-Step Guide
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/how-to-finance-a-semi-truck/
Published: 2026-10-21

Learning **how to finance a semi truck** is mostly about understanding what lenders want and what the loan really costs over its full term. The right loan keeps your payment affordable on slow weeks; the wrong one can take over your business. This guide walks through the process step by step with a hypothetical example. It is general education, not financial advice, so review any offer with your CPA or a trusted advisor before you sign.

## How semi truck loans work

Most truck financing is an **equipment loan**: the lender pays the seller, you make monthly payments, and the truck serves as collateral. If you stop paying, the lender can repossess it. The main terms to understand:

- **Price financed:** purchase price plus any taxes, fees or warranties rolled into the loan, minus your down payment.
- **Interest rate (APR):** what borrowing costs per year.
- **Term:** how many months you will pay.
- **Monthly payment:** the result of the three items above.
- **Fees and conditions:** documentation fees, prepayment penalties, balloon payments, insurance requirements.

## What lenders look at

Every lender weighs things differently, but most review:

- **Personal and business credit history**, including late payments and recent collections
- **Time in business** and time under your own authority
- **CDL experience**, especially in the type of equipment you are buying
- **Down payment** you can bring
- **The truck:** age, mileage, make, condition and whether it suits the work
- **Cash reserves** and other debts
- **Income history**, such as bank statements, settlement sheets or tax returns

New authorities can usually still get financing, but expect tighter terms. Clean, up-to-date books help a lot.

## Documents to have ready

Lenders move faster when your file is complete. Gather these before you apply:

- Driver's license and CDL
- Business formation papers and EIN letter, if you have a business entity
- USDOT and MC numbers, if you already have authority
- Recent business and personal bank statements
- Tax returns or settlement statements showing income
- The truck's details: year, make, model, VIN, mileage and the seller's quote
- Proof of insurance or an insurance quote

## Step by step: financing your truck

1. **Know your numbers first.** Calculate your cost per mile and what payment the business can afford on a slow month.
2. **Check your credit** and fix errors before you apply.
3. **Save your down payment and a reserve.** Plan for both. A truck with no repair fund is one breakdown away from a missed payment.
4. **Choose the truck carefully.** If buying used, follow our [used semi truck buying guide](/blog/buying-a-used-semi-truck.html) before you commit.
5. **Get several written offers** from different types of lenders (banks, credit unions, equipment finance companies, dealer financing).
6. **Compare total cost,** not only the monthly payment.
7. **Read every condition:** prepayment penalties, late fees, required insurance, balloon payments.
8. **Have a CPA or advisor review** the final offer before you sign.

## Worked example: the same truck, two offers

Here is a **hypothetical** example. The numbers are made up to show the math, not to suggest real rates.

You are financing **$80,000** over **60 months**.

| | Offer A | Offer B |
|---|---|---|
| APR | 12% | 18% |
| Monthly payment (approx.) | $1,780 | $2,030 |
| Total paid over 60 months | about $106,800 | about $121,800 |
| Total interest | about $26,800 | about $41,800 |

The $250 difference in monthly payment looks small, but over five years Offer B costs about **$15,000 more**. Run your own scenarios with the [truck loan calculator](/truck-loan-calculator.html).

Now convert the payment to a per-mile cost. If the truck runs a hypothetical 9,000 miles a month:

- Offer A: $1,780 / 9,000 = about **$0.20 per mile**
- Offer B: $2,030 / 9,000 = about **$0.23 per mile**

That per-mile figure goes straight into your [break-even calculator](/break-even-calculator.html). If a slow month drops you to 6,000 miles, Offer B becomes about $0.34 per mile. Always test the payment against a bad month, not your best month.

## Common loan features to understand

### Balloon payments
Some loans have lower monthly payments with a large lump sum due at the end. Make sure you know exactly how you would pay it.

### Prepayment penalties
Some lenders charge a fee if you pay the loan off early. If you plan to refinance or sell, this matters.

### Add-ons rolled into the loan
Extended warranties, GAP coverage and fees may be added to the amount financed. You then pay interest on them. Ask for an itemized breakdown.

### Insurance requirements
Lenders usually require physical damage coverage naming them as loss payee. Get an insurance quote before you sign so the true monthly cost is clear.

## Red flags in truck financing

- Pressure to sign the same day
- A payment quoted with no APR, term or total cost in writing
- Requests to pay large upfront "approval fees" before any written offer
- Terms that change between the quote and the final contract
- A seller and lender who will not let you inspect the truck or review documents with an advisor

When something feels wrong, walk away. There is always another truck.

## Financing vs leasing

Financing means you own the truck and build equity, but you carry repair risk. Leasing can mean lower upfront cash but different long-term costs. Read [lease vs buy a truck](/blog/lease-vs-buy-a-truck.html) to compare the two side by side.

## How Texas Solutions can help

Texas Solutions is a dispatch service, not a lender, broker or motor carrier. Our dispatchers find and negotiate loads with your truck payment and cost per mile in mind, handle broker packets and paperwork, and work 24/7, while you approve every load. Steady, well-planned miles are what make a truck payment manageable. See our [dispatch services](/dispatch.html) or [talk to a dispatcher](/contact.html).

### How to File Form 2290: Heavy Vehicle Use Tax for Truckers
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/how-to-file-form-2290/
Published: 2026-10-21

**Form 2290** is the IRS return you use to report and pay the federal Heavy Vehicle Use Tax (HVUT) on trucks that run on public highways. If you own a heavy truck in your own name or your company's name, filing it on time is part of keeping your plates and your authority working.

## What Form 2290 is and who must file

The HVUT is a yearly federal tax on heavy highway motor vehicles. Form 2290 is how you report each vehicle and pay the tax. In general, you must file if:

- You own (or are the registered owner of) a highway motor vehicle,
- Its **taxable gross weight** is at or above the IRS threshold (historically 55,000 pounds), and
- It is used on public highways during the tax period.

Taxable gross weight is not the same as the empty weight of the truck. It is roughly the truck's actual unloaded weight, plus the unloaded weight of trailers you usually pull with it, plus the heaviest load you customarily carry. Many owner-operators simply use the weight they register the truck for in their state, but check the Form 2290 instructions for how weight categories work.

The amount of tax depends on the weight category, and the IRS publishes the current rate table in the instructions. We do not quote amounts here because they can change; always use the table for the tax year you are filing.

## When Form 2290 is due

The HVUT tax period runs from **July 1 to June 30**. Two dates matter:

- **Trucks in use in July:** the return for the new period is generally due by the last day of August.
- **Trucks first used later in the period:** the return is generally due by the last day of the month after the month of first use. For example, a truck first put on the road in October would generally be due by the end of November.

If the due date lands on a weekend or legal holiday, the IRS usually moves it to the next business day. Confirm the exact dates for your situation in the current IRS instructions.

## What you need before you file

Gather this before you sit down to file:

1. **EIN** for the owner (an SSN is not accepted).
2. **Business name and address** exactly as the IRS has them for that EIN.
3. **VIN** for every truck you are reporting. A typo here is one of the most common reasons owners must file a correction.
4. **Taxable gross weight category** for each truck.
5. **Month of first use** in the tax period.
6. **Payment method**, such as electronic funds withdrawal or another IRS-approved option.
7. Whether any truck qualifies as **suspended** (low mileage).

## Step-by-step: how to file Form 2290

1. **Choose how to file.** The IRS encourages e-filing, and it is required if you report 25 or more vehicles. Most owner-operators e-file through an IRS-authorized e-file provider. Make sure the provider is listed by the IRS; providers charge their own service fees separate from the tax.
2. **Enter business and vehicle details.** Double-check the EIN, name and every VIN.
3. **Select the weight category and month of first use** for each truck.
4. **Mark suspended vehicles** if a truck is expected to stay under the mileage limit.
5. **Choose a payment option** and submit.
6. **Download your stamped Schedule 1.** With e-filing, the IRS-watermarked Schedule 1 usually comes back quickly. Paper returns take much longer.
7. **Store copies.** Keep the return, Schedule 1 and payment proof with your truck records.

### Why the stamped Schedule 1 matters

Schedule 1 is your proof of payment (or proof of suspension). You typically need it to:

- Register or renew plates, including apportioned plates under IRP.
- Show proof to a leasing carrier if you run under someone else's authority.
- Answer questions during an audit or a lease onboarding.

Keep a digital copy on your phone and a paper copy in the office. Many owner-operators also keep one in the truck.

## Suspended vehicles and low-mileage trucks

If you expect a truck to be driven no more than the IRS mileage limit during the tax period (5,000 miles in general, with a higher limit for agricultural vehicles), you can report it as suspended. No tax is due, but you still file.

If the truck later goes over the limit, the tax becomes due. The IRS instructions explain the deadline for reporting that change, so mark the date in your calendar if a truck is close.

## Worked example: due date for a new truck

Say you buy a truck and first run it on the highway in **March**.

- The tax period is the one that started the previous July 1 and ends June 30.
- Because you first used it in March, the return is generally due by the **end of April**.
- The tax for a partial period is prorated by the month of first use, using the IRS table.
- On **July 1** a new tax period starts, and that truck will be due again by the end of **August**.

That means a truck bought late in the period can need two 2290 filings within a few months. Plan cash flow for both.

## Common Form 2290 mistakes to avoid

- **Wrong VIN.** Fix it with an amended or corrected filing as the instructions describe.
- **Using an SSN** instead of an EIN.
- **Waiting until late August,** when e-file systems are busiest and a new EIN may not be active yet.
- **Wrong weight category,** especially after changing trailer type or what you haul.
- **Not tracking miles** on a suspended truck that ends up working more than expected.
- **Assuming a leasing carrier filed for you.** Unless your lease clearly says so in writing, the registered owner is usually responsible.

Track your highway miles carefully, too. The same mileage records help with your fuel tax filings; see our guide to [IFTA for owner-operators](/blog/ifta-for-owner-operators-how-to-file.html) and the [IFTA mileage calculator](/ifta-mileage-calculator.html).

Form 2290 is one of several recurring items for a carrier with its own authority. Others include UCR registration, the MCS-150 biennial update, IFTA returns and IRP renewal. Our guide on how to [keep your MC authority active](/blog/keep-your-mc-authority-active.html) puts these on one calendar, and our [trucking back office services](/trucking-back-office-services.html) page explains the paperwork support we offer.

This guide is general information, not tax advice. Rates, thresholds and deadlines are set by the IRS and can change, so confirm everything in the current Form 2290 instructions at IRS.gov or with a CPA who works with trucking companies.

Our dispatchers find and negotiate loads, handle broker packets and paperwork, and are available 24/7, while you approve every load. Keeping your Schedule 1, insurance and authority documents current makes broker setup faster, so we help you stay organized.
