### How to Dispute a Roadside Violation With DataQs
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/how-to-dispute-a-violation-dataqs/
Published: 2026-10-21

If a roadside inspection report or crash record on your USDOT number is wrong, you do not have to live with it. FMCSA's **DataQs** system lets carriers and drivers ask for a review of inaccurate safety data, and a successful request can remove or change a violation that is hurting your CSA percentiles.

## What DataQs is (and is not)

DataQs is FMCSA's online system for submitting a **Request for Data Review (RDR)**. FMCSA routes each request to the agency that owns the data, which for roadside inspections is usually the state enforcement agency whose officer did the inspection.

DataQs is for data that is **wrong or incomplete**. It is not a way to argue that a correct violation was unfair or to remove a violation because you later fixed the problem. Requests that only express disagreement tend to be closed quickly.

## Situations where a DataQs request makes sense

- **Wrong carrier.** The inspection was assigned to your USDOT number but the truck was running under another carrier's authority, or the number was entered wrong.
- **Wrong driver or vehicle.** A different driver's name, license or VIN appears on the report.
- **Duplicate record.** The same inspection or crash shows up twice.
- **Factually wrong violation.** For example, an hours-of-service violation your ELD records clearly disprove, or a defect code that does not match what was found.
- **Citation dismissed or found not guilty.** If a violation also led to a citation that was later dismissed or ended in a not-guilty result in court, FMCSA policy generally allows the violation to be updated in its data. A conviction of a different or lesser charge may also change how it is recorded.
- **Crash preventability.** For certain types of crashes, FMCSA's Crash Preventability Determination Program lets you submit a request through DataQs to have a crash reviewed as not preventable. Eligible crash types are defined by FMCSA, so check the current list.

## Evidence that tends to help

A request is only as strong as the proof attached. Gather what applies:

- The **inspection report** itself, with the report number.
- **ELD records** and supporting documents (fuel receipts, bills of lading, toll records) for hours-of-service disputes.
- **Lease agreement** and the operating carrier's information for wrong-carrier disputes.
- **Photos** taken at the scene with date and time.
- **Court documents** showing dismissal or not-guilty results for citations.
- **Police reports** and other records for crash reviews.
- A **repair invoice dated before** the inspection, if it proves a part was compliant at the time.

Label files clearly and keep them readable. A reviewer should understand your point without hunting through pages.

## Step-by-step: filing a DataQs request

1. **Find the record.** Pull the inspection or crash from your FMCSA portal or SMS results, and note the report number, date and state.
2. **Create or log in to your DataQs account.** Use the account type that matches you: motor carrier, driver, or other.
3. **Start a new request** and choose the correct category, such as inspection or crash, and the specific issue type.
4. **Identify the record** by report number and state.
5. **Write a short, factual explanation.** Say what is wrong, what is correct, and what evidence shows it. Keep the tone professional.
6. **Attach your evidence.**
7. **Submit and save your confirmation.**
8. **Watch for updates.** Reviewers may ask questions. Respond quickly, inside DataQs, so the request does not stall or close.
9. **Check your data** once a decision is made. Changes can take some time to flow into your SMS results.

### A sample explanation

Here is the kind of short, specific statement that works well. Adjust it to your facts:

> Inspection report [number], [state], [date]. Violation 395.8(e) (false log) was recorded. The driver's ELD records and the attached fuel receipts, timestamped in [city] at [time], show the logged location and duty status were accurate. We request the violation be reviewed and removed. ELD data file and receipts attached.

Avoid long stories, blame, or comments about the officer. Stick to the record and the evidence.

## If your request is denied

Read the reason. Sometimes a request fails only because evidence was missing or unclear. In that case you may be able to submit a **request for reconsideration** with better documentation, depending on the state's process. If the record is accurate, the best path is to let time and clean inspections reduce its effect; see [CSA scores explained](/blog/csa-scores-explained.html) for how violations age.

If a citation is involved and you plan to fight it in court, talk to an attorney who handles traffic and trucking cases. The court outcome can matter for what you can later request in DataQs.

## Mistakes that sink DataQs requests

- Filing without any evidence.
- Arguing a violation is minor instead of showing it is inaccurate.
- Filing the same request many times.
- Ignoring reviewer questions until the request closes.
- Waiting too long. Older records are harder to document, and the violation is affecting your scores the whole time.

## Prevent the next one

The cheapest violation is the one that never gets written. Keep your truck and paperwork ready for [DOT roadside inspections](/blog/dot-roadside-inspections.html), run legal hours, and review every inspection report before leaving the site. Know which defects put you [out of service](/blog/out-of-service-criteria.html), because those carry the most weight. If you share a truck under someone else's authority, read our guide to [MC lease options](/mc-lease.html) so records land on the right USDOT number.

This guide is general information. Procedures, eligible request types and state processes can change, so check the current guidance in DataQs and on FMCSA's website.

## How Texas Solutions can help

Texas Solutions is a dispatch service, not a broker or motor carrier. Our dispatchers find and negotiate loads, handle broker packets and paperwork, and are available 24/7, while you approve every load. A clean safety record makes broker setup easier, and we help you keep documents organized when you need them. See our [dispatch services](/dispatch.html) or [talk to a dispatcher](/contact.html).

### How to Choose an ELD: Features and Questions to Ask
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/how-to-choose-an-eld/
Published: 2026-10-21

Every ELD on the market claims to be simple and compliant, so **how to choose an ELD** comes down to asking the right questions. The right device keeps you legal at inspections, does not fight you every morning and does not lock you into a contract you regret.

This guide compares ELDs by features and questions instead of brands. Rules mentioned here are summarized from the federal ELD rule as we understand it; confirm current requirements with FMCSA.

## Step 1: Make sure you actually need one

The federal ELD rule applies to most drivers who must keep records of duty status. Common exceptions include:

- **Older engines.** Vehicles with an engine model year older than 2000.
- **Short-haul drivers** who qualify for the short-haul exception and use time records instead of logs.
- **Drivers who keep logs 8 days or fewer** in any 30-day period.
- **Driveaway-towaway operations**, in certain situations.

If you fit an exception, you may still choose an ELD for tracking and IFTA mileage, but you are not required to use one. Confirm with FMCSA before you skip it.

## Step 2: Check compliance first

An ELD that is not properly registered is a violation waiting to happen.

- **Registered list.** ELDs are self-certified by the manufacturer and listed on FMCSA's registered ELD list. Confirm the exact model and version you are buying is on it.
- **Revoked list.** FMCSA also publishes revoked devices. If yours is revoked, you have a limited time to replace it. Check both lists before you buy and every few months after.
- **Data transfer at inspections.** The rule allows telematics transfer (web services and email) or local transfer (USB and Bluetooth). Ask which method the device supports and practice it before an inspector asks you to.
- **Malfunction support.** The provider should give you the instruction sheets you must carry. See our [ELD malfunction rules](/blog/eld-malfunction-rules.html) guide for what that packet includes.

## Step 3: Compare the features that matter day to day

Most ELDs record the same required data. The differences show up in daily use.

| Feature | What to look for | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Driver app | Clear clocks for 11, 14, 30-minute break and 60/70 cycle | You check it dozens of times a day |
| Split sleeper support | Calculates 7/3 and 8/2 pairings automatically | Avoids manual math mistakes |
| PC and yard moves | Can be enabled per driver, with annotations | Needed for honest off-duty and yard movement |
| Unidentified driving | Easy to accept, assign or annotate | Unresolved records cause audit headaches |
| Edits | Clear workflow for proposed edits and driver approval | Keeps your logs accurate and defensible |
| DVIR | Electronic inspection reports | Saves paper and creates a record |
| IFTA mileage | Miles by state, exportable | Speeds up quarterly fuel tax filing |
| GPS tracking | Location and history | Helpful for dispatch and detention proof |
| Document scanning | Upload BOLs and receipts | Faster billing and factoring |
| Offline mode | Records properly without cell signal | Rural lanes and dead zones |

Do not pay for fleet features you will never use. A one-truck owner-operator needs a reliable driver app, accurate clocks and easy IFTA reports more than a complex fleet dashboard.

## Step 4: Check hardware fit

- **Connector type.** Heavy trucks commonly use 9-pin diagnostic ports, while some newer trucks use different connectors. Ask which cables are included and what an adapter costs.
- **Mounting.** A portable ELD (phone or tablet) generally must be mounted in a fixed position while the truck is moving and be visible from the normal driving position. A solid mount matters.
- **Phone or tablet.** Bring your own device or use a provided tablet? Dedicated devices avoid conflicts with personal apps and notifications.
- **Installation.** Plug-and-play units are easy to move between trucks. Hardwired units may be more stable but harder to swap.

## Step 5: Understand the real cost

ELD pricing comes in many shapes. Compare total cost over the contract, not just the monthly number.

**Hypothetical example:** Option A has no hardware cost and a higher monthly fee on a 36-month contract. Option B charges for hardware up front with a lower monthly fee and no contract.

- Option A: 36 months x $40 = $1,440
- Option B: $250 hardware + (36 months x $30) = $1,330

Option B is cheaper over three years and can be canceled any time, but costs more on day one. These numbers are made up for illustration; get written quotes and run your own comparison. Add the result to your fixed costs in the [cost per mile calculator](/cost-per-mile-calculator.html).

Watch for these extras:

- Activation or setup fees
- Early termination fees
- Charges for extra cables, mounts or replacement hardware
- Paid add-ons for IFTA reports, tracking history or document scanning
- Price increases after a promotional period

## Questions to ask before you sign

Use this checklist when you talk to any ELD provider:

- [ ] Is this exact model on FMCSA's registered ELD list today?
- [ ] Which inspection transfer methods does it support?
- [ ] Is support available 24/7, including nights and weekends, by phone?
- [ ] What happens if the device fails on the road? How fast is replacement hardware shipped?
- [ ] How does the app handle split sleeper, PC and yard moves?
- [ ] Can I export my logs and IFTA data if I leave?
- [ ] What is the contract length, and what does it cost to cancel early?
- [ ] Which phones or tablets are supported?
- [ ] Does it work without cell signal, and how does it sync later?
- [ ] Can it share location with a dispatcher or customer, and can I control that?

Read online reviews from other small carriers, but focus on patterns about support and reliability, not single complaints.

## Leased on or under your own authority?

If you are leased to a carrier, the carrier usually chooses the ELD and you must use theirs. When you get your own authority, the choice becomes yours. Add ELD setup to your startup list in our [how to start a trucking company](/blog/how-to-start-a-trucking-company.html) guide. For other tools worth comparing the same way, see [trucking apps for owner-operators](/blog/trucking-apps-for-owner-operators.html).

## How Texas Solutions can help

Texas Solutions is a dispatch service, not a broker or motor carrier. Our dispatchers find and negotiate loads, handle broker packets and paperwork 24/7, and can plan around your ELD clocks so loads fit your available hours. You approve every load. Learn about [dispatch services](/dispatch.html) or [talk to a dispatcher](/contact.html).

### How to Choose a Factoring Company: Features and Questions to Ask
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/how-to-choose-a-factoring-company/
Published: 2026-10-21

Choosing a **factoring company** is one of the most important money decisions an owner-operator makes. The right one keeps cash moving and helps you avoid bad brokers. The wrong one can drain margins with hidden fees and lock you into a contract that is hard to leave. This guide compares factoring by features and gives you the questions to ask.

If you are new to factoring, start with our guide to [freight factoring for owner-operators](/blog/freight-factoring-for-owner-operators-explained.html), then come back here to compare offers.

## Recourse vs non-recourse

This is the first big choice.

- **Recourse factoring.** If the broker does not pay within a set period, you buy back the invoice or it is deducted from future funding. Usually lower rates.
- **Non-recourse factoring.** The factoring company absorbs the loss if a broker cannot pay, usually only for credit reasons like insolvency. Usually higher rates.

Ask exactly what "non-recourse" covers. In many contracts it does not cover disputes, short pays, claims or missing paperwork. Those come back to you either way.

## Know the real cost per invoice

The headline percentage is only part of the cost. Ask for every fee in writing.

### Fees to ask about

- Factoring rate, and whether it rises the longer an invoice stays unpaid
- Same-day funding, wire or ACH fees
- Fuel advance fees
- Application, setup or onboarding fees
- Monthly minimum or low-volume fees
- Invoice processing or document fees
- Credit check fees
- Termination or early exit fees
- Fees for sending paper mail or originals

### Worked example

Hypothetical example comparing two offers on $20,000 of monthly invoices from 8 loads:

| Item | Offer A | Offer B |
|---|---|---|
| Rate | 2.5% = $500 | 3.0% = $600 |
| Funding fee per transfer | $15 x 8 = $120 | Included |
| Monthly minimum fee | $50 | None |
| Total monthly cost | **$670** | **$600** |

Offer A looks cheaper but costs more once fees are added. Always calculate total cost per month for your real volume. Then plug factoring cost into your [cost per mile calculator](/cost-per-mile-calculator.html) so it is reflected in the rates you accept.

## Advance rate and reserve

Some factoring companies advance a portion of the invoice up front and hold the rest as a reserve, released when the broker pays (minus fees). Others advance nearly the full amount minus the fee.

Ask:

- What percent is advanced?
- How long is the reserve held, and when is it released?
- Can the reserve be used to cover chargebacks on other invoices?

A lower reserve means more cash in hand, but compare it against the total fees.

## Contract terms and how you leave

Many carriers find out about contract terms only when they try to leave. Read these sections carefully:

- **Contract length** and whether it auto-renews
- **Notice period** required to cancel, and how notice must be given
- **Exit fees** or liquidated damages
- **Full-turnover requirement**: must you factor every invoice from approved customers?
- **UCC-1 filing**: what it covers and how fast it is released
- **Notice of assignment (NOA)**: how and when the NOA is released so brokers pay you directly again

Have an attorney or trusted advisor review the agreement before you sign. If anything is unclear, ask for the explanation in writing.

## Funding speed and process

Cash flow is why you factor, so test the process:

- How fast are invoices funded after submission?
- What is the daily cutoff time, and do they fund on weekends or holidays?
- How do you submit paperwork: mobile app, scan, email?
- Which documents are required? Usually a signed rate con, signed BOL or POD, and your invoice.
- How are lumper receipts and accessorials handled?

Our guides on [how to read a rate confirmation](/blog/how-to-read-a-rate-confirmation.html) and [TONU, layover and lumper pay](/blog/tonu-layover-and-lumper-pay.html) explain the paperwork that makes funding smooth.

## Broker credit tools

A good factoring company helps you avoid bad payers. Ask:

- Can I check a broker's credit before I book, and is it instant?
- Do you share days-to-pay data?
- What happens if I haul for a broker you do not approve?
- Do you alert me to fraud warnings or brokers with payment problems?

Credit checks are not a substitute for your own vetting. See [how to vet a freight broker](/blog/how-to-vet-a-freight-broker.html).

## Support and extras

- Is there a real person to call, and during what hours?
- Is there a dedicated account rep?
- Do they offer fuel discounts or fuel advances, and at what cost?
- Do they provide reporting for your bookkeeping?
- How do they handle collections, and how do they treat your broker relationships?

Extras are only worth it if you would use them and the core terms are fair.

## Factoring company checklist

Before you sign, confirm you have:

1. Every fee in writing and a calculated monthly total at your volume
2. A clear explanation of recourse and what non-recourse really covers
3. The advance rate and reserve terms
4. Contract length, renewal, notice period and exit costs
5. Full-turnover requirements, if any
6. UCC and NOA release process
7. Funding times and cutoffs
8. Broker credit check access
9. A support contact you have actually spoken to
10. Your own reviewer's read on the contract

Once you choose, our guide on [working with a factoring company](/blog/working-with-a-factoring-company.html) covers the day-to-day.

## How Texas Solutions can help

Texas Solutions is a dispatch service, not a broker, motor carrier or factoring company. Our dispatchers find and negotiate loads, check broker credit with your factoring company before booking, and handle broker packets and paperwork 24/7, and you approve every load. See our [dispatch services](/dispatch.html) or [talk to a dispatcher](/contact.html).

### Hiring Your First Truck Driver: A Step-by-Step Guide
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/hiring-your-first-truck-driver/
Published: 2026-10-21

**Hiring your first truck driver** is the moment an owner-operator becomes a fleet owner. It can double your revenue, but it also doubles your compliance, insurance and cash flow exposure, and you are now responsible for someone else's driving. This guide walks through the decision and the hiring steps in the order that keeps you out of trouble.

## Before you hire

### Step 1: Make sure the numbers work

Before you post a job, confirm a second truck can pay a driver and still make money for you.

**Hypothetical example** (made-up numbers for illustration):

| Item | Per week |
|---|---|
| Miles | 2,500 |
| Gross revenue at $2.40/mile | $6,000 |
| Fuel | $1,900 |
| Truck and trailer payment | $700 |
| Insurance for the added unit | $400 |
| Maintenance and tires reserve | $375 |
| Other (ELD, permits, tolls, dispatch, admin) | $500 |
| **Before driver pay** | **$2,125** |
| Driver pay at $0.60/mile | $1,500 |
| Payroll taxes and benefits (estimate) | $200 |
| **Left for you** | **$425** |

In this example the second truck makes money, but a slow week, one repair or a low-paying lane can wipe it out. Run your own numbers with the [driver pay calculator](/driver-pay-calculator.html), and check your full cost per mile and break-even point before committing. Keep a cash reserve covering several weeks of expenses, because you pay the driver before some brokers pay you.

### Step 2: Decide employee or contractor

This is a legal and tax question, not a preference. Generally, if you control when, where and how the driver works, provide the truck and set the rules, the driver may be an employee under IRS and state tests. Some states apply stricter tests than others.

Hiring a company driver as a W-2 employee means payroll, withholding, unemployment tax and workers' compensation where required. Leasing on an owner-operator who brings their own truck is a different arrangement with its own federal leasing rules.

Talk to a CPA or employment attorney before the first paycheck. If you might work with leased owner-operators later, ask about that arrangement too.

### Step 3: Get insurance approval first

Call your insurance agent before you interview seriously. Ask:

- What are the minimum age and experience requirements for an added driver?
- What will adding a driver and unit do to my premium?
- Which violations or accidents on an MVR would disqualify a candidate?
- Do I need occupational accident or workers' compensation coverage?

Many insurers want a few years of verifiable experience. Finding out after you have made an offer is a costly mistake. Get the answers in writing.

## Finding and qualifying the driver

### Step 4: Find and screen candidates

Write a job post that is honest about the lane, home time, equipment and pay plan. Then screen in stages:

1. **Phone screen:** experience, equipment type, home time expectations, any recent tickets or accidents.
2. **Application:** the full DOT-compliant employment application.
3. **MVR and insurance check:** send the MVR to your agent for approval.
4. **Interview:** ask how they plan a trip, handle a late appointment, or deal with a broker who will not pay detention. Listen for communication skills.
5. **Road test** (or accept a valid CDL in place of it, where the rules allow), plus a ride-along if you can.
6. **References** from previous drivers or dispatchers, not just HR offices.

### Step 5: Qualify the driver before the first load

Nothing moves until these are done:

- [ ] Signed employment application
- [ ] MVRs from every state licensed in the past three years
- [ ] Previous employer safety performance history requests sent
- [ ] Road test certificate or CDL copy
- [ ] Current medical card and National Registry verification
- [ ] Clearinghouse pre-employment full query with driver consent
- [ ] Negative pre-employment drug test result received
- [ ] Driver added to your random testing pool
- [ ] Insurance approval in writing
- [ ] Driver added to your ELD account

Use the [driver qualification file checklist](/blog/driver-qualification-file-checklist.html) and the [drug and alcohol testing program](/blog/drug-and-alcohol-testing-program.html) guide for details. Confirm current requirements with FMCSA.

## Pay and onboarding

### Step 6: Choose a pay plan and put it in writing

Common structures:

- **Per mile:** simple and common. Decide whether you pay practical, loaded or all miles.
- **Percentage of load revenue:** rewards good rates but varies week to week.
- **Hourly or daily:** common for local and regional work.
- **Weekly salary:** steady for the driver, risky for you in slow weeks.

Whatever you choose, write down extra pay for detention, layovers, stop-offs, breakdowns and tarping if it applies. Explain how and when you pay, and any deductions. Clear rules prevent most driver disputes.

### Step 7: Onboard properly

First impressions shape retention. A simple orientation covers:

- Company policies: speed, idling, passengers, pets, personal conveyance
- Truck walkaround and [pre-trip inspection](/blog/pre-trip-inspection-checklist.html) expectations
- ELD login, logs and hours of service
- Fuel card limits and where to fuel
- Paperwork: bills of lading, PODs, lumper receipts and how to send them
- Who to call for breakdowns, accidents and load problems, day or night

Ride with the driver for the first day or two if you can.

### Step 8: Check in and keep good drivers

The first 90 days decide whether a driver stays. Set a short call at the end of week one, week four and month three. Ask what is working, what is frustrating and whether pay settlements are clear. Fix small problems fast: a late paycheck or a truck that keeps breaking down will cost you a good driver sooner than a slightly lower rate per mile.

Keep the recurring compliance tasks on a calendar too: medical card expiration, CDL renewal, the annual MVR review and the annual Clearinghouse query. Missing one of these can make a good driver unqualified on paper overnight.

## Mistakes first-time fleet owners make

- Hiring before insurance approval
- Letting a driver run "just one load" before the drug test result comes back
- No written pay agreement
- Not tracking medical card and license expiration dates
- Handing a driver your worst lanes and expecting them to stay

Fix these early and growing beyond two trucks gets much easier.

## How Texas Solutions can help

Texas Solutions is a dispatch service, not a broker or motor carrier. When you add a truck, our dispatchers find and negotiate loads for each unit, handle broker packets and paperwork, and work 24/7, while you approve every load. See our [small fleet dispatch](/small-fleet-dispatch.html) service or [talk to a dispatcher](/contact.html).

### Hazmat Endorsement Guide for Owner-Operators
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/hazmat-endorsement-guide/
Published: 2026-10-21

A **hazmat endorsement** (the "H" on your CDL) lets you drive a vehicle carrying hazardous materials in amounts that require placards. It opens up freight many drivers cannot touch, but it comes with a federal background check, extra training, and real business obligations. This guide walks through how to get it and what it changes for an owner-operator.

## What the hazmat endorsement covers

Under federal rules, a driver needs the H endorsement to operate a commercial motor vehicle transporting hazardous materials in a quantity that requires placarding under the Hazardous Materials Regulations (49 CFR Parts 171-180). Small quantities that do not require placards generally do not trigger the endorsement, although other hazmat rules (shipping papers, training, emergency response information) can still apply.

Related endorsements you will hear about:

- **H** - placarded hazardous materials
- **N** - tank vehicles (liquids or gases in bulk tanks)
- **X** - a combination of H and N that many states print when you hold both

Interstate CDL drivers must be at least 21, and the hazmat endorsement follows that same minimum for interstate work. Check your state's rules for intrastate operations.

## Who is eligible

To get an H endorsement you must pass a **TSA Security Threat Assessment**. TSA reviews criminal history, immigration status, and certain other records. Broadly:

- You must be a US citizen, lawful permanent resident, or fall into one of the other immigration categories TSA accepts.
- Certain serious crimes permanently disqualify an applicant, and others disqualify for a period of years after conviction or release.
- Some disqualifications can be waived or appealed through a TSA process.

The disqualifying offense list is specific and changes from time to time, so read it on the TSA website before you pay for training. If you have anything on your record, it is worth looking it up first.

## Step-by-step: getting your H endorsement

1. **Confirm your CDL is in good standing** and your medical certificate is current. Your state will not add an endorsement to a suspended or downgraded license.2. **Complete hazmat theory training.** Since February 2022, first-time H applicants must complete Entry-Level Driver Training hazmat theory from a provider listed on FMCSA's Training Provider Registry. The provider submits your completion electronically. Read more in our [ELDT guide](/blog/entry-level-driver-training-eldt.html).
3. **Apply for the TSA threat assessment.** Enroll online or by phone through TSA's hazmat endorsement program, then visit an enrollment center for fingerprints and identity documents. You pay the TSA fee at enrollment.
4. **Pass the state hazmat knowledge test.** Study the hazmat section of your state's CDL manual: placards, shipping papers, segregation tables, loading rules and emergency response.
5. **Wait for the state to issue the endorsement.** TSA sends its determination to your state. Once the state has both the TSA approval and your test results, it updates your CDL. Some states issue a new card; some require a visit.

Order matters in some states. A few want the knowledge test first, others want the TSA application first. Ask your licensing office before you start so you do not have to repeat anything.

## Renewal and keeping it active

The TSA threat assessment is valid for up to five years, but your state may line up the renewal with your CDL renewal date. Common mistakes:

- **Waiting until the last month.** If TSA has not cleared you when your endorsement expires, the state may drop the H from your license until it does.
- **Assuming the knowledge test is a one-time thing.** Federal rules require a hazmat knowledge test at renewal; check how your state handles it.
- **Forgetting carrier training.** Separate from the endorsement, hazmat employees must receive hazmat training from their employer at least every three years under 49 CFR 172.704. As an owner-operator with your own authority, you are both employer and employee, so keep your own training record.

## What changes for your business

Having the H on your license is only the driver side. If you haul hazmat under your own MC number, the company side matters just as much.

| Area | What to check |
|---|---|
| Insurance | Federal minimum financial responsibility for many hazmat classes is higher than for general freight, and brokers often want more. Talk to your insurance agent before you book. |
| MCS-150 | Your USDOT registration should show that you haul hazardous materials. |
| PHMSA registration | Required for many placarded loads. See our [PHMSA hazmat registration guide](/blog/phmsa-hazmat-registration.html). |
| Hazmat safety permit | Certain high-hazard materials need an FMCSA hazmat safety permit on top of everything else. |
| Equipment | Placards, a fire extinguisher of the required rating, and a place to keep shipping papers within reach. |
| Inspections | Hazmat loads tend to get closer roadside attention. |

## Is the hazmat endorsement worth it?

For many drivers, yes, even if they rarely haul placarded freight. Reasons it pays off:

- **More loads qualify.** Plenty of dry van and reefer freight includes small amounts of placarded product. Without the H you have to turn those down.
- **Rates are often higher.** Hazmat loads can pay a premium because fewer carriers can take them. This varies by lane and season, so compare each offer to your [cost per mile](/cost-per-mile-calculator.html).
- **Tanker and fuel work** require it (along with N, as X).

The trade-offs are cost, time, a stricter compliance load, and higher insurance. A quick hypothetical check: if the endorsement, training and extra insurance costs added up to $2,500 in a year, and hazmat loads paid you an extra $150 each compared with your normal freight, you would need about 17 hazmat loads that year to break even ($2,500 / $150). Plug in your real numbers with the [load profitability calculator](/load-profitability-calculator.html).

## Quick checklist before your first hazmat load

- H endorsement on your CDL (and N or X if tank)
- Current hazmat training record for yourself
- Insurance that covers the hazmat class at the required limits
- PHMSA registration certificate or number on board, if required
- Correct placards for the load, and you know how to read the shipping papers
- Emergency response information with the shipping papers
- Route checked for hazmat restrictions, tunnels and bridges

Rules and fees change. Confirm current requirements with TSA, FMCSA, PHMSA and your state licensing agency before you apply or book.

## How Texas Solutions can help

Texas Solutions is a dispatch service, not a broker or a motor carrier. Once you are endorsed and set up, our dispatchers can look for hazmat-eligible loads, negotiate rates, and handle broker packets and paperwork 24/7, and you approve every load. Learn more about our [dispatch services](/dispatch.html) or [talk to a dispatcher](/contact.html).

### How to Grow From 1 to 5 Trucks Without Breaking Your Business
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/grow-from-1-to-5-trucks/
Published: 2026-10-21

Learning how to **grow from 1 to 5 trucks** is a different skill than running one truck well. At one truck, you are the driver, dispatcher, bookkeeper and safety manager, and your own hard work covers mistakes. Once you add trucks, your systems and cash have to do that work. This guide explains when to grow, what changes at each step, and how to check whether a new truck will actually make money.

## Signs you are ready to add a truck

Before you buy, honestly check these:

- **Steady profit per mile** on your first truck for many months, not one strong season
- **Cash reserves** that cover fixed costs for every truck through a slow period
- **Clean safety record:** few violations, no major unresolved crash or compliance issues
- **Organized books:** you know your cost per mile and your average days to get paid
- **Freight you can count on:** repeat brokers, lanes or shippers that need more capacity
- **Time:** a way to handle more calls, paperwork and problems while you still drive

If you are not sure about your numbers, start with [trucking KPIs to track](/blog/trucking-kpis-to-track.html).

## What changes at truck number two

### You become an employer or contractor manager
You now need drivers. That means recruiting, checking records, onboarding and keeping them. Read [hiring your first truck driver](/blog/hiring-your-first-truck-driver.html) before you post a job ad.

### Compliance work multiplies
Every driver needs a complete qualification file, must be in your drug and alcohol testing program, and must be queried in the FMCSA Drug and Alcohol Clearinghouse as the rules require. Your hours-of-service, vehicle maintenance and inspection records now cover more people and units. Use the [driver qualification file checklist](/blog/driver-qualification-file-checklist.html), and confirm current requirements with FMCSA.

### Insurance changes
Your premium depends on each driver's record and experience and each truck's value. A driver with a poor record may be expensive or impossible to insure.

### Registrations grow
Each new unit needs to be added to your IRP registration, IFTA account and insurance, and UCR fees are based on fleet size. Plan the timing so a new truck is legal on day one.

### Driver classification and payroll
Whether drivers are employees or independent contractors affects taxes, insurance and liability. Talk to an attorney or CPA before you decide, and set up payroll properly.

## Worked example: does truck two pay for itself?

All numbers below are **hypothetical**. The point is the method, not the figures.

Truck two will run 9,000 total miles a month at an average of $2.30 per total mile.

| Item | Per month |
|---|---|
| Revenue (9,000 x $2.30) | $20,700 |
| Driver pay at $0.65 per mile | $5,850 |
| Employer payroll costs or contractor costs (estimate) | $600 |
| Fuel ($0.85 per mile) | $7,650 |
| Truck payment | $2,000 |
| Insurance | $1,800 |
| Maintenance and tires ($0.15 per mile) | $1,350 |
| Dispatch, ELD, tolls, permits and other | $1,200 |
| **Total cost** | **$20,450** |
| **Profit before overhead** | **$250** |

At $2.30 per mile, this truck barely breaks even, and one repair or a slow week puts it underwater. Now try $2.55 per total mile: revenue rises to $22,950 and profit before overhead rises to about $2,500, with little change in cost. That small rate difference decides whether truck two is an asset or a burden. Model your own version with the [driver pay calculator](/driver-pay-calculator.html) and your cost per mile.

Notice also that driver pay is a cost that did not exist at truck one, when the profit was your pay. That is why many second trucks earn far less than owners expect.

## A step-by-step growth plan

1. **Document everything you do on truck one:** how you book loads, track maintenance, file IFTA and handle paperwork.
2. **Build your reserve** for two trucks before you buy the second.
3. **Line up freight** that needs more capacity.
4. **Get insurance quotes** for the specific truck and the driver candidates.
5. **Hire carefully,** complete qualification files and testing before the driver's first dispatch.
6. **Add truck two and run it for several months.** Track its KPIs separately from your own truck.
7. **Fix what breaks** in your systems: communication, maintenance scheduling, settlements.
8. **Repeat for trucks three, four and five** only when each truck's numbers hold up.

## Systems you need by five trucks

- **Dispatch:** someone always available to plan loads and handle problems for every truck
- **Maintenance:** a schedule per unit, a trusted shop network and a repair fund per truck
- **Safety and compliance:** driver files, testing, Clearinghouse queries, HOS audits and inspection records
- **Back office:** invoicing, factoring or collections, settlements, IFTA and payroll
- **Reporting:** weekly KPIs by truck and by driver

## Common growth mistakes

- Buying trucks faster than you can find good drivers
- Hiring a driver you would not trust with your own truck because the truck is sitting
- Letting compliance paperwork fall behind as you get busy
- Counting gross revenue instead of profit per truck
- Spending the reserve on the next down payment

## How Texas Solutions can help

Texas Solutions is a dispatch service, not a broker or motor carrier. As you grow, our dispatchers find and negotiate loads for every truck, plan lanes to keep units moving, handle broker packets and paperwork, and work 24/7, while you approve every load. ### Fuel-Saving Tips for Truckers: Cut Your Diesel Bill
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/fuel-saving-tips-for-truckers/
Published: 2026-10-21

Fuel is usually one of the largest costs an owner-operator controls. Prices move with the market, but how much fuel you burn is largely up to you. These **fuel-saving tips for truckers** focus on habits and maintenance that cost little or nothing and pay back on every mile.

## Know your real mpg first

You cannot improve what you do not measure. Track fuel for each fill-up and the miles driven between fill-ups, then calculate mpg for each week and each load type. The dash display is helpful, but your own records are more reliable.

Watch for patterns:

- Heavier loads and hilly routes lower mpg.
- Winter fuel blends and cold weather often reduce mpg.
- A sudden drop with no obvious cause can point to a mechanical problem.

Put your numbers into the [truck fuel cost calculator](/truck-fuel-cost-calculator.html) to see what fuel costs you per mile.

## Driving habits that save fuel

### Slow down and stay steady

Wind resistance grows fast as speed rises, so a few miles per hour can make a clear difference in fuel burned. A steady, moderate cruising speed is one of the easiest ways to save. Running slower does add some time, so weigh it against your appointments and hours of service.

### Smooth acceleration and braking

Hard acceleration and late braking waste fuel. Look far ahead, ease off early for traffic and lights, and let momentum carry the truck where it is safe to do so.

### Use cruise control wisely

On flat and gently rolling roads, cruise control keeps speed steady. In steep terrain, many drivers do better managing the throttle themselves so the truck is not downshifting hard to hold a set speed on climbs.

### Shift efficiently

With a manual transmission, shift progressively and keep the engine in its efficient RPM range. With an automated transmission, learn the eco settings and let the system work as designed.

### Cut idle time

Idling burns fuel while the truck earns nothing, and it adds engine hours that bring maintenance due sooner. Ways to reduce it:

- Use an auxiliary power unit, battery HVAC system or bunk heater for rest breaks.
- Shut the engine off during loading, unloading and long waits when weather and safety allow.
- Use shore power at truck stops that offer it.
- Check state and city anti-idling rules where you park, because limits and exemptions vary.

## Tires and maintenance

### Tire pressure

Underinflated tires increase rolling resistance and wear. Check pressure regularly with a gauge, not just a thump, and set it to the manufacturer's recommendation for your load. Consider low-rolling-resistance tires when it is time to replace.

### Alignment

Poor alignment drags the truck and wears tires unevenly. Have it checked after hitting a curb or pothole hard, and at regular intervals.

### Engine and filters

Clean air and fuel filters, proper oil, healthy injectors and a working aftertreatment system all help mpg. Our [truck maintenance schedule](/blog/truck-maintenance-schedule.html) guide covers what to check and when.

## Aerodynamics, weight and equipment

### Aerodynamics

Air resistance is a big share of fuel burned at highway speeds. Helpful steps:

- Keep the tractor-trailer gap as small as safely possible.
- Make sure fairings, side extenders and trailer skirts are in place and undamaged.
- Remove unneeded exterior items such as extra lights or racks that catch wind.
- On flatbeds, keep tarps tight and loads low and neat where possible.

### Weight and equipment choices

Every extra pound has to be pulled up every hill. Clear out tools, spare parts and personal items you do not need, and keep the fuel tanks only as full as your route requires when you are close to weight limits.

When buying or replacing equipment, ask how the choice affects fuel. Engine and transmission specs, rear axle ratio, tire type and aerodynamic packages all play a part. A truck spec'd for the work you actually do, such as regional versus long haul, usually burns less fuel than one built for a different job.

## Smart fueling and trip planning

### Plan fuel stops by price

Diesel prices vary between states and between stops on the same highway, partly because fuel taxes differ by state. Plan where to fill up instead of buying wherever the tank runs low.

### Use a fuel card that fits your lanes

Fuel cards can offer discounts at participating stops and make record keeping easier for IFTA. Compare network coverage, fees and discount types before choosing. See [how to choose a fuel card for truckers](/blog/how-to-choose-a-fuel-card-for-truckers.html).

### Cut empty miles

The cheapest gallon is the one you never burn. Planning reloads before delivery, avoiding long deadheads and choosing balanced lanes all save fuel. Planning the full loop is covered in our guide to [plan a profitable round trip](/blog/plan-a-profitable-round-trip.html).

### Avoid congestion

Stop-and-go traffic is hard on fuel. Where your schedule allows, time trips through big cities outside rush hours.

## Worked example: what better mpg is worth

Hypothetical numbers: you drive 100,000 miles a year and diesel averages $4.00 per gallon.

| | At 6.0 mpg | At 6.5 mpg |
|---|---|---|
| Gallons used | about 16,667 | about 15,385 |
| Fuel cost | about $66,667 | about $61,538 |

Raising mpg by half a mile per gallon saves about 1,280 gallons, or roughly $5,100 a year in this example. That is why small habits matter.

## Fuel-saving checklist

- [ ] Track mpg by fill-up and by week.
- [ ] Set a steady, moderate cruising speed.
- [ ] Limit idling; use an APU or other idle-reduction option.
- [ ] Check tire pressure regularly and fix alignment issues.
- [ ] Keep filters, engine and aftertreatment in good shape.
- [ ] Keep aerodynamic parts in place and the trailer gap tight.
- [ ] Plan fuel stops by price and use a card that fits your lanes.
- [ ] Plan reloads to cut deadhead.

## How Texas Solutions can help

Texas Solutions is a dispatch service, not a broker or motor carrier. Our dispatchers plan loads to reduce empty miles, negotiate rates, and handle broker packets and paperwork 24/7, and you approve every load. To keep the truck loaded and moving efficiently, [talk to a dispatcher](/contact.html).

### Freight Market Calendar: Busy and Slow Months for Truckers
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/freight-market-calendar/
Published: 2026-10-21

Freight does not move evenly through the year. Harvests, retail stocking, holidays and weather all shift how many loads are posted and how many trucks are chasing them. A simple **freight market calendar** helps you plan cash flow, maintenance and home time around the months that tend to pay best and the months that tend to drag.

## Why seasonality matters for an owner-operator

Spot rates move with the balance between loads and trucks. When shippers have more freight than the market has trucks, rates rise. When trucks outnumber loads, rates fall and brokers have more leverage.

For a one-truck operation, those swings show up directly in weekly gross. Knowing roughly when they happen lets you:

- Build a cash reserve during strong months to cover the slow ones.
- Schedule maintenance and home time when the truck would earn the least.
- Position the truck near busy regions before demand peaks.
- Negotiate harder when capacity is tight, and accept that some weeks are about covering costs.

Keep in mind that the wider economy, fuel prices and regulations can override normal seasonal patterns. Treat this calendar as a starting point, then watch what your own lanes do.

## Month-by-month freight calendar

| Period | What usually happens | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| January | Post-holiday slowdown, returns freight, winter weather | Expect softer rates; plan maintenance and paperwork |
| February | Still soft in many lanes; early produce from southern regions | Watch southern reefer freight; protect cash |
| March | Freight builds; quarter-end push; spring produce grows | Look for better outbound options; firm up rates |
| April - May | Produce moves north; construction picks up; inspection blitzes | Strong month for reefer and flatbed in many areas |
| June | Quarter-end push; hurricane season begins | Watch for storm-related disruptions and relief freight |
| July | Holiday week squeeze around July 4; summer produce | Plan around the holiday; check reefer demand |
| August - October | Retail stocking for back-to-school and the holidays; harvest freight | Often the strongest stretch for dry van and reefer |
| November | Thanksgiving squeeze; holiday food and retail freight | Book ahead; expect tight capacity around the holiday |
| December | Early month busy, then slows near Christmas | Decide on home time; book loads before the holiday lull |

This table is a general pattern, not a forecast. Your region, trailer type and customer base can shift every line of it.

### Spring: produce and construction

Produce season is one of the biggest seasonal drivers for refrigerated freight. Harvests usually start in the southern states and move north as the weather warms, which pulls reefer capacity toward those growing regions. If you run a reefer, the [reefer loads guide](/blog/reefer-loads-refrigerated-dispatch-guide.html) covers how to work those markets.

Spring also brings construction back. Flatbed demand for lumber, steel and building materials usually firms up as job sites reopen after winter.

**Inspection blitzes.**

CVSA runs enforcement events during the year, including a multi-day roadside inspection blitz that is usually held in spring. Some drivers park during those days, which can tighten capacity in certain areas. Check the CVSA website for the dates each year, and make sure your truck and paperwork are ready regardless.

### Summer: holidays, heat and storms

Holiday weeks such as Memorial Day, July 4 and Labor Day usually cause short capacity squeezes. Many drivers take time off, while shippers still need loads moved before and after the holiday.

Hurricane season in the Atlantic runs roughly from June through November. Storms can shut down lanes, delay pickups and create sudden demand for relief and rebuilding freight. Keep an eye on the weather when you book loads into the Gulf Coast or the Southeast.

Summer heat also matters for reefer operators, since temperature-sensitive loads need reliable equipment and careful pre-cooling.

### Fall: peak season

For many dry van and reefer carriers, late summer and fall are the strongest stretch of the year. Retailers stock up for back-to-school and holiday sales, and harvest freight adds to the volume. Read our [peak season guide](/blog/peak-season-trucking-loads-holiday-freight.html) for how to make the most of it.

Peak season is also when rate confirmations get rushed. Read every rate con carefully, confirm detention and layover terms, and do not let a busy week push you into a load that does not cover your costs.

### Winter: the slow stretch

After the holidays, retail freight drops and many lanes go soft. January and February are often the hardest months for owner-operators who rely only on the spot market. Winter weather also adds risk, delays and chain-law requirements in mountain states.

Use this time to:

1. Do major maintenance and inspections.
2. Review last year's numbers and your cost per mile.
3. Update your broker packet and insurance certificates.
4. Build relationships with shippers or brokers that move steady freight year-round.

## Weekly and monthly patterns too

Seasonality is not just about months. Many lanes also have weekly rhythms:

- **Monday and Friday** can be busier for posted loads in some markets.
- **Friday afternoon** loads may pay more if a broker needs a truck before the weekend.
- **Month-end and quarter-end** often bring a push as shippers try to move product before the books close.

Track these patterns in your own lanes for a few months. A simple spreadsheet with date, lane, rate and load count will show you more than any general rule.

## Worked example: planning a slow month

Here is a hypothetical example. Say your all-in cost is $1.90 per mile and you usually run 10,000 miles a month. That is $19,000 a month in costs.

- In a strong month, you average $2.60 per mile: $26,000 gross, about $7,000 above cost.
- In a slow month, you average $2.05 per mile: $20,500 gross, only $1,500 above cost.

If you set aside part of the strong-month profit, the slow month stops being a crisis. Check your own numbers with the [cost per mile calculator](/cost-per-mile-calculator.html).

## How Texas Solutions can help

Texas Solutions is a dispatch service, not a broker or motor carrier. Our dispatchers watch the market every day, find and negotiate loads, handle broker packets and paperwork 24/7, and you approve every load before it is booked. If you want help planning around the busy and slow seasons, [talk to a dispatcher](/contact.html) or see our [dispatch services](/dispatch.html).

### Flatbed Cargo Securement: Rules, Math and a Checklist
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/flatbed-cargo-securement/
Published: 2026-10-21

**Flatbed cargo securement** is where flatbed drivers earn their pay and protect their record. The federal rules are in 49 CFR 393.100 through 393.136, and inspectors check them closely. This guide covers the core math, the commodity rules you need to know, and a checklist you can use on every load.

## The performance standard behind the rules

The securement system as a whole must be strong enough to hold the cargo against set forces. In plain terms, it must keep the load from moving under:

- **0.8 g** forward deceleration (hard braking)
- **0.5 g** rearward acceleration
- **0.5 g** sideways (lateral) force
- Enough downward force to prevent vertical movement when the cargo is not otherwise fully contained

You do not need to calculate g-forces on every load. The tiedown and working load limit rules below are designed to meet these standards for typical freight.

## Rule 1: working load limit (WLL)

Every tiedown has a working load limit, which should be marked on the strap, chain or binder by the manufacturer. The rule:

> The aggregate WLL of all tiedowns must be **at least 50% of the weight of the cargo**.

How each tiedown counts:

- **Indirect tiedown** (trailer, over or through the cargo, back to the trailer): counts its **full** WLL.
- **Direct tiedown** (trailer straight to an attachment point on the cargo): counts **half** its WLL.
- The weakest component sets the WLL. A strong chain with a weak binder or hook is only as strong as the binder or hook.

## Rule 2: minimum number of tiedowns

Separately from WLL, each article needs a minimum number of tiedowns based on its length and weight. If the article is **not** blocked at the front by a headboard or another article:

| Article | Minimum tiedowns |
|---|---|
| 5 ft or shorter and 1,100 lbs or less | 1 |
| 5 ft or shorter and over 1,100 lbs | 2 |
| Longer than 5 ft, up to 10 ft | 2 |
| Longer than 10 ft | 2, plus 1 for each additional 10 ft or part of 10 ft |

If the article **is** blocked against forward movement by a headboard, bulkhead or other cargo that is itself secured, the minimum is generally one tiedown for each 10 ft of length or part of it.

You must satisfy **both** rules. Plenty of loads meet the WLL with three heavy chains but still need more tiedowns because of their length.

## Worked example

Hypothetical load: three bundles of steel tubing, each 20 ft long and 12,000 lbs, for 36,000 lbs total, loaded side by side and **not** blocked by the headboard.

**Count per bundle:** 20 ft is longer than 10 ft, so 2 for the first 10 ft plus 1 for the next 10 ft = **3 tiedowns per bundle**, or 9 total.

**WLL:** half of 36,000 lbs is 18,000 lbs. If you use straps over the top (indirect) each marked with a WLL of 5,000 lbs, nine straps give 45,000 lbs of aggregate WLL. That clears 18,000 lbs comfortably.

Both rules are met. If the bundles were blocked against the headboard, the minimum count would drop to 2 per bundle, but most drivers still add extra straps for real-world safety margin.

## Commodity-specific rules

Some cargo has its own section in the regulations, and those rules apply on top of (or instead of) the general rules. The main ones:

- **Logs**
- **Dressed lumber and similar building products**
- **Metal coils** (different rules for eyes vertical, eyes crosswise and eyes lengthwise)
- **Paper rolls**
- **Concrete pipe**
- **Intermodal containers**
- **Automobiles, light trucks and vans**
- **Heavy vehicles, equipment and machinery** (for example, items over 10,000 lbs generally need at least four tiedowns, with accessories like blades and buckets lowered and secured)
- **Flattened or crushed vehicles**
- **Roll-on/roll-off and hook-lift containers**
- **Large boulders**

If you haul any of these regularly, read that section of the regulations and FMCSA's driver's handbook on cargo securement until you know it well. Metal coils and heavy machinery are the two that trip up new flatbedders most often.

## Condition of your gear

Securement violations are often about worn equipment, not the number of straps. Inspectors look for:

- Cuts, tears, burns or broken stitching on straps
- Knots in straps or chains
- Cracked, stretched or damaged chain links, hooks and binders
- Missing WLL markings
- No edge protection where a strap crosses a sharp edge

Use edge protectors on any sharp or abrasive edge. Retire damaged gear right away; it is cheaper than an out-of-service order. Our guide on [out-of-service criteria](/blog/out-of-service-criteria.html) explains what can sideline a truck.

## When to re-check

Under the driver inspection rule:

1. Inspect cargo and securement **before** the trip.
2. Re-check **within the first 50 miles** and adjust as needed.
3. Re-check **when your duty status changes, or after 3 hours or 150 miles of driving, whichever comes first.**

Straps loosen as loads settle and as temperatures change, especially with lumber and tarped loads. Build these stops into your trip plan so they do not eat into your hours unexpectedly. Add them to your [pre-trip inspection checklist](/blog/pre-trip-inspection-checklist.html).

## Overhang and wide loads

- Cargo extending **more than 4 ft beyond the rear** (or projecting beyond the sides) must be marked with red or orange warning flags, and with lights when lamps are required.
- Anything wider than legal width or taller than the state's height limit needs a permit. See [oversize and overweight permits](/blog/oversize-overweight-permits.html).

## Pre-departure securement checklist

- Weight of each article known and written down
- Tiedown count meets the length rule for each article
- Aggregate WLL is at least half the cargo weight
- All gear marked with WLL and in good condition
- Edge protection on sharp edges
- Commodity-specific rules checked if they apply
- Loose items, dunnage and tarps secured
- Overhang flagged; permits on board if oversize
- Re-check stops planned at 50 miles and every 3 hours or 150 miles

Rules can be updated and interpretations vary. Confirm current requirements with FMCSA and the CVSA out-of-service criteria, and follow any stricter shipper instructions.

## How Texas Solutions can help

Texas Solutions is a dispatch service, not a broker or a motor carrier. Our [flatbed dispatch](/flatbed-dispatch.html) team finds and negotiates loads that match your trailer and securement gear, handles broker packets and paperwork 24/7, and you approve every load. You can also [talk to a dispatcher](/contact.html).

### How to Start a Final Mile Delivery Business
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/final-mile-delivery-business/
Published: 2026-10-21

A **final mile delivery business** handles the last step of the supply chain: taking furniture, appliances, fitness equipment and other bulky goods from a local hub to the customer's door. It is a local, route-based business with steady volume in many markets, but it is very different from running loads off a load board. You manage crews, customer service and damage risk every single day.

## How final mile works

Retailers and manufacturers ship goods to a regional warehouse or cross-dock. From there, a final mile carrier picks up a planned route each morning and delivers to homes or businesses within a set area. Service levels vary:

- **Threshold:** drop at the door or garage.
- **Room of choice:** carry the item inside to the room the customer picks.
- **White glove:** carry in, unpack, assemble or install, and remove packaging.
- **Haul-away:** take the old item back to the hub or a disposal site.

Higher service levels pay more but take longer per stop and carry more damage risk.

## Who you work for

Most final mile carriers do not find their own freight day to day. They usually work through:

- **Logistics companies** that hold contracts with big retailers and hire contract carriers to run routes.
- **Retailers or manufacturers** directly, often after you build a track record.
- **Regional furniture and appliance stores** that need delivery help without running their own trucks.

Some carriers mix final mile with over-the-road box truck freight to fill slow days or weeks. That gives you flexibility but takes planning.

## Equipment and crew

### Truck

The workhorse of final mile is the non-CDL box truck, commonly around 26 feet with a liftgate. Contracts often set rules on truck age, length, liftgate capacity and appearance. Smaller vans can work for parcels and light items. See [box truck vs cargo van](/blog/box-truck-vs-cargo-van.html) for the trade-offs.

### Gear checklist

- Liftgate in good working order
- Hand trucks and an appliance dolly
- Moving blankets and pads
- Straps, load bars and E-track
- Basic tools for assembly and install
- Floor protection and shoe covers
- A phone mount and a reliable delivery app (usually provided by the contractor)

### Crew

Bulky goods usually need a two-person team: a driver and a helper. Your crew is the face of the business, since they are in customers' homes. Hire for reliability and attitude, and train on lifting, customer service and damage prevention. Talk to an attorney or CPA about whether crew members should be employees or contractors, because misclassification can be costly.

## Paperwork and insurance

Requirements depend on your state, your vehicle weight and whether you cross state lines. Confirm with FMCSA and your state. A typical setup includes:

1. Business entity and EIN
2. USDOT number, and operating authority if you haul for-hire across state lines or the contract requires it
3. Commercial auto liability, cargo insurance and general liability
4. Workers' compensation if you have employees (rules vary by state)
5. DOT medical cards and hours-of-service compliance where your vehicle weight requires them

Contractors often require specific insurance limits and name themselves as additional insured. Ask your insurance agent to review the contract's requirements before you sign. Our [trucking authority setup](/trucking-authority-setup.html) service can help with the registration side.

## How the money works

Pay models vary by contract: per stop, per route, per day or a combination, sometimes with bonuses or extra pay for assembly and haul-away. The details that hurt carriers most are often in the fine print:

- **Damage chargebacks** deducted from settlements
- **Customer complaint penalties** or service score requirements
- **Failed delivery** pay (or no pay) when the customer is not home
- **Fuel** whether it is included or paid separately

### Hypothetical daily example

Say a route pays $55 per stop and you run 12 stops.

- Revenue: 12 x $55 = **$660**
- Helper pay for the day: $180
- Fuel (120 miles at 9 mpg, $3.80/gal): about $51
- Truck, insurance and maintenance share per day: $220
- Daily cost before your pay: **$451**
- Left for you: **$209**

One damage chargeback can wipe out that margin. That is why route density, careful handling and a good crew matter so much. Track your true cost with the [cost per mile calculator](/cost-per-mile-calculator.html) and your crew costs with the [driver pay calculator](/driver-pay-calculator.html).

## Questions to ask before signing a contract

- How many stops per route on average, and how are routes assigned?
- How are damage claims investigated and charged back?
- What happens to pay on failed or refused deliveries?
- What are the truck, insurance and background check requirements?
- How often and how fast are settlements paid?
- Can I run other freight on days with no route?

Get the answers in writing.

## Tips to protect your margin

- **Photograph every item** at pickup and after delivery, including the packaging. Photos are your best defense against damage claims.
- **Inspect before you load.** Note any box damage on the paperwork at the hub, not after the customer opens it.
- **Plan the load order** so the last stop goes in first and nothing gets moved twice.
- **Call ahead** to confirm the customer is home and to ask about stairs, tight doors or elevators.
- **Keep your crew steady.** Training a new helper every month costs time, damage and customer scores.
- **Track results per route** so you know which routes make money and which only keep the truck busy.

## How Texas Solutions can help

Texas Solutions is a dispatch service, not a broker or motor carrier. If you run box trucks and want over-the-road or regional loads alongside your routes, our [box truck dispatch](/box-truck-dispatch.html) team finds and negotiates loads, handles broker packets and paperwork 24/7, and you approve every load. [Talk to a dispatcher](/contact.html) to see if it fits your schedule.

### Expedited Freight: How It Works and How to Haul It
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/expedited-freight-guide/
Published: 2026-10-21

**Expedited freight** is the part of trucking where time matters more than anything else. A factory line is down waiting for a part, a hospital needs supplies tonight, or a shipment missed its original truck. The shipper pays for a dedicated vehicle that goes straight to the receiver, and the carrier that answers fast and delivers on time gets the next call.

## What makes freight "expedited"

Expedited freight usually has these traits:

- **Time-critical delivery.** Often same-day, overnight or a guaranteed appointment.
- **Exclusive use.** The vehicle carries only that shipment, with no other pickups or drops on the way.
- **Short notice.** Loads can come in with an hour or less before pickup.
- **Direct routing.** The driver goes from pickup to delivery with only legal breaks and fuel stops.
- **Close tracking.** Shippers and brokers expect regular updates and fast proof of delivery.

The freight itself can be small, like a box of parts, or a full truckload. What makes it expedited is the service, not the size.

## Vehicle types in expedite

| Vehicle | Typical freight | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Cargo or sprinter van | Small, light shipments | Lowest cost, lots of competition |
| Straight truck (box truck) | Several pallets, often with liftgate | Popular for regional expedite |
| Hotshot (pickup plus trailer) | Machinery parts, oilfield, construction | Often flatbed or gooseneck |
| Semi with team drivers | Full loads over long distances | Team keeps the truck moving around the clock |

Many expedite carriers equip vehicles with E-track, load bars, pallet jacks and sometimes temperature control. Some customers also ask for drivers with hazmat endorsements, TWIC cards or the ability to cross into Canada, since those widen the freight you can take. Our [hotshot business guide](/blog/how-to-start-a-hotshot-business.html) covers the pickup-and-trailer side.

## How expedited rates work

Expedite is usually priced per mile or as a flat rate for the run, with the premium reflecting speed and exclusive use. Things that raise the rate:

- Very short notice
- Tight or overnight delivery windows
- Team service
- Special requirements (liftgate, temperature, hazmat, security)
- Weekend and holiday runs

The catch is that expedite can be lumpy. You might run hard for three days, then sit waiting for the next load. Some carriers wait close to freight-heavy areas so they can respond fast when a call comes in. That waiting time is usually unpaid.

### Hypothetical weekly example

A straight truck runs three expedited loads in a week:

- Load 1: 450 miles at $2.60/mile = $1,170
- Load 2: 300 miles at $2.80/mile = $840
- Load 3: 620 miles at $2.50/mile = $1,550
- Total revenue: **$3,560** on 1,370 loaded miles
- Empty repositioning between loads: 400 miles
- Effective rate per total mile: $3,560 / 1,770 = **about $2.01**

That is still decent, but it is a lot lower than the rate on any single load. Check your own numbers with the [deadhead miles calculator](/deadhead-miles-calculator.html).

## Hours of service and team driving

Expedite tempts drivers to push, but hours-of-service rules still apply to vehicles covered by them. A solo driver in a covered vehicle has limits on daily driving and on-duty time, plus weekly limits. When a delivery is too far to reach legally solo, the answer is a team, not a falsified log. Learn the limits in our [hours of service guide](/blog/hours-of-service-rules-explained-11-14-70-hour.html), and if you are thinking of running with a partner, read the [team driving guide](/blog/team-driving-guide.html). Always confirm current rules with FMCSA.

## What it takes to succeed in expedite

1. **Be reachable.** Many loads go to the first qualified carrier who answers. Missing calls means missing freight.
2. **Be honest about ETAs.** Give a realistic pickup and delivery time, then beat it. A missed promise on a critical load loses the customer.
3. **Keep the vehicle ready.** Fuel up, keep equipment stocked, and stay ahead on maintenance. A breakdown on an expedited load is a disaster for everyone.
4. **Communicate constantly.** Send pickup confirmation, regular location updates and proof of delivery right away.
5. **Position smartly.** Learn which areas generate expedited freight and where you can get reloaded.
6. **Keep paperwork clean.** Current insurance, authority and carrier packets let you get set up with new brokers quickly.

## Pros and cons

**Pros**

- Higher pay per loaded mile than standard freight in many cases
- Often quicker loading and unloading, since the freight is urgent for the receiver too
- Strong repeat business once customers trust you

**Cons**

- Irregular schedule and unpaid waiting time
- High pressure on every load
- More empty miles repositioning
- Little room for mechanical problems

## Is expedite right for you?

Expedite fits drivers who like to move fast, stay on the phone and do not mind an unpredictable schedule. If you want a regular home time and the same lanes every week, dedicated or regional freight may suit you better. Many carriers mix both, taking expedited loads when they pay well and standard freight to fill the gaps.

## How Texas Solutions can help

Texas Solutions is a dispatch service, not a broker or motor carrier. For box trucks, hotshots and semis, our dispatchers find and negotiate loads, including urgent ones, handle broker packets and paperwork, and work 24/7 so short-notice freight does not slip by, and you approve every load. See our [dispatch services](/dispatch.html) or [talk to a dispatcher](/contact.html).

### Entry-Level Driver Training (ELDT): What New CDL Drivers Need
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/entry-level-driver-training-eldt/
Published: 2026-10-21

**Entry-level driver training (ELDT)** is the federal minimum training standard for new commercial drivers. It changed how people get a CDL: you can no longer just study the manual, practice with a friend and show up for the skills test. For carriers, it also changes how you think about hiring new drivers. Here is how it works.

## What ELDT is

FMCSA's ELDT rules (49 CFR Part 380) took effect on February 7, 2022. They set a minimum training curriculum for certain CDL applicants, require that training come from a registered provider, and require the provider to report completion electronically to FMCSA before the driver can take the related test.

The rules set a floor. They do not replace state CDL testing, and they do not guarantee a carrier or insurer will consider the driver experienced.

## Who needs ELDT

In general, you need ELDT if you are:

- Getting a **Class A CDL** for the first time
- Getting a **Class B CDL** for the first time
- **Upgrading** from Class B to Class A
- Getting a **hazmat (H)** endorsement for the first time
- Getting a **passenger (P)** or **school bus (S)** endorsement for the first time

Generally, you do **not** need ELDT if you already held the CDL or endorsement before February 7, 2022, or if you got a commercial learner's permit (CLP) before that date and got your CDL before the CLP expired. There are some other exceptions (for example, certain military drivers and drivers covered by specific waivers). Check the current list on the FMCSA website and with your state licensing agency.

## The two parts of training

### Theory (classroom or online)

Theory covers topics such as basic vehicle operation, safe driving, hours of service, cargo, trip planning, wellness and whistleblower rights. It can be delivered online or in a classroom. There is no minimum hour requirement, but the student must pass a final assessment with the score the rule requires (80 percent).

### Behind-the-wheel (BTW)

BTW has two pieces:

- **Range training** on a closed course: pre-trip inspection, straight backing, offset backing, parallel parking, alley dock and coupling.
- **Public road training**: turns, lane changes, intersections, railroad crossings, highway driving, night operation where applicable, and more.

BTW also has no federal minimum hours. The instructor decides when the student shows proficiency. Hazmat endorsement training is theory only.

## The Training Provider Registry

The Training Provider Registry (TPR) is FMCSA's online list of approved providers. Every provider that delivers ELDT must be listed there, from large schools to a single carrier training its own drivers.

How it works, step by step:

1. **Pick a provider** listed on the TPR. Confirm it offers the specific class or endorsement you need.
2. **Get your CLP** from your state (for Class A or B). Many states require you to hold it for a minimum period before the skills test.
3. **Complete theory and BTW training.**
4. **The provider submits your completion** to the TPR. The rule gives providers a short deadline (by the end of the second business day after completion).
5. **FMCSA passes the record to your state**, which then lets you schedule the skills test (or the hazmat knowledge test).
6. **Take and pass the state test.**

If your state will not schedule your test, the most common cause is a missing or delayed TPR record. Contact the provider first.

## Checklist for new CDL candidates

- [ ] Confirm whether you need ELDT for your license class or endorsement
- [ ] Choose a provider listed on the Training Provider Registry
- [ ] Pass your DOT physical and get a medical certificate (see the [medical card and DOT physical](/blog/medical-card-and-dot-physical.html) guide)
- [ ] Get your CLP and note how long you must hold it before testing
- [ ] Complete theory and pass the assessment
- [ ] Complete range and public road BTW training
- [ ] Confirm the provider submitted your record to the TPR
- [ ] Schedule and pass the skills test
- [ ] For hazmat, also complete the TSA security threat assessment

## What carriers should know before hiring an ELDT graduate

A new CDL holder is legally able to drive, but insurance and real-world readiness are different questions.

- **Insurance:** many commercial auto insurers set experience and age minimums for drivers they will cover. A driver fresh out of school may not be acceptable, or may raise your premium. Ask your insurance agent before you make an offer.
- **Finishing training:** ELDT is a minimum. Many carriers add their own orientation, ride-along time or a mentoring period, especially for backing, docking and trip planning.
- **Qualification still applies:** a new driver needs a full DQ file, a pre-employment drug test and a Clearinghouse query just like anyone else. Use the [driver qualification file checklist](/blog/driver-qualification-file-checklist.html) and the [drug and alcohol testing program](/blog/drug-and-alcohol-testing-program.html) guide.
- **Interstate age rule:** drivers generally must be at least 21 to drive a CMV in interstate commerce. Confirm any current pilot programs with FMCSA.

If you are building toward hiring, our guide to [hiring your first truck driver](/blog/hiring-your-first-truck-driver.html) walks through the full process.

## Hypothetical example: cost of getting a Class A

The numbers below are made up to show the parts of the total cost, not real prices.

| Item | Hypothetical cost |
|---|---|
| ELDT theory and BTW (school) | $5,000 |
| DOT physical | $100 |
| CLP and CDL state fees | $150 |
| Hazmat endorsement plus TSA check | $200 |
| **Total** | **$5,450** |

Some carriers pay for training in exchange for a work commitment. Read those contracts carefully, especially repayment terms if you leave early, and talk to an attorney if anything is unclear.
