Read about [semi truck dispatch](/semi-truck-dispatch.html) or [talk to a dispatcher](/contact.html).

### ELD Malfunction Rules: What to Do When Your ELD Fails
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/eld-malfunction-rules/
Published: 2026-10-21

An ELD that freezes, loses its connection to the engine or stops recording can stop your day in its tracks if you do not know the **ELD malfunction rules**. The good news is that the federal rule gives drivers a clear procedure, so a broken device does not have to mean a violation or a parked truck.

This guide explains what counts as a malfunction, what the driver must do, what the carrier must do, and how to stay ready before anything goes wrong. The rule lives in 49 CFR 395.34. Always confirm the current text with FMCSA, since guidance and interpretations can change.

## What counts as an ELD malfunction

Registered ELDs are required to monitor themselves and flag problems. Problems fall into two groups:

- **Malfunctions.** The device cannot reliably do one of its core jobs. The rule lists malfunction types such as power compliance, engine synchronization, timing, positioning, data recording, data transfer and "other" malfunctions identified by the manufacturer.
- **Data diagnostic events.** Something is wrong with the data, but the device may still be working. Examples include power data diagnostics, engine synchronization diagnostics, missing required data elements, data transfer issues and unidentified driving records.

Most ELDs show an "M" indicator for a malfunction and a "D" indicator for a data diagnostic event, along with a code. Your ELD user manual explains what each code means for your specific device. A data diagnostic event usually means you should fix the data (for example, accept or reject unidentified driving, or re-pair a tablet), while a malfunction triggers the formal procedure below.

## Driver steps when the ELD malfunctions

When the device shows a malfunction, or you notice it is not recording properly, follow these steps:

1. **Note the malfunction.** Write down the date, time, what happened and any code shown on the screen. A photo of the screen is a useful backup.
2. **Notify your motor carrier in writing within 24 hours.** A text, email or message through your company's system creates a record. If you are leased on, this goes to the carrier whose authority you run under.
3. **Reconstruct your records.** If the ELD cannot display your logs, recreate your records of duty status on paper for the current 24-hour period and the previous 7 consecutive days. Skip any days you can still pull from the device or another source.
4. **Keep paper logs until the ELD is fixed.** Continue on graph-grid paper logs (or another method allowed by the rule) until the device is repaired or replaced and working again.
5. **Show the inspector what you have.** At a roadside inspection, explain the malfunction, show your notice to the carrier and present your paper logs.

### What to keep in the cab at all times

The rule requires an ELD information packet in the truck. Use this as a quick checklist:

- [ ] ELD user manual (paper or electronic)
- [ ] Instruction sheet explaining how to transfer data to an inspector
- [ ] Instruction sheet explaining malfunction reporting and recordkeeping
- [ ] Blank paper graph-grid logs for at least 8 days
- [ ] A pen and a copy of your recent hours, if you can print or save them

Missing instruction sheets or blank logs is an easy violation to avoid. Check the packet each time you do a pre-trip inspection or change trucks.

## Carrier steps and the repair deadline

The motor carrier also has duties once it learns about a malfunction:

- **Repair or replace the ELD within 8 days** of discovering the problem or receiving the driver's notice, whichever comes first.
- **Make sure drivers keep paper records** in the meantime.
- **Request an extension if needed.** If the carrier cannot fix the problem in time, it can ask FMCSA for an extension. The request generally goes to the FMCSA Division Administrator for the carrier's principal place of business, within 5 days after the driver's notice, with an explanation of the problem and the plan to fix it.

Keep copies of the driver's notice, repair or replacement records and any extension request. These are the first things an auditor will ask for if a malfunction shows up during an investigation.

## A simple timeline example

Here is a hypothetical example of how this plays out:

| Day | What happens |
|---|---|
| Monday 2 p.m. | ELD shows an engine sync malfunction. Driver notes the time and code and takes a photo. |
| Monday 3 p.m. | Driver emails the carrier about the malfunction (well inside 24 hours). |
| Monday 3 p.m. | Driver reconstructs the day and the prior 7 days on paper, since the tablet cannot display them. |
| Tuesday to Thursday | Driver runs on paper logs. Carrier orders a replacement cable. |
| Friday | New cable installed, ELD reconnects, driver goes back to electronic logs. Carrier files the repair record. |

The device was repaired 4 days after the notice, inside the 8-day window. If the part had been backordered, the carrier would have needed to request an extension before the deadline rather than letting the driver run on paper indefinitely.

## Common causes and quick fixes

Many "malfunctions" are connection problems you can solve in minutes:

- **Loose or damaged cable** at the diagnostic port. Reseat it and check for bent pins.
- **Bluetooth or tablet pairing lost.** Restart the app and the tablet, then re-pair.
- **Outdated app or firmware.** Update on Wi-Fi before trips, not at a weigh station.
- **Power issues** after a jump start, battery swap or wiring work.
- **Poor GPS signal** in terminals or tunnels, which often clears on its own.

If a quick fix works and the indicator clears, note what happened anyway. If it does not clear, treat it as a malfunction and start the procedure. Never unplug the device to avoid recording time. Tampering is a serious violation and can lead to penalties for both the driver and the carrier.

## How malfunctions affect your trip planning

Paper logs do not change your hours of service limits. You still have the same 11-hour driving limit, 14-hour window and 60/70-hour cycle. They do mean more work at every stop and more scrutiny at inspections, so build in a little extra time. Our [hours of service rules guide](/blog/hours-of-service-rules-explained-11-14-70-hour.html) covers the limits, and the [hours of service calculator](/hours-of-service-calculator.html) helps you plan a day by hand when the ELD is down.

If you keep running into malfunctions, the device itself may be the problem. See [how to choose an ELD](/blog/how-to-choose-an-eld.html) for the features and support questions to ask before you switch.

Our dispatchers find and negotiate loads, handle broker packets and paperwork 24/7, and plan around your available hours, including days when you are on paper logs, while you approve every load. ### DOT Drug and Alcohol Testing Program for Owner-Operators
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/drug-and-alcohol-testing-program/
Published: 2026-10-21

A **DOT drug and alcohol testing program** is one of the first things a new carrier needs and one of the most common reasons new carriers fail their safety audit. If you or any of your drivers need a CDL for the vehicle you operate, the program is not optional. Here is how it works and how to set it up as a one-truck or small fleet operation.

## Who must have a testing program

The FMCSA testing rules (49 CFR Part 382, with procedures in Part 40) apply to employers of drivers who operate commercial motor vehicles that require a CDL. That includes owner-operators who are both the employer and the driver. Typical semi trucks are covered.

Non-CDL operations, such as many cargo van, box truck and hotshot setups under the CDL weight thresholds, are generally outside Part 382. Some brokers, shippers or insurers may still ask for testing as a business requirement. When in doubt, check with FMCSA about your exact equipment.

## Setup checklist for a new carrier

Do these in order, before your first load:

1. [ ] **Choose a consortium or third-party administrator (C/TPA).** It manages the random pool, schedules tests through collection sites, and keeps many of the records. Ask what is included: random selection, collection site network, medical review officer, annual summary, Clearinghouse support and post-accident help after hours.
2. [ ] **Adopt a written testing policy** that covers the required topics, and give a copy to every driver. Keep signed receipts.
3. [ ] **Name a designated employer representative (DER)**, the person who receives results and removes drivers from duty. For a one-truck carrier, that is usually you.
4. [ ] **Register in the Clearinghouse** as an employer and, if you are an owner-operator, designate your C/TPA so it can report on your behalf.
5. [ ] **Get a pre-employment drug test** with a verified negative result before any safety-sensitive work.
6. [ ] **Run a pre-employment full Clearinghouse query** on each CDL driver, with the driver's electronic consent in the Clearinghouse.
7. [ ] **Enroll every CDL driver in the random pool**, including yourself.
8. [ ] **Train supervisors** on reasonable suspicion if you have anyone supervising drivers. The rules require training on both drug and alcohol signs.
9. [ ] **Set up a confidential file** for testing records, separate from the DQ file.

## The six types of tests

| Test | When it happens | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Pre-employment | Before first safety-sensitive work | Drug test required; negative result must be received first |
| Random | Unannounced, throughout the year | FMCSA sets minimum annual rates for drugs and alcohol |
| Post-accident | After qualifying crashes | Time limits apply for alcohol and drug tests |
| Reasonable suspicion | When a trained supervisor observes specific signs | Must be documented |
| Return-to-duty | After a violation, before returning | Directly observed collection for drugs |
| Follow-up | After return to duty | Unannounced, set by the substance abuse professional |

FMCSA publishes the minimum random testing rates each year. In recent years they have been 50 percent of the average number of driver positions for drugs and 10 percent for alcohol, but confirm the current rates on the FMCSA website, since they can change.

### Post-accident testing basics

Post-accident testing is where small carriers most often get confused. In general, testing is required after a crash involving a fatality, and after a crash where the CMV driver gets a citation and someone is injured and treated away from the scene, or a vehicle is towed away with disabling damage. Alcohol tests have short time limits (the rule targets within 2 hours and sets an outer limit of 8 hours), and drug tests have a longer outer limit (32 hours). Keep your C/TPA's after-hours number in the truck and confirm the current criteria in Part 382.

## How the Clearinghouse fits in

The FMCSA Drug and Alcohol Clearinghouse is an online database of CDL driver violations: positive tests, refusals and return-to-duty progress. It works in a few directions:

- **Employers query it** before hiring a CDL driver and at least once a year for current drivers.
- **Employers and C/TPAs report** violations and certain other information.
- **Drivers register** so they can give consent and view their own records.

State licensing agencies now use Clearinghouse information too. Under rules that took effect in late 2024, a driver in "prohibited" status can lose the commercial driving privilege on their license until they complete return to duty. Confirm current details with FMCSA.

Clearinghouse queries are purchased in plans through the Clearinghouse itself. Budget for them as a small, recurring cost.

## What happens with a violation

If a driver tests positive, refuses a test or otherwise violates the rules:

1. **Remove the driver from safety-sensitive work immediately.**
2. **Report the violation** to the Clearinghouse within the required time (your C/TPA or MRO may handle part of this).
3. **Give the driver a list of substance abuse professionals (SAPs).**
4. The driver completes the SAP's evaluation and recommended education or treatment.
5. The driver passes a **return-to-duty test**.
6. The driver is placed on a **follow-up testing plan** set by the SAP.

The carrier does not have to rehire a driver after a violation. But no carrier can let that driver operate a CDL vehicle until return to duty is complete.

## Records to keep

Retention periods differ by record. In general, positive results, refusals and SAP records are kept longer (several years), while negative results are kept for a shorter period. Your C/TPA may hold many of these, but you are still responsible for being able to produce them. Ask your provider exactly which records they keep and for how long, and check Part 382 Subpart D for the current schedule.

A missing testing program is on FMCSA's list of automatic failure violations in the [new entrant safety audit](/blog/new-entrant-safety-audit-guide.html). For the rest of your driver paperwork, see the [driver qualification file checklist](/blog/driver-qualification-file-checklist.html), and if you are adding a driver, read [hiring your first truck driver](/blog/hiring-your-first-truck-driver.html).

## Hypothetical budget example

Here is a made-up example for a one-truck owner-operator, to show which costs to expect. Real prices vary by provider and region.

- Consortium membership: $150 per year (hypothetical)
- Pre-employment drug test: $75 (hypothetical)
- Clearinghouse queries: a few dollars each
- Random tests: often included in membership or charged per test

Even at a few hundred dollars a year, the program costs far less than a failed audit or an uninsured crash. Add the total to your overhead in the [cost per mile calculator](/cost-per-mile-calculator.html).

## How Texas Solutions can help

Texas Solutions is a dispatch service, not a broker or motor carrier, so your testing program stays with you and your C/TPA. Our dispatchers find and negotiate loads, handle broker packets and paperwork, and are available 24/7, and you approve every load. See our [owner-operator dispatch](/owner-operator-dispatch.html) service or [talk to a dispatcher](/contact.html).

### Driver Qualification File Checklist for Small Carriers
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/driver-qualification-file-checklist/
Published: 2026-10-21

A **driver qualification file checklist** keeps you from finding out during an audit that one missing form makes a driver unqualified on paper. Federal rules require interstate carriers to keep a file for every driver, and that includes the owner-operator who drives under their own MC number. Here is what goes in the file, when each item gets updated, and the gaps that cause trouble most often.

## Who needs a DQ file

The driver qualification rules in 49 CFR Part 391 apply to drivers of commercial motor vehicles in interstate commerce. In general that means vehicles with a gross weight or weight rating over 10,001 pounds, vehicles placarded for hazmat, and certain passenger vehicles. A CDL is not the trigger: a non-CDL hotshot or box truck over the weight threshold usually still needs a qualified driver and a DQ file.

If you are a one-truck carrier, you keep the file on yourself. Many new carriers miss this, then struggle during the [new entrant safety audit](/blog/new-entrant-safety-audit-guide.html) because the "company" never qualified its own driver.

Intrastate rules vary by state. Texas and most other states adopt much of Part 391, but with differences, so check your state rules if you run only in-state.

## The DQ file checklist

Use this list for each driver. Check the current text of 49 CFR 391.51 on the FMCSA website before you rely on it, because rules get updated.

### Before the driver's first dispatch

- [ ] **Employment application** with the information required by 391.21, signed and dated by the driver. It must list employers for the past three years, plus any commercial driving jobs going back further as the rule requires.
- [ ] **Motor vehicle record (MVR)** from every state where the driver held a license or permit in the past three years, requested within 30 days of the hire date.
- [ ] **Safety performance history request** sent to each DOT-regulated employer the driver worked for in the past three years, plus the responses or a record of your good-faith efforts to get them.
- [ ] **Road test certificate**, or a copy of a valid CDL (or an equivalent document the rules accept) in place of the road test.
- [ ] **Medical examiner's certificate** (the "medical card") that is current.
- [ ] **Proof that the medical examiner is on the National Registry** of Certified Medical Examiners, such as a dated printout or note of your verification.
- [ ] **Clearinghouse pre-employment full query** completed and clear for CDL drivers. The query record is kept with drug and alcohol records, but note in your hiring checklist that it was done. See the [drug and alcohol testing program](/blog/drug-and-alcohol-testing-program.html) guide.
- [ ] **Pre-employment drug test** with a verified negative result before any safety-sensitive work, for CDL drivers. Again, file the result in the separate testing file.

### Every year

- [ ] **Annual MVR** from each state where the driver holds a license or permit.
- [ ] **Annual review** of the driving record, signed by the person who did it, noting whether the driver still meets minimum requirements.
- [ ] **Annual Clearinghouse limited query** (or full query) for CDL drivers.

### As needed

- [ ] **New medical certificate** every time the old one expires. Exams can be valid for up to 24 months but are often shorter. Read the [medical card and DOT physical](/blog/medical-card-and-dot-physical.html) guide.
- [ ] **Updated CDL copy** after renewal, upgrade or endorsement change.
- [ ] **Skill performance evaluation certificate** or medical exemption letter, if the driver relies on one.

## A simple filing system that passes an audit

You do not need software to stay organized, but you do need consistency. A setup that works for many small fleets:

1. **One folder per driver**, paper or digital, with the same section order every time: application, MVRs, previous employer history, road test or CDL, medical, annual reviews.
2. **A separate locked folder** for drug and alcohol records and Clearinghouse queries.
3. **A tracking sheet** with one row per driver and columns for medical card expiration, CDL expiration, annual MVR due date and annual Clearinghouse query due date.
4. **Calendar reminders 30 days before** each expiration.
5. **A quarterly self-check** where you open every file and compare it against the checklist above.

Digital files are generally acceptable as long as you can produce them promptly when asked. Keep backups.

## Common DQ file mistakes

These are the problems that show up again and again:

- **Expired medical card** with no new one on file. Driving with an expired medical certificate is treated as using an unqualified driver.
- **No National Registry verification** for the examiner. The card alone is not enough.
- **Missing previous employer inquiries**, or inquiries sent but no follow-up documented. Write down every attempt, with dates.
- **MVR pulled from only one state** when the driver held licenses in more than one during the three-year window.
- **Annual review not signed or dated.**
- **Application missing required employment history**, especially gaps that are not explained.
- **Testing records mixed into the DQ file**, which creates a confidentiality problem.

## How long to keep it

The general rule: keep the DQ file for the length of employment plus three years after the driver leaves. Certain recurring documents, such as MVRs, annual reviews, and medical certificates, may be removed from the file three years after the date they were executed. Drug and alcohol records follow their own retention schedule under Parts 382 and 40. When in doubt, keep it, and confirm the current periods with FMCSA.

## Worked example: a two-truck carrier

Say you run your own truck and just hired one driver. Your file workload looks like this:

| Task | For you | For your driver | How often |
|---|---|---|---|
| MVR review | 1 | 1 | Yearly |
| Clearinghouse query | 1 | 1 | Yearly |
| Medical card check | 1 | 1 | At each expiration |
| Full new-hire file | Already done | 1 | Once |

That is about four routine tasks a year plus medical renewals. It takes a few hours, which is far less time than a failed audit or an insurance claim denied because a driver was not qualified on paper. If you are about to make your first hire, read [hiring your first truck driver](/blog/hiring-your-first-truck-driver.html) for the full onboarding flow.

## How Texas Solutions can help

Texas Solutions is a dispatch service, not a broker or motor carrier, so your safety files stay your responsibility. What we take off your plate is the load side: our dispatchers find and negotiate loads, handle broker packets and paperwork, and work 24/7, while you approve every load. That frees up time to keep your files in order. See our [dispatch services](/dispatch.html) or [talk to a dispatcher](/contact.html).

### Double Brokering and Freight Fraud: How Carriers Protect Themselves
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/double-brokering-and-freight-fraud/
Published: 2026-10-21

**Double brokering** is one of the most expensive problems in trucking today. A carrier hauls a load in good faith, then finds out the "broker" never had the right to tender it and the money is gone. Freight fraud also includes identity theft, fake brokers and stolen loads. The good news: most scams rely on the same few tricks, and a simple verification routine stops the majority of them.

## What double brokering is

In legitimate freight, a licensed broker arranges a load with a carrier, and that carrier hauls it. Double brokering happens when someone takes a load and passes it to another carrier without authorization. Common versions:

- **Unauthorized re-brokering.** A carrier accepts a load, then hands it to another carrier and keeps the difference. This breaks the broker agreement and, without broker authority, generally breaks federal law.
- **Fraudulent double brokering.** A scammer poses as a carrier or broker using a stolen or fake identity, books a load, re-brokers it to a real carrier, collects payment from the original broker and disappears. The carrier who hauled it often goes unpaid.

Either way, the shipper loses visibility, insurance may not cover the load, and the hauling carrier is left chasing money.

## Other common freight fraud schemes

- **Carrier identity theft.** Scammers use your MC and DOT number, sometimes after changing contact details on public records, to book loads in your name.
- **Fake broker identities.** Lookalike email domains or spoofed phone numbers pretending to be a real brokerage.
- **Fictitious pickups.** A load is booked to steal the freight itself, often high-value goods.
- **Phishing.** Emails or texts with links to fake login pages for load boards, email or government portals.
- **Bank change requests.** Fake requests to change where payments go, sent to brokers or factoring companies.
- **Upfront fee scams.** Someone asks you to pay a fee to "unlock" a load or join a dispatch list.

## Red flags to watch for

| Red flag | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| Email from a free account or a domain slightly different from the broker's real one | Common sign of impersonation |
| Phone number not matching FMCSA records | Could be a fake identity |
| Rate far above the market for the lane | Bait to get you to skip checks |
| Pressure to book immediately without paperwork | Cuts out verification |
| BOL shows a different broker than your rate con | The load may be double brokered |
| Pickup or delivery details change suddenly by text | Possible fictitious pickup or theft |
| Request to pay any fee to get the load | Legit brokers pay carriers, not the reverse |
| New authority with no history offering many high-paying loads | Higher risk, check carefully |

## A verification routine for every load

Use this before you sign any rate confirmation:

1. **Look up the broker's MC with FMCSA.** Confirm broker authority is active and a broker bond or trust is on file.
2. **Contact the broker using details from official records,** not only the number or email that contacted you.
3. **Check the email domain** on the rate con against the broker's known domain.
4. **Run a credit check** through your factoring company or credit service.
5. **Match the rate con to the load.** Broker name, MC and load number should be consistent. See [how to read a rate confirmation](/blog/how-to-read-a-rate-confirmation.html).
6. **Check the BOL at pickup.** If it lists a different broker or carrier, call the broker on the BOL before leaving.
7. **Never pay to get a load.**

Our guide on [how to vet a freight broker](/blog/how-to-vet-a-freight-broker.html) goes deeper into setup checks.

## Protect your own identity and accounts

Fraudsters want your authority as much as your truck.

- Turn on multi-factor authentication for email, FMCSA portal access, load boards, factoring portals and banking
- Use a business email on your own domain, and tell brokers which addresses you use
- Check your FMCSA registration details regularly for unexpected changes to contact info
- Never click login links in unexpected emails or texts; type the address yourself
- Verify any bank or payment change by calling a known number
- Limit who has access to your accounts, and remove access when people leave
- Keep your authority and filings current; see [how to keep your MC authority active](/blog/keep-your-mc-authority-active.html)

Brokers will ask for a carrier packet with sensitive documents. Send it only to verified brokers. The [carrier packet checklist](/blog/carrier-packet-checklist.html) lists what is normally required.

## What to do if you suspect fraud

- **Before pickup:** do not haul it. Tell the broker listed on official records what you found.
- **At pickup:** if the BOL does not match, call the broker on the BOL before leaving the shipper.
- **After delivery and unpaid:** collect every document and message, contact the original broker and shipper, and file a complaint with FMCSA.
- **If your identity was used:** notify FMCSA, your insurer, your factoring company and the brokers you work with, and change all passwords. Consider talking to an attorney.
- **If freight was stolen:** call local law enforcement and your insurer right away.

Fast reporting matters. The sooner others know, the less damage a scammer can do with your name.

## Dispatch scams are freight fraud too

Some scammers pose as dispatchers, charge upfront fees and then vanish or book double-brokered loads. A legitimate dispatcher should have a clear written agreement and should not need your login credentials for government portals. See [how to choose a truck dispatcher and avoid scams](/blog/how-to-choose-a-truck-dispatcher-avoid-scams.html).

## How Texas Solutions can help

Texas Solutions is a dispatch service, not a broker or motor carrier. Our dispatchers verify brokers before booking, check that rate cons and BOLs match, and handle broker packets and paperwork 24/7, and you approve every load. See our [dispatch services](/dispatch.html) or [talk to a dispatcher](/contact.html).

### DOT Roadside Inspections: Levels, What Officers Check, How to Pass
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/dot-roadside-inspections/
Published: 2026-10-21

**DOT roadside inspections** are a routine part of trucking. How you prepare decides whether one costs you ten minutes or a tow, a lost load and a mark on your CSA record. This guide covers the inspection levels, what officers look at, and a practical checklist.

## Who does roadside inspections

Most roadside inspections are done by state enforcement officers trained to the **North American Standard** used across the US, Canada and Mexico. The Commercial Vehicle Safety Alliance (CVSA) sets the inspection procedures and the out-of-service criteria. Results are uploaded to FMCSA and feed into your Safety Measurement System (CSA) data.

## The CVSA inspection levels

| Level | Name | What it covers |
|---|---|---|
| I | North American Standard Inspection | Full driver and vehicle check, including going under the truck |
| II | Walk-Around Inspection | Driver check plus a vehicle walk-around, without getting under the truck |
| III | Driver/Credential Inspection | Driver license, medical card, hours of service, paperwork |
| IV | Special Inspection | A one-time check of a specific item, often for a study |
| V | Vehicle-Only Inspection | Vehicle check without the driver present, often at a carrier location |
| VI | Enhanced Inspection for Radioactive Shipments | Certain radioactive material loads |
| VII | Jurisdictional Mandated Inspection | State-specific programs that do not fit other levels |
| VIII | Electronic Inspection | Data collected electronically without officer contact |

For most owner-operators the common ones are Levels I, II and III.

## What officers check

### The driver

- **Commercial driver's license** valid for the vehicle and any endorsements needed.
- **Medical examiner's certificate** where required. Check current FMCSA and state rules on how medical status is recorded with your license.
- **Hours of service** and the ELD: the officer may request a data transfer and review your record of duty status.
- **ELD documents in the cab:** the user manual, data transfer instructions, malfunction instruction sheet and a supply of blank paper logs.
- **Seat belt use** and signs of fatigue, illness, alcohol or drugs.
- **Shipping papers,** and hazmat documents and placards if applicable.

See our guide to [hours of service rules](/blog/hours-of-service-rules-explained-11-14-70-hour.html) to understand the limits you will be checked against.

### The vehicle

On a Level I, expect the officer to look at:

- **Brakes:** adjustment, air leaks, linings, drums, hoses, and the warning device.
- **Tires and wheels:** tread depth, cuts, bulges, inflation, loose or missing lug nuts.
- **Lights and reflectors:** headlamps, brake lamps, turn signals, clearance lamps.
- **Coupling devices:** fifth wheel, kingpin, safety chains for converter gear or trailers that use them.
- **Steering and suspension:** play, leaks, broken springs.
- **Frame, exhaust and fuel system:** cracks, leaks, loose parts.
- **Cargo securement:** tiedowns, number and condition, blocking and bracing.
- **Windshield, wipers, mirrors** and emergency equipment.
- **Periodic (annual) inspection** proof for the truck and trailer.

Brakes, tires and lights are among the most commonly cited problems, which is also why they are easy wins in a good pre-trip routine.

## Documents to keep in the cab

Use this as a quick check before every trip:

- [ ] CDL and medical certificate (if you carry a paper copy)
- [ ] Truck and trailer registration (cab card)
- [ ] Proof of insurance
- [ ] Annual inspection reports or decals for truck and trailer
- [ ] Lease agreement if running under another carrier's authority
- [ ] ELD manual, data transfer instructions, malfunction sheet, blank paper logs
- [ ] Bill of lading and shipping papers
- [ ] IFTA license and decals, and IRP cab card where applicable
- [ ] Copy of stamped Form 2290 Schedule 1 (often requested at registration and sometimes useful on the road)
- [ ] Permits for oversize, overweight or specific states if needed

## How to handle the inspection itself

1. **Pull in safely and follow instructions.** Have paperwork organized in one folder.
2. **Stay polite and brief.** Answer questions directly. Arguing on the roadside rarely helps.
3. **Do what is asked** during the brake check or lights check.
4. **Read the report** before you leave. Make sure your USDOT number, the VIN, plates and your name are right.
5. **Take photos** of anything you believe is wrong, with time and location.
6. **Fix defects** listed, and keep the repair receipt.
7. **Return the report** to the carrier if you are a leased driver. Many reports need a signed certification that defects were repaired, returned within the time stated on the report.

If something on the report is inaccurate, you can request a review later. See [how to dispute a violation with DataQs](/blog/how-to-dispute-a-violation-dataqs.html).

### Out-of-service orders

Some violations are serious enough that the driver or the truck cannot move until the problem is corrected. Examples include certain brake defects, badly worn or damaged tires, and driving over hours. These are listed in the CVSA North American Standard Out-of-Service Criteria. Our guide to [out-of-service criteria](/blog/out-of-service-criteria.html) explains how it works and what to do.

## Inspection blitzes

CVSA runs enforcement events across North America, such as the yearly International Roadcheck and Brake Safety Week. During these events more trucks are inspected, often at Level I, with a focus area announced in advance. Watch CVSA's announcements and plan extra time.

## A pre-trip routine that prevents violations

A solid 15-minute walk-around catches most problems before an officer does:

1. Lights on, walk around: every lamp, both directions on turn signals, brake lamps.
2. Tires: tread, sidewalls, pressure, lug nuts.
3. Air system: build-up, leaks, low-air warning, brake stroke where you can check it.
4. Coupling: fifth wheel locked, kingpin engaged, glad hands and lines secure.
5. Cargo: tiedowns tight, load not shifted.
6. Paperwork folder in place.

Inspection results feed directly into your [CSA scores](/blog/csa-scores-explained.html), so this routine pays for itself.

This is general information. Inspection procedures and out-of-service criteria are updated, so check CVSA and FMCSA for current rules.

## How Texas Solutions can help

Texas Solutions is a dispatch service, not a broker or motor carrier. Our dispatchers find and negotiate loads, handle broker packets and paperwork, and work 24/7, and you approve every load. We plan pickups with time for pre-trips and legal hours, so you are not rushing past problems. Learn about our [dispatch services](/dispatch.html) or [talk to a dispatcher](/contact.html).

### Load Board vs Dispatcher: Should You Self-Dispatch or Hire a Truck Dispatcher?
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/dispatcher-vs-self-dispatch-load-board/
Published: 2026-10-21

Every owner-operator ends up asking the same question: **load board vs dispatcher**. Do you keep paying for a load board and book your own freight, or hand that work to a truck dispatcher for a percentage? There is no single right answer. This guide lays out the real costs of **dispatcher vs self-dispatch** so you can decide with your own numbers.

## What self-dispatch really costs

Self-dispatch looks free apart from the board subscription. It is not. Here is where the cost hides:

- **Time.** Searching boards, calling brokers, sending carrier packets, negotiating and checking rate confirmations easily takes a couple of hours a day. Those hours come out of driving time, sleep or home time.
- **Rate negotiation.** Brokers negotiate all day. If you take the posted rate because you are tired or in a hurry, you leave money on the table on every load.
- **Deadhead.** Booking one load at a time often means delivering into a market with no outbound freight and driving empty to the next one. See [what deadhead is and how to reduce it](/blog/what-is-deadhead-in-trucking-how-to-reduce-it.html).
- **Paperwork.** Invoices, detention claims and lumper receipts get missed when you are also the driver.

## What a dispatcher costs

A dispatcher usually charges a percentage of weekly gross. At Texas Solutions it is 5% for OTR semis, 7% for hotshots and 8% for box trucks, with no setup fee and no long-term contract. On a semi grossing $8,000 a week, 5% is $400.

## A worked example (hypothetical)

Take a dry van semi grossing $8,000 a week on self-dispatch, with 18% deadhead.

| | Self-dispatch | With a dispatcher |
|---|---|---|
| Weekly gross | $8,000 | $8,400 (better rates on 4 loads) |
| Dispatch fee | $0 | $420 (5%) |
| Empty miles | 450 | 300 |
| Fuel saved on 150 fewer empty miles (about 6.5 mpg, $3.70/gal) | | about $85 |
| Hours on the phone per week | about 12 | about 2 |

In this example the fee is roughly covered by the higher rates and lower fuel cost, and the carrier gets about 10 hours a week back. Change the numbers and the answer changes. That is the point: run your own. The [load profitability calculator](/load-profitability-calculator.html) and [deadhead miles calculator](/deadhead-miles-calculator.html) help.

## When self-dispatch makes sense

- You already have steady direct freight or a dedicated lane.
- You enjoy negotiating and have the time to do it well.
- You run local or regional loads with the same customers every week.
- Your margins are so tight that any fee breaks the budget, and you would rather spend the time.

## When a dispatcher makes sense

- You spend more time on the phone than you want to, or you are calling brokers while driving.
- Your deadhead percentage is high and you keep getting stuck in weak markets.
- You have new authority and need brokers who will set you up.
- You run more than one truck and are dispatching at night.
- Paperwork is slipping and invoices are going out late.

## How to find high paying loads either way

Whether you self-dispatch or not, the same habits pay:

1. **Judge loads per total mile, including deadhead.** A $3.20 load with 120 empty miles can pay less than a $2.90 load next door. See [best paying loads per mile](/blog/what-is-a-good-rate-per-mile-trucking-2026.html).
2. **Plan the reload before you accept the load.** Check outbound freight in the delivery market.
3. **Negotiate every time.** Ask for more, especially on short-notice and hard-to-cover loads. Our guide on [rate negotiation with brokers](/blog/how-to-negotiate-freight-rates.html) has scripts.
4. **Build repeat lanes.** Brokers rebook carriers who deliver on time and answer the phone.

## A middle path

You do not have to choose all or nothing. Some carriers keep the board for their own repeat freight and use a dispatcher for the rest, or try a dispatcher for a few weeks and compare. With Texas Solutions your first load is dispatched free, so you can compare one real week. [Talk to a dispatcher](/contact.html) or read [is a truck dispatcher worth it](/blog/is-a-truck-dispatcher-worth-it.html).

### CSA Scores Explained: How FMCSA Measures Your Safety
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/csa-scores-explained/
Published: 2026-10-21

**CSA scores** are how the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA) sorts carriers by safety performance between full audits. Brokers, shippers and insurers look at the same data, so your numbers can affect whether you get loaded and what you pay for coverage.

## What CSA is

CSA stands for Compliance, Safety, Accountability. It is FMCSA's enforcement program, and its scoring engine is the **Safety Measurement System (SMS)**. SMS takes data from:

- Roadside inspections and the violations written on them,
- Reportable crashes,
- Investigation results.

It then groups that data into categories and compares your carrier to others with a similar amount of activity. The result is a **percentile from 0 to 100** in each category. Higher is worse: a percentile of 80 means your measure is worse than about 80% of similar carriers.

FMCSA has been working on changes to the SMS methodology, including how categories are grouped and how carriers are compared. The basics below describe how the system has generally worked; check FMCSA's CSA website for the current version.

## The seven BASICs

SMS sorts data into Behavior Analysis and Safety Improvement Categories, or **BASICs**:

| BASIC | What feeds it |
|---|---|
| Unsafe Driving | Speeding, improper lane changes, texting, seat belt, reckless driving |
| Crash Indicator | Reportable crash history |
| Hours-of-Service Compliance | Logbook and ELD violations, driving over hours |
| Vehicle Maintenance | Brakes, lights, tires, other defects (cargo securement is also scored here in the current system) |
| Controlled Substances/Alcohol | Drug or alcohol possession or use violations |
| Hazardous Materials Compliance | Placarding, shipping papers, packaging |
| Driver Fitness | Invalid license, missing medical certificate, unqualified driver |

Each BASIC has an **intervention threshold**. Thresholds are lower (stricter) for passenger carriers and hazmat carriers, and some BASICs are treated as higher-risk than others. Cross a threshold and you may be flagged for an FMCSA intervention. Some percentiles, such as the Crash Indicator, are not shown to the public.

## How the score is calculated

You do not need the full formula, but three ideas explain most of it.

### 1. Severity weight

Each violation carries a severity weight, roughly 1 to 10. A minor paperwork issue weighs much less than a brake or tire defect. Violations that put a driver or vehicle **out of service** get extra weight. See our guide to [out-of-service criteria](/blog/out-of-service-criteria.html).

### 2. Time weight

SMS generally looks at the last **24 months**. Recent events count more:

- Last 6 months: highest weight
- 6 to 12 months: medium weight
- 12 to 24 months: lowest weight

After 24 months the event drops out of the SMS calculation.

### 3. Normalizing by exposure

Your weighted violations are divided by your exposure, such as the number of relevant inspections or, for some BASICs, a measure based on power units and miles. This is why one bad inspection hurts a small carrier with few inspections far more than a large fleet.

## Worked example: why clean inspections matter

Take a simplified example. These numbers are hypothetical and the real formula has more parts.

- A one-truck carrier has **2 inspections** in the Vehicle Maintenance BASIC. One has a lighting violation with a weighted total of 6. Measure: 6 / 2 = **3.0**.
- Over the next months the truck gets **4 more clean inspections**. Same violation, now 6 / 6 = **1.0**.
- As that violation ages past 6 and 12 months, its time weight drops, so the measure falls further.

The lesson: one violation on a thin record looks bad, and the cure is time plus clean inspections. That is also why a Level I inspection with no violations is a good outcome, not a hassle. Our guide to [DOT roadside inspections](/blog/dot-roadside-inspections.html) explains how to prepare.

## What happens when scores are high

FMCSA uses a stepped approach. Depending on your data, it may:

- Send a **warning letter**,
- Conduct an **offsite or onsite investigation**,
- Require a corrective action plan,
- In serious cases, issue a proposed safety rating or penalties.

Outside FMCSA, high percentiles can mean brokers decline to set you up, shippers reject you, and insurance quotes go up. A new authority also faces the new entrant safety audit, where poor roadside results can count against you.

## How to keep your CSA scores low

### Before the trip

- Do a real pre-trip inspection every day. Lights, tires and brakes cause many vehicle violations.
- Fix defects before dispatch, not "next week."
- Keep the cab paperwork current: registration, insurance, annual inspection, medical card, ELD instruction sheet and blank paper logs.

### On the road

- Run legal hours and keep ELD logs accurate. Our guide to [hours of service](/blog/hours-of-service-rules-explained-11-14-70-hour.html) covers the 11, 14 and 70-hour rules.
- Avoid speeding and phone use. Unsafe Driving violations tend to be weighted heavily.
- Wear a seat belt. It is an easy violation to avoid.

### After the inspection

- Read every report before the driver leaves the scale.
- If a violation is wrong, dispute it through FMCSA's DataQs system. See [how to dispute a violation with DataQs](/blog/how-to-dispute-a-violation-dataqs.html).
- Check your SMS profile monthly so you see problems before a broker does.

## Checking your own data

You can view your public SMS results on FMCSA's website by USDOT number. Logging in to the FMCSA portal shows more detail, including non-public BASICs. Review each inspection for accuracy: right USDOT number, right truck, right driver. Inspections are sometimes assigned to the wrong carrier, and you can request a correction through DataQs.

## How Texas Solutions can help

Texas Solutions is a dispatch service, not a broker or motor carrier. Our dispatchers find and negotiate loads, handle broker packets and paperwork, and work 24/7, and you approve every load. We plan loads around legal hours so drivers are not pushed into violations. See our [owner-operator dispatch](/owner-operator-dispatch.html) service or [talk to a dispatcher](/contact.html).

### Crossing Into Canada and Mexico: A Trucker's Guide
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/crossing-into-canada-and-mexico/
Published: 2026-10-21

**Cross-border trucking** can open up good-paying lanes, especially into Canada and to the Texas-Mexico border, but it adds paperwork that domestic loads never touch. A missing manifest or the wrong document can leave you parked at the border for hours. Here is what a US owner-operator needs to know before taking the first cross-border load.

## Is cross-border right for you?

It fits best if you:

- Run near the northern border or the major Texas crossings
- Have a clean driving and criminal record
- Can handle a few extra filings per load, or work with someone who can
- Have insurance that will cover the trip

If you mostly run the Southeast, cross-border may not be worth the setup. If you are based in the upper Midwest, Northeast or South Texas, it can add steady freight.

## Driver documents

**For Canada:**

- A passport, or another accepted document such as a FAST card
- A valid CDL and medical certificate (the US and Canada recognize each other's commercial licenses for this purpose)
- A clean admissibility history. Criminal convictions, including impaired driving, can make a driver inadmissible to Canada.

**For Mexico:**

- A passport if you actually enter Mexico
- In practice, most US drivers only go as far as a US border yard or warehouse

Rules on documents and admissibility change. Check with US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) and the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) before your first trip.

## Carrier setup

Before you haul the first load, your company typically needs:

| Item | What it is |
|---|---|
| SCAC code | A carrier identifier used in US customs filings. |
| CBSA carrier code | Canada's carrier identifier for advance manifests. |
| eManifest access | A way to file advance manifests with both countries, either directly or through a service provider. |
| US import user fee decal | An annual fee paid by commercial trucks entering the US. |
| IFTA and IRP | Canadian provinces take part in IFTA and IRP, so add the provinces you will run to your IRP account and track miles by jurisdiction. See our [IFTA guide](/blog/ifta-for-owner-operators-how-to-file.html). |
| Insurance | Confirm your policy covers Canadian operations. US policies generally do not cover driving in Mexico. Read [trucking insurance explained](/blog/trucking-insurance-explained.html). |
| Bond (if needed) | Some in-bond moves require a bonded carrier. Ask your customs broker. |

## Advance eManifest: the step people miss

Both countries require advance electronic manifests from highway carriers:

- **Into Canada:** an ACI eManifest filed with CBSA before arrival, generally at least an hour before you reach the border.
- **Into the US:** an ACE eManifest filed with CBP before arrival, generally at least an hour before, with a shorter window for some FAST shipments.

The shipper or consignee usually uses a **customs broker** to clear the goods themselves. Your job is to make sure the broker has the shipment information and that your manifest references it correctly. Expect barcoded cover sheets or reference numbers that tie the shipment to the customs entry.

Step by step for a typical load into Canada:

1. Get the commercial invoice and the customs broker's name and contact from the shipper.
2. Confirm the broker has received the documents and is ready to clear.
3. File the ACI eManifest with the correct carrier code, driver, truck, trailer and shipment details.
4. Print or keep the shipment reference sheet and documents in the cab.
5. Arrive at the port of entry you declared, and answer the officer's questions directly.
6. For the return trip, repeat the process for the US side with an ACE eManifest.

Exact timing windows and filing methods change. Confirm them with CBSA and CBP.

## Cabotage: no domestic moves

Canada restricts foreign carriers from hauling **domestic** freight from one Canadian point to another, and the US has similar limits on foreign carriers. The narrow exceptions are tightly defined. Practically, Canadian work means: load in the US, deliver in Canada, then reload back to the US. Plan the reload before you cross. Our guide on [planning a profitable round trip](/blog/plan-a-profitable-round-trip.html) covers how to price both legs together.

## Hours of service and ELDs in Canada

Canada has its own federal hours of service rules, and they differ from US rules. As a general picture, Canada uses a daily limit of 13 hours of driving and 14 hours on duty, a 16-hour elapsed work shift limit, and two cycle options (70 hours in 7 days or 120 hours in 14 days). Canada also requires electronic logging devices certified for Canadian use.

When you are in Canada, you follow Canadian rules; when you return, you follow US rules, and your recent hours carry over. Make sure your ELD supports both rule sets and that you know how to switch. Review the [US hours of service rules](/blog/hours-of-service-rules-explained-11-14-70-hour.html) and confirm Canadian details with Transport Canada.

## Hauling to Mexico: the border handoff

Most US-Mexico freight moves in stages:

1. A US carrier hauls the trailer to a border city such as Laredo, El Paso or McAllen.
2. A **transfer (drayage) carrier** takes the trailer across the bridge through both customs processes.
3. A Mexican carrier handles the inland leg in Mexico, and the reverse happens northbound.

For a US owner-operator, this means most Mexico freight looks like a domestic load to or from a border warehouse. The things to watch:

- Long wait times at border yards; negotiate detention up front.
- Trailer interchange: confirm who is responsible for your trailer while it is in Mexico if it crosses.
- Mexican liability insurance is required for any US truck operating in Mexico.

## Border-day tips

- Keep documents organized in one folder, in the order officers ask for them.
- Do not carry firearms, cannabis or other prohibited items. Rules on these differ sharply between countries.
- Budget time. A smooth crossing can be quick; a document problem can take hours.
- Be honest and direct with officers. Do not joke.

Cross-border rules, fees and programs change often. Confirm current requirements with CBP, CBSA, Transport Canada, FMCSA and your customs broker, and talk to your insurance agent before your first trip.

## How Texas Solutions can help

Texas Solutions is a dispatch service, not a broker or a motor carrier. Our dispatchers find and negotiate loads, plan reloads back to the US, handle broker packets and paperwork 24/7, and you approve every load. See our [dispatch services](/dispatch.html) or [talk to a dispatcher](/contact.html).

### Cheapest Truck Dispatch Service? How to Compare Dispatch Fees and Their Real Cost
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/cheapest-truck-dispatch-service-real-cost/
Published: 2026-10-21

Everyone wants the **cheapest truck dispatch service**. That is fair: the fee comes straight out of your gross. But the lowest number in an ad is often not the lowest cost once the extras are added. This guide shows how **truck dispatch cost** is calculated, how a **dispatch fee percentage** compares with a **flat rate** or **weekly dispatch fee**, and what to check before you sign.

## The three ways dispatchers charge

| Model | How it works | Good for | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Percentage of weekly gross | A set % of what the truck books each week | Carriers whose weeks vary | Check what "gross" includes |
| Flat weekly fee | Same dollar amount every week | Steady, high-gross trucks | Due even when the truck sits |
| Per load | A fee on each load booked | Occasional dispatch | Can add up on short loads |

Most independent dispatchers use a percentage, commonly quoted from about 3% to 10% depending on equipment and services. Read more in [dispatch percentage vs flat fee](/blog/dispatch-percentage-vs-flat-fee.html).

## What 5% truck dispatch really costs

At 5% of weekly gross, the fee moves with your week:

| Weekly gross | 5% fee | 7% fee (hotshot) | 8% fee (box truck) |
|---|---|---|---|
| $4,000 | $200 | $280 | $320 |
| $6,000 | $300 | $420 | $480 |
| $8,000 | $400 | $560 | $640 |
| $10,000 | $500 | $700 | $800 |

Now compare a hypothetical flat weekly fee of $350. In a $10,000 week it is cheaper than 5%. In a $4,000 week, or a week the truck is in the shop, you still pay $350, and $350 on zero gross is the most expensive dispatch there is. Run your own numbers in the [dispatch fee calculator](/estimate.html).

## Hidden costs that make "cheap" expensive

A low percentage can hide a high total. Ask about:

- **Setup or onboarding fees** charged before a single load.
- **Weekly minimums** that apply even when you do not run.
- **Paperwork charges** per broker packet, invoice or rate confirmation.
- **Long contracts** with penalties for leaving. Look for **no contract truck dispatch**: a signed agreement with a short notice period, not a 12-month lock-in.
- **Forced dispatch.** A dispatcher paid on volume may push cheap loads. **No forced dispatch** means you approve every load.
- **Low rates.** A dispatcher who books the first posted rate costs you more per load than any fee difference.

## Cheapest fee vs best value

Two dispatchers, same semi, same week:

- Dispatcher A charges 4%, takes the posted rates and leaves you with 20% deadhead.
- Dispatcher B charges 5%, negotiates $150 more across the week and plans the reload so you run 100 fewer empty miles.

Dispatcher B costs about $80 more in fee on $8,000 gross but puts more money in your pocket. Use the [load profitability calculator](/load-profitability-calculator.html) to compare offers on your own lanes.

## Questions to ask about price

1. Is the fee a percentage of gross, a flat weekly amount or per load?
2. What counts as gross: linehaul only, or detention and fuel surcharge too?
3. Is there a setup fee, minimum or contract term?
4. What paperwork is included in the fee?
5. Do I approve every load?
6. Can I try a load first?

## Texas Solutions pricing, in writing

- 5% of weekly gross for OTR semis (dry van, reefer, flatbed, step deck, power only).
- 7% for hotshots, 8% for box trucks and straight trucks.
- No flat rate, no setup fee, no monthly subscription, no long-term contract.
- Broker packets, rate confirmations and invoicing included.
- You approve every load. First load dispatched free.

Local and regional work is quoted separately. See the full [truck dispatch rates](/truck-dispatch-rates.html) page or [talk to a dispatcher](/contact.html).

### Carrier Packet Checklist: Documents Brokers Ask For
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/carrier-packet-checklist/
Published: 2026-10-21

A **carrier packet** is the set of documents a broker needs before it can give you a load. Every broker has its own setup process, but they all ask for roughly the same things. If your packet is complete, accurate and ready to send, you can get approved in minutes instead of losing a good load while you hunt for paperwork.

## What a carrier packet is for

Brokers are responsible for choosing carriers carefully. The packet lets them confirm that:

- You are a real, active motor carrier with operating authority
- Your insurance meets their requirements
- They know who to pay and where
- You have agreed to their terms in writing

Many brokers now use online onboarding systems, but the documents behind them are the same. For how setup fits into booking loads, see [broker setup, rate confirmations, spot vs contract](/blog/broker-setup-rate-confirmation-spot-vs-contract.html).

## The carrier packet checklist

Keep a digital folder with clear PDF scans of each item below, named so you can find them quickly.

### Core documents

- [ ] **Operating authority letter** (your MC authority grant from FMCSA)
- [ ] **USDOT number and MC number** written the same way on every document
- [ ] **W-9** with your legal business name and EIN, signed and dated
- [ ] **Certificate of insurance (COI)** showing auto liability and cargo coverage, policy numbers, limits and dates
- [ ] **Signed broker-carrier agreement** (the broker provides this)

### Payment documents

- [ ] **Voided check or bank letter** if the broker pays you directly
- [ ] **Notice of assignment (NOA)** from your factoring company, if you factor
- [ ] **Remit-to address and email** for invoices and payment notices
- [ ] **Quick pay preference** if the broker offers it

### Contact and company information

- [ ] Company legal name, DBA (if any) and physical address
- [ ] Main contact, dispatch contact and after-hours phone
- [ ] Billing and accounting email
- [ ] Equipment list: truck and trailer types, sizes and any special features
- [ ] Preferred lanes or regions
- [ ] Driver and truck count

### Sometimes requested

- [ ] Copy of your BOC-3 confirmation or process agent details
- [ ] Hazmat registration or permits for hazmat freight
- [ ] TWIC card copies for port work
- [ ] References from other brokers or shippers
- [ ] Safety rating or recent inspection information

Requirements vary, so read each broker's instructions and send exactly what they ask for.

## Getting your certificate of insurance right

The COI is the item that causes the most setup delays. Tips:

1. **Ask your insurance agent to issue a COI for each broker**, listing the broker as certificate holder with their exact legal name and address.
2. **Check the limits** against the broker's requirements before you apply. If a broker needs higher cargo coverage than you carry, ask your agent about the cost before agreeing.
3. **Match the names.** Your insured name on the COI should match the name on your authority and W-9.
4. **List equipment correctly.** Some policies list scheduled vehicles or exclude certain freight. Know your exclusions so you do not book a load your policy does not cover.
5. **Send it from the agent when asked.** Many brokers want the COI to come directly from the insurance agency to prevent fake certificates.

Learn more about coverage types in [trucking insurance explained](/blog/trucking-insurance-explained.html).

## Factoring and the notice of assignment

If you factor your invoices, the factoring company will send brokers a notice of assignment telling them to pay the factor instead of you. Make sure:

- Every broker has the NOA before you invoice the first load
- Your W-9 and remit-to information match what the factor expects
- You understand how to change factors later, since brokers need a release letter

Paying the wrong party is a common cause of late payments. Our guide to [freight factoring](/blog/freight-factoring-for-owner-operators-explained.html) explains the process.

## Protect yourself while sharing documents

Your carrier packet contains information criminals can use to impersonate your company. A few habits help:

- Verify the broker's authority and contact details through FMCSA records before sending a packet
- Send documents only to email domains that match the broker's official website and records
- Be cautious with unexpected setup requests or links from people you have not worked with
- Watch for anyone booking loads in your name that you did not authorize

Read [double brokering and freight fraud](/blog/double-brokering-and-freight-fraud.html) for the warning signs.

## Keep your packet current

An outdated packet causes rejections and payment holds. Review it on a schedule:

- **When your insurance renews:** request new COIs and update every broker you work with
- **When you change banks or factors:** update payment details and send a new NOA or release letter
- **When you add trucks or trailers:** update your equipment list and insurance schedule
- **When your address or contact changes:** update FMCSA records first, then brokers
- **Every January:** check that your W-9 and contact details are still accurate

Also confirm that your authority and registrations stay active, since an inactive status will stop setups immediately.

Our dispatchers keep your carrier packet organized, handle broker setup and paperwork 24/7, find and negotiate loads, and you approve every load. New carriers can start with our [dispatch for new authority](/dispatch-for-new-authority.html) service or [talk to a dispatcher](/contact.html).

### Cargo Claims Guide: How to Prevent, Handle and Settle Them
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/cargo-claims-guide/
Published: 2026-10-21

A **cargo claim** is a demand for payment when freight is damaged, short, lost or delayed while in a carrier's care. One claim can wipe out a month of profit or put your insurance at risk, so the best strategy is preventing claims and documenting every load so you can defend the ones that happen.

## How cargo liability works, in plain terms

For most interstate truckload freight, carrier liability falls under a federal law known as the Carmack Amendment. In simple terms, a motor carrier is generally responsible for actual loss or damage to the goods it hauls, with limited exceptions such as acts of God, acts of the shipper or the inherent nature of the goods. Liability can be limited by agreement in some cases.

Brokers usually require you to carry cargo insurance, often with a specific minimum limit, and their contracts may add their own claim terms. Federal cargo insurance requirements apply to some carrier types, such as household goods movers, but not to most general freight carriers. Confirm the current rules with FMCSA and talk to your insurance agent about the right coverage for what you haul. Our guide to [trucking insurance](/blog/trucking-insurance-explained.html) explains the main policy types.

This is a summary, not legal advice. For a specific claim, talk to your insurance agent or a transportation attorney.

## Prevention starts at pickup

Most claims are won or lost before the truck leaves the shipper.

### Pickup checklist

- Verify piece count, pallet count and condition against the BOL
- Watch loading when the shipper allows it
- Photograph the freight, the load pattern and any visible damage before the doors close
- Note exceptions on the BOL, such as "2 pallets shrink-wrap torn" or "crushed corner on 1 carton"
- If you could not count or watch loading, request "shipper load and count" (SLC) on the BOL
- Record the seal number on the BOL and photograph the seal
- For reefer: confirm the setpoint on the rate con and BOL, pre-cool the trailer, record product temperature if allowed, and keep the unit download
- For flatbed: secure and tarp to the shipper's requirements and federal securement rules

Never sign a clean BOL for freight you know has a problem. Once you sign without exceptions, you have accepted it in good condition.

## Protect the load in transit

- Drive for the freight: smooth braking and turns, especially with tall or top-heavy loads
- Check securement within the required early miles and at regular stops on open-deck loads; see [flatbed cargo securement](/blog/flatbed-cargo-securement.html)
- Monitor reefer temperature and respond to alarms immediately
- Park in well-lit, secure locations and avoid leaving loaded trailers unattended in high-theft areas
- Never break a seal unless instructed in writing by the broker or shipper, and document it if a scale or inspection officer opens it

## At delivery: document everything

If something is wrong at the receiver:

1. **Do not argue at the dock.** Stay calm and focus on documentation.
2. **Photograph** the seal before it is cut, the trailer before unloading, and all damaged product.
3. **Make sure exceptions are written** on the delivery receipt. The receiver will note damage or shortage; make sure the notes are accurate and specific.
4. **Call the broker immediately** from the dock. Do not leave without instructions on refused or partially refused freight.
5. **Get refused freight instructions in writing.** If the receiver refuses product, the broker should tell you where to take it. Do not dump or salvage freight on your own.
6. **Notify your insurance agent** as soon as you know there may be a claim.

## How the claim process usually works

1. **Written claim filed.** The shipper, consignee or broker files a written claim with supporting documents: invoice, BOL, delivery receipt with exceptions, photos.
2. **Acknowledgment.** Federal regulations for interstate carriers set time frames to acknowledge a claim and then pay, decline or make a firm offer. Confirm the current requirements with FMCSA or your attorney.
3. **Investigation.** You and your insurer review the documents, the seal records, temperature downloads and photos.
4. **Resolution.** The claim is paid, partly paid, declined with reasons, or negotiated.
5. **Salvage.** Damaged freight often has salvage value, which may reduce the claim amount.

### Worked example

Hypothetical example: a claim comes in for $8,000 of damaged product. Your cargo policy has a $2,500 deductible. If the claim is covered and paid in full, your insurer pays $5,500 and you pay $2,500. If the damaged product is sold for salvage at $1,000 and the claim is reduced to $7,000, the insurer's share drops to $4,500 and your deductible stays the same. That is why salvage and accurate claim amounts matter. Ask your agent how your own policy handles deductibles and salvage.

## Common claim types and your best evidence

| Claim type | Typical cause | Strongest evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Damage | Load shift, poor packaging, handling | Pickup photos, BOL exceptions, securement photos |
| Shortage | Miscount at pickup | Seal intact, SLC on BOL, piece count notes |
| Temperature | Wrong setpoint, unit failure, warm product | Rate con setpoint, reefer download, pulp temps |
| Theft | Unattended trailer, fraud pickup | Parking records, police report, tracking history |
| Delay | Breakdown, missed appointment | Communications log, repair records |

## Watch for claim terms in broker agreements

Before you sign a broker-carrier agreement, read the claims section. Watch for:

- Clauses letting the broker deduct claims from unrelated loads
- Holding payment on all loads while any claim is open
- Liability for "full invoice value" without limits on high-value freight
- Short deadlines for you to respond

You do not have to accept every term. Ask questions, and have an attorney review your standard agreements. Our guide on [how to vet a freight broker](/blog/how-to-vet-a-freight-broker.html) covers other contract terms to check, and [how to read a rate confirmation](/blog/how-to-read-a-rate-confirmation.html) shows where commodity and value notes appear.

Our dispatchers check commodity, value and special requirements before you accept a load, keep broker communication and paperwork organized 24/7, and you approve every load. See our [dispatch services](/dispatch.html) or [talk to a dispatcher](/contact.html).

### Buying a Used Semi Truck: Inspection Checklist and Red Flags
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/buying-a-used-semi-truck/
Published: 2026-10-21

**Buying a used semi truck** is how many owner-operators get started, and it can be a smart move if you buy the right truck at the right price. The risk is that you inherit someone else's expensive problems. This guide gives you a practical checklist, the records to ask for, red flags and a hypothetical budget so you buy with your eyes open.

## Start with what the truck needs to do

Before looking at listings, decide:

- **What freight will you haul?** Dry van, reefer, flatbed and power only have different needs. See [dry van vs reefer vs flatbed](/blog/dry-van-vs-reefer-vs-flatbed-which-trailer.html).
- **Where will you run?** Regional, OTR, mountains, or states with strict emissions rules.
- **What is your total budget?** Price plus taxes, registration, insurance, and a repair reserve.
- **Sleeper or day cab?** Long-haul work usually requires a sleeper.

A cheap truck that does not fit your freight or your lanes is not a good deal.

## Paperwork checks before you inspect

Do these first. If the paperwork fails, you do not need to drive across the state to see the truck.

1. **Title:** the seller's name matches, and the title is clean (not salvage or rebuilt unless you accept that).
2. **Liens:** confirm there is no outstanding loan, or that it will be paid off at sale with written proof.
3. **VIN match:** the VIN on the title matches the truck's door plate and frame.
4. **Maintenance records:** oil changes, major repairs, overhauls, aftertreatment work.
5. **Annual DOT inspection record:** the most recent periodic inspection report.
6. **Emissions compliance:** if you plan to run in states with special rules, confirm the engine qualifies.

A seller who cannot or will not provide records is telling you something.

## Used semi truck inspection checklist

Bring an independent heavy-truck mechanic you choose, not one the seller recommends. Have them check:

### Engine and drivetrain
- **ECM report:** fault codes, engine hours, idle time, total miles, hard braking events. Compare ECM miles with the odometer.
- **Oil analysis:** a lab sample can reveal coolant in the oil, fuel dilution or unusual metal wear.
- Blow-by, leaks, smoke on start-up and under load
- Turbo, injectors and cooling system condition
- Transmission shifting, clutch wear, differentials and driveline

### Emissions and aftertreatment
- DPF condition and regeneration history
- EGR and SCR/DEF system faults
- Any signs the emissions system was removed or tampered with. Deleted systems can create legal, inspection and resale problems; ask a qualified professional before buying any truck in that condition.

### Frame, suspension and body
- Frame cracks, welds, rust and alignment
- Air suspension bags, leaf springs, shocks and fifth wheel
- Cab mounts, doors, windows, sleeper condition

### Brakes, tires and electrical
- Brake linings, drums, air system leaks and pushrod travel
- Tire tread depth, matching, and age
- Lights, gauges, dash warnings and HVAC

### Test drive
- Drive loaded if possible, including a hill
- Watch temperature, oil pressure and boost
- Listen for noises at highway speed and while braking

Our [pre-trip inspection checklist](/blog/pre-trip-inspection-checklist.html) is a useful reminder of the items DOT inspectors look at too.

## Red flags that should make you slow down

- Seller refuses an independent inspection or ECM download
- ECM miles and odometer do not match
- Fresh paint on the frame or engine hiding leaks or welds
- No maintenance records at all
- Active fault codes cleared just before your visit
- Price far below similar trucks with no clear reason
- Pressure to send a deposit before you see the truck, especially by wire or gift card
- Title held in a different name or state with a story attached

Scams exist in truck sales. Never pay for a truck you have not verified in person or through a trusted inspector, and confirm ownership before money moves.

## Worked example: a realistic first-year budget

These are **hypothetical** numbers to show how to plan, not real market prices.

| Item | Hypothetical amount |
|---|---|
| Purchase price | $60,000 |
| Taxes, title and registration | $5,000 |
| Pre-purchase inspection and oil analysis | $600 |
| Immediate repairs found in inspection | $4,000 |
| Repair reserve for the first year | $10,000 |
| **Total to plan for** | **$79,600** |

The truck "costs" $60,000, but the money you actually need is close to $80,000. Many new owner-operators budget only for the price and get stuck after the first major repair. Use the [maintenance budget calculator](/maintenance-budget-calculator.html) to size your reserve. Our guide on [how to finance a semi truck](/blog/how-to-finance-a-semi-truck.html) explains what lenders look for in a used unit.

## After you buy

- Change all fluids and filters unless records show it was just done
- Start your own maintenance log on day one
- Set a monthly amount aside for repairs and do not touch it
- Get your insurance, registration and IFTA set up before the first load

The first few months tell you a lot about the truck. Watch fuel economy, oil consumption and any new fault codes closely, and fix small problems before they grow into roadside breakdowns that cost you loads as well as repair bills.
