Once your truck is ready, our dispatchers find and negotiate loads that fit your equipment and lanes, handle broker packets and paperwork, and work 24/7 while you approve every load. See our [dispatch services](/dispatch.html) or [talk to a dispatcher](/contact.html).

### Box Truck vs Cargo Van: Which Is Better for Your Business?
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/box-truck-vs-cargo-van/
Published: 2026-10-21

Choosing between a **box truck vs cargo van** is one of the first big decisions for a small freight business. Both can be run without a CDL in many cases, and both haul freight that semis do not want. But they differ a lot in cost, rules, capacity and the customers they attract.

## The short version

- **Cargo van:** lower cost, fewer rules, small loads, lower pay per load. Good for courier, expedite and testing the business.
- **Box truck:** higher cost, more compliance, pallets and liftgate freight, more customer types. Good for regional freight, final mile and retail or furniture work.

## Side-by-side comparison

| Factor | Cargo van | Box truck (non-CDL) |
|---|---|---|
| Typical cargo | Boxes, parts, a few pallets | Multiple pallets, furniture, appliances |
| Liftgate | Rare | Common, often required |
| Driver license | Regular license | Regular license if under the CDL weight threshold |
| Federal rules | Fewer, since most vans are under main weight thresholds | More, often including DOT medical card, hours of service and inspections |
| Fuel use | Lower | Higher |
| Purchase price | Lower | Higher |
| Rate per mile | Lower | Higher |
| Customer types | Courier, expedite, small parcels | LTL-style loads, final mile, retail, partial loads |

Weight thresholds and exact rules change, so confirm current requirements with FMCSA and your state before buying either one.

## Startup cost and running cost

A cargo van is usually the cheapest way into for-hire freight. The purchase price is lower, insurance is often lower, and fuel and tires cost less. If money is tight, that matters, because a big payment in the slow first months is one of the most common reasons new carriers fail.

A box truck costs more in almost every line: purchase, insurance, fuel, tires, liftgate maintenance and possibly an ELD. In exchange, each load carries more freight and usually pays more.

### A simple hypothetical comparison

Say both vehicles run 8,000 miles a month.

- **Cargo van:** total monthly cost of $4,000, or $0.50 per mile. Average rate $1.20 per loaded mile with 25% empty miles. Revenue: 6,000 loaded miles x $1.20 = $7,200. Profit before your pay: **$3,200**.
- **Box truck:** total monthly cost of $7,200, or $0.90 per mile. Average rate $2.00 per loaded mile with 20% empty miles. Revenue: 6,400 loaded miles x $2.00 = $12,800. Profit before your pay: **$5,600**.

These numbers are made up for illustration. Your real rates and costs depend on your lanes, season and equipment. Plug in your own figures with the [cost per mile calculator](/cost-per-mile-calculator.html) and the [load profitability calculator](/load-profitability-calculator.html).

The key point: the box truck earns more in good months, but it also loses more in slow months. Its break-even is higher.

## Freight and customers

**Cargo vans** fit small, urgent freight: auto parts, medical samples, documents, small business deliveries and long-distance expedite runs where one small shipment needs to move right away.

**Box trucks** open more doors:

- Partial and LTL-style pallet loads from brokers
- Final mile and home delivery, often with a two-person crew
- Retail store deliveries and restocks
- Furniture, appliances and trade show freight
- Dedicated routes for local distributors

Many shippers require a liftgate because their receivers do not have a dock. A box truck with a working liftgate can take those loads; a van usually cannot.

## Rules and compliance

This is where the two differ the most. Many federal motor carrier rules apply once a vehicle crosses certain weight thresholds in interstate commerce. Most cargo vans stay under them. Most box trucks are over at least the first one.

For a box truck in interstate commerce, expect to deal with:

- USDOT number and, for for-hire freight, FMCSA operating authority
- DOT medical card for the driver
- Hours-of-service rules and, in many cases, an ELD
- Annual vehicle inspection and driver qualification records
- Drug and alcohol testing only if the vehicle requires a CDL

A for-hire van hauling across state lines generally still needs operating authority. Confirm all of this with FMCSA, since thresholds and exceptions are specific. Our guide on [how to get an MC number](/blog/how-to-get-mc-number-authority-owner-operator.html) covers the authority side.

## Which should you choose?

Start with a **cargo van** if:

- Your budget is limited and you want low fixed costs
- You have local courier or expedite customers lined up
- You want to learn the business before taking on more risk

Start with a **box truck** if:

- You have access to pallet, liftgate or final mile freight
- You can handle the extra compliance work
- You have enough cash reserve to survive a slow month or two

Either way, decide based on freight you can actually get. A vehicle without customers is just a payment.

## Moving from a van to a box truck

If you already run a van, these are signs it may be time to step up:

1. You turn down loads every week because they will not fit.
2. Customers keep asking about liftgate service.
3. Your van runs full most days and you have steady demand.
4. You have savings to cover the larger payment and a few slow weeks.

Before you buy, read [how to start a box truck business](/blog/how-to-start-a-box-truck-business.html) for setup steps specific to straight trucks.

## How Texas Solutions can help

Texas Solutions is a dispatch service, not a broker or motor carrier. We do not currently dispatch cargo vans, but our [box truck dispatch](/box-truck-dispatch.html) team finds and negotiates loads, handles broker packets and paperwork, and works 24/7, and you approve every load. We can also help with authority setup and back-office work. [Talk to a dispatcher](/contact.html) when you are ready to move up.

### BOC-3 Filing Explained: Process Agents for Trucking Authority
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/boc-3-filing-explained/
Published: 2026-10-21

The **BOC-3 filing** is one of the first things FMCSA looks for when you apply for operating authority, and one of the easiest to overlook later. It is a short form, but without it your MC authority will not be granted, and problems with it can put existing authority at risk.

## What a BOC-3 is

BOC-3 stands for **Designation of Process Agents**. A process agent is a person or company in a given state that can receive court papers (service of process) on behalf of your business if someone files a legal action against you in that state.

Because trucks cross many states, FMCSA requires interstate carriers, brokers and freight forwarders to name an agent in each state where they operate. For carriers, that generally means every state you drive through or do business in, and in practice most carriers designate agents in all states plus the District of Columbia.

## Who needs a BOC-3

- **For-hire motor carriers** applying for interstate operating authority (an MC number).
- **Freight brokers.**
- **Freight forwarders.**

Owner-operators who lease onto another carrier and run under that carrier's authority generally do not need their own BOC-3. If you later get your own authority, you will. See [how to get your MC number](/blog/how-to-get-mc-number-authority-owner-operator.html) for the whole sequence.

## Blanket agents vs. naming your own agents

### Blanket process agent company

Most carriers use a **blanket agent**: a company that maintains agents in every state and files one BOC-3 that covers them all. Benefits:

- One filing, all states.
- Filed electronically with FMCSA, so it usually shows up faster.
- The company keeps the agent list current.

When comparing blanket agent companies, ask:

- Is the fee one-time or annual? Are there renewal charges?
- Do they file electronically with FMCSA, and how fast?
- Will they send you a copy of the filing confirmation?
- How do they forward legal papers to you, and how fast?
- Do they offer anything you do not need, bundled into the price?

### Naming your own agents

You can name individuals or companies yourself and, under FMCSA rules, a carrier can file its own BOC-3 on paper. This takes more work, because you need a valid agent in every required state, and paper filings are slower. Few owner-operators go this route.

## Step-by-step: getting your BOC-3 filed

1. **Apply for your USDOT number and operating authority** through FMCSA's registration system.
2. **Choose a blanket process agent company** (or arrange your own agents).
3. **Give them your exact legal name, USDOT and MC or docket number, and address** as they appear on your FMCSA application.
4. **They file the BOC-3** with FMCSA electronically.
5. **Get a copy** of the filing for your records.
6. **Make sure insurance is also filed.** Authority is generally not granted until both the BOC-3 and required insurance filings are on record and the protest period has passed.
7. **Check FMCSA's public lookup** to confirm the BOC-3 shows as on file.

Our [trucking authority setup](/trucking-authority-setup.html) page explains the support we offer if you want help with the full sequence.

## When to update or replace your BOC-3

A BOC-3 does not usually expire, but you need a new filing when:

- **You change process agent companies.** The new company files a new BOC-3.
- **Your agent company goes out of business** or cancels your service.
- **Your legal business name changes,** such as moving from a sole proprietorship to an LLC with a new USDOT number. In that case, check whether you need new authority altogether.
- **FMCSA or a broker says it is missing.** Fix it right away.

## Worked example: a typical new-authority timeline

Every case is different, but here is a simplified sequence for a new carrier:

| Step | Who files | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Apply for USDOT and MC | You | Through FMCSA's online registration |
| BOC-3 | Blanket agent company | Usually filed within a short time after you order |
| Liability insurance filing | Your insurance company | Often the step that takes the longest |
| Protest period | FMCSA | A waiting period before authority becomes active |
| Authority granted | FMCSA | Check status online, then start broker setups |

If authority does not activate when you expect, check both the BOC-3 and insurance status first. A missing filing is the most common hold-up.

## Common BOC-3 problems

- **Name mismatch.** The name on the BOC-3 must match your FMCSA record.
- **Wrong docket number** entered by the agent company.
- **Assuming the insurance agent filed it.** Insurance agents file insurance, not BOC-3s, unless they say otherwise.
- **Paying for "annual BOC-3 renewal"** you may not need. Read the terms before you pay.
- **Ignoring legal papers** forwarded by your agent. If you receive service of process, talk to an attorney promptly.

The BOC-3 is one of several items that keep your authority in good standing, along with insurance, UCR and the MCS-150 update. Our guide on how to [keep your MC authority active](/blog/keep-your-mc-authority-active.html) puts all of them on one calendar.

This guide is general information, not legal advice. Requirements and procedures can change, so confirm current rules with FMCSA.

Our dispatchers find and negotiate loads, handle broker packets and paperwork, and are available 24/7, while you approve every load. Once your authority is active, we can help you get set up with brokers and running. See our [dispatch services](/dispatch.html) or [talk to a dispatcher](/contact.html).

### Best Truck Dispatch Service for Owner-Operators in 2026: How to Compare
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/best-truck-dispatch-service-for-owner-operators-2026/
Published: 2026-10-21

Searching for the **best truck dispatch service for owner-operators in 2026** gives you dozens of companies that all say they are the best. None of those claims can be checked. What you can check is how a dispatch service charges, what it puts in writing and how it treats you on the first load. This guide gives you a way to compare truck dispatching services across the USA on the things that actually affect your weekly gross.

## What a truck dispatch service should do for you

A truck dispatch service works for the carrier. Under your own MC authority, a dispatcher:

- Searches load boards and broker networks for freight that fits your equipment and lanes.
- Negotiates the rate before the load reaches you.
- Sends your carrier packet to brokers and checks every rate confirmation.
- Plans the next load so you do not deadhead across a state for it.
- Handles invoicing, detention and lumper paperwork, and factoring documents if you factor.

If a "dispatcher" wants you to haul under their MC or asks for the broker's payment to go to them, that is not dispatch. Read [how to choose a truck dispatcher and avoid scams](/blog/how-to-choose-a-truck-dispatcher-avoid-scams.html) before you sign anything.

## Seven things to compare

| What to check | Good sign | Warning sign |
|---|---|---|
| Fee | A published percentage or rate, in writing | "We'll talk about price later" |
| Upfront cost | No setup fee, or a small one you understand | Large payment before any load is booked |
| Contract | No long-term contract, clear notice period | 6 or 12 month lock-in with penalties |
| Load approval | You approve every load: no forced dispatch | Loads booked without your OK |
| Equipment | Experience with your trailer or truck type | "We do everything" with no detail |
| Availability | Reachable 24/7 by phone, text or WhatsApp | Office hours only, email replies next day |
| Paperwork | Broker packets, rate cons and invoicing included | Extra charge for every document |

### 1. The fee and how it is calculated

Ask what the fee is based on. A percentage of weekly gross means you pay more in a good week and less in a slow one. A flat weekly fee is due even when your truck sits. Compare both in [dispatch percentage vs flat fee](/blog/dispatch-percentage-vs-flat-fee.html) and work out your own number with the [dispatch fee calculator](/estimate.html).

### 2. No contract truck dispatch

A good dispatcher keeps you because the loads are good, not because a contract says you cannot leave. You still need a signed dispatch agreement: it sets your percentage, what is included and how either side can end the service. Look for no long-term contract and a short notice period.

### 3. No forced dispatch

You own the truck and the authority, so you decide which loads run. A dispatcher can recommend; you approve. If you ever feel pushed into a cheap load "to keep the relationship", the relationship is the problem.

### 4. Equipment experience

Reefer, flatbed, hotshot, box truck and power only freight each move through different brokers and boards. Ask the dispatcher how they find loads for your exact setup. Our pages for [reefer dispatch](/reefer-dispatch.html), [flatbed and step deck dispatch](/flatbed-dispatch.html), [box truck dispatch](/box-truck-dispatch.html), [hotshot dispatch](/hotshot-dispatch.html), [dry van dispatch](/dry-van-dispatch.html) and [power only dispatch](/power-only-dispatch.html) show what that looks like.

### 5. Help with new authority

If your MC number is new, many brokers will not book you yet. The best dispatch service for a new carrier knows which brokers accept new authority. See [how to get loads with a new MC number](/blog/how-to-get-loads-with-new-mc-number.html).

### 6. A 24/7 truck dispatch service

OTR freight does not stop at 5 p.m. A cancelled load at 9 p.m. or a reload on Sunday morning needs someone who answers. Ask who picks up the phone at night.

### 7. Paperwork included

Broker setup packets, rate confirmations, invoicing and detention claims take hours every week. Check whether they are part of the fee or billed on top.

## Independent truck dispatcher or dispatch company?

An independent truck dispatcher is often one person working a handful of trucks. That can mean very personal service, but nobody covers when that person sleeps or takes a day off. A dispatch company has a team, so there is cover around the clock, but you should still have a main contact who knows your truck. Ask both how many trucks each dispatcher handles.

## Questions to ask before you sign

1. What is your fee, and is it a percentage of gross or a flat weekly amount?
2. Is there a setup fee, a minimum or a contract term?
3. Do I approve every load before it is booked?
4. Who signs rate confirmations?
5. How do you find loads for my equipment and lanes?
6. Do you work with new MC authority?
7. What paperwork is included?
8. How do I reach you at night and on weekends?
9. Can I try one load before I commit?

## How Texas Solutions answers those questions

- **Fee:** 5% of weekly gross for OTR semis (dry van, reefer, flatbed, step deck, power only), 7% for hotshots, 8% for box trucks and straight trucks. Local and regional work is quoted separately.
- **Upfront cost:** none. No setup fee, no flat rate, no monthly subscription.
- **Contract:** no long-term contract. A signed dispatch agreement sets your percentage and notice period.
- **Load approval:** you approve every load. No forced dispatch.
- **New authority:** we work with new MC numbers from day one.
- **Availability:** dispatchers available 24/7 by call, text or WhatsApp at (838) 910-3147.
- **Trial:** your first load is dispatched with no dispatch fee.

We do not guarantee rates or earnings; nobody honest can. What we can promise is a clear fee, your approval on every load and someone who answers. [Talk to a dispatcher](/contact.html) or check the [dispatch rates](/truck-dispatch-rates.html).

### Truck Loads and Load Boards: How They Work for Carriers
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/truck-loads-and-load-boards-guide/
Published: 2026-10-13

For most small carriers, the search for truck loads starts on a load board. It is often the first place a new authority finds freight, and it remains a daily tool for many experienced owner-operators. This guide explains what a **load board** is, how carriers use one, and how to judge the loads for trucks you see posted.

If you are working out how to find loads for trucks you own or drive, the load board is where most carriers start. You will also hear them called truck boards, a loading board or a loads board; a load board for truckers is the same tool whatever the name, and most load boards for trucking list truckload, partial and expedited freight side by side. Some carriers keep one truckload load board for long hauls and a second, smaller board for local freight; load boards for truckers differ mainly in which brokers post on them.

## What a load board is

A load board is an online marketplace. Freight brokers, and sometimes shippers, post loads that need a truck. Carriers and dispatchers search those posts and contact the poster to book.

A typical load post shows:

- Origin and destination
- Pickup date and sometimes a delivery window
- Equipment type (van, reefer, flatbed, step deck, power only, hotshot and so on)
- Weight and length
- Posted rate, or no rate at all
- The broker's company name, contact and MC number
- Sometimes the broker's credit score and average days to pay

Carriers can also **post their truck**: where it will be empty and when. Brokers search those posts and call carriers with matching loads.

## Common load boards

These are some of the well-known names. We describe them only in general terms, because features and prices change. Check each provider's website for current details.

- **DAT load board.** One of the largest load board networks in the US, with load search, truck posting, market rate data and broker credit information depending on the plan.
- **Truckstop load board.** Another large, long-running network, with load search, rate tools and broker payment and credit information on its plans.
- **123Loadboard.** A load board often used by smaller carriers, with load search and related tools.
- **Amazon Relay.** Not a traditional broker board. It is Amazon's own platform for booking Amazon freight with carriers who hold their own authority.

Each of these has paid plans with different levels of access. We compare features in more detail in our guide to [the best load boards for owner-operators](/blog/best-load-boards-for-owner-operators.html).

## Free load boards: what to expect

A free load board can be a good way to start, especially for a brand-new carrier with a tight budget. Free options include free tiers of some boards and brokers' own load portals.

Typical trade-offs:

- Fewer loads and less coverage of some lanes
- Fewer search filters
- Little or no broker credit and payment data
- More competition for each posted load

If you use a free board, take extra care checking the broker before you book.

## How carriers use a load board, step by step

1. **Set your search.** Choose your equipment, empty location, search radius and date.
2. **Set the destination.** Search to a specific market, a region, or anywhere, depending on your plans.
3. **Sort and filter.** Look at deadhead to pickup, total miles and rate. Hide brokers you will not work with.
4. **Check the broker.** Look up its MC number on FMCSA, and review credit score and days to pay if the board shows them.
5. **Call or message.** Confirm the details and ask about anything missing: appointment times, commodity, tarps, lumpers, detention policy.
6. **Negotiate.** Use market data and your own cost per mile to counter.
7. **Book and get the rate confirmation.** Read it before pickup.

## How to judge a posted load

The posted rate per loaded mile is not the whole story. What matters is the rate on **every** mile you drive, including empty miles to the pickup.

**Worked example: two dry van posts (assumptions labelled)**

- **Load A:** $2,400 for 700 loaded miles, 90 miles deadhead
- **Load B:** $2,250 for 680 loaded miles, 15 miles deadhead

Rate per loaded mile:

- Load A: $2,400 / 700 = **$3.43**
- Load B: $2,250 / 680 = **$3.31**

Rate per total mile:

- Load A: $2,400 / (700 + 90) = $2,400 / 790 = **$3.04**
- Load B: $2,250 / (680 + 15) = $2,250 / 695 = **$3.24**

Load B pays less on paper but more on every mile driven. Then ask where each load leaves you. A slightly lower rate into a strong freight market can beat a high rate into a dead one. Try your own numbers with the [deadhead miles calculator](/deadhead-miles-calculator.html) and the [load profitability calculator](/load-profitability-calculator.html). For more on empty miles, read [what deadhead is and how to reduce it](/blog/what-is-deadhead-in-trucking-how-to-reduce-it.html).

## Load board safety tips

Fraud is a real problem on open marketplaces. Protect yourself:

- Verify the broker's MC number and contact details independently
- Be cautious if the phone number or email does not match the company's official records
- Never pay anyone to "release" a load
- Do not share login details for your load board, ELD or factoring account
- Watch for double brokering signs, such as a load that suddenly changes hands

## Limits of load boards

Load boards are useful, but they have limits:

- **Competition.** Many carriers see the same post, which can push rates down.
- **Time.** Searching and calling can take hours a day, often while you should be driving or resting.
- **Spot only.** Most posts are one-off loads, not repeat lanes.

That is why many carriers combine boards with broker relationships and direct freight. See [how to find loads for your truck](/blog/how-to-find-loads-for-your-truck.html) for a broader plan.

## Using a dispatcher instead of searching yourself

A truck dispatch service uses load boards and broker networks on your behalf. Texas Solutions searches, calls and negotiates while you drive, then sends you the details to approve. We dispatch dry van, reefer, flatbed, step deck, power only, hotshot, box truck and straight truck, with remote dispatchers available 24/7 across the USA.

Fees for OTR are 5% of weekly gross for semi trucks, 7% for hotshots and 8% for box trucks and straight trucks, with no setup fee and no long-term contract. See how our [owner-operator dispatch service](/owner-operator-dispatch.html) works or [get a free estimate](/estimate.html).

### Non-CDL Box Truck and Hotshot Loads: Weight Rules and How to Find Freight
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/non-cdl-box-truck-and-hotshot-loads/
Published: 2026-10-13

Running without a CDL is one of the most common ways people start in box truck or hotshot trucking. It lowers the barrier to entry, but it comes with a hard ceiling on weight, and misreading the rules can lead to fines, out-of-service orders or an insurance problem after a claim.

This post explains the federal thresholds in plain language, shows how much payload they leave, and covers how to find non-CDL box truck loads and non-CDL hotshot loads. It is general information, not legal advice. Rules can change and states can add their own, so **confirm your situation with FMCSA and your state licensing agency** before buying equipment or booking freight.

## The key terms

- **GVWR (gross vehicle weight rating):** the maximum loaded weight the manufacturer rates a single vehicle for. It is on the door-jamb certification label.
- **GVW (gross vehicle weight):** what the vehicle actually weighs at a given moment, cargo included.
- **GCWR (gross combination weight rating):** the rating for a truck and trailer together. Federal rules define it as the greater of the manufacturer's value (when shown on the certification label) or the sum of the truck and trailer ratings or weights.
- **GCW (gross combination weight):** what the truck and trailer actually weigh together.

An important detail: the federal CDL definitions use **the rating or the actual weight, whichever is greater**. A truck rated at 26,000 lbs that is loaded to 27,000 lbs is treated as over the line.

## The federal CDL thresholds

Under the federal definitions:

- **Class A CDL:** a combination with a GCWR or GCW of **26,001 lbs or more**, when the towed unit has a GVWR or GVW of **more than 10,000 lbs**.
- **Class B CDL:** a single vehicle with a GVWR or GVW of **26,001 lbs or more**, or such a vehicle towing a trailer of 10,000 lbs or less.
- **Class C CDL:** smaller vehicles that carry 16 or more passengers including the driver, or haul hazardous materials that require placards.

If your vehicle does not fall into one of those groups, a CDL is generally not required federally. States can have their own requirements, especially for intrastate operations, so check locally.

## Non-CDL box trucks

For a box truck, the question is simple: is the truck rated and loaded at **26,000 lbs or less**? Many 26 ft box trucks are built with a GVWR right at or just under that number for this reason.

### Payload example

Assumptions, for illustration only:

- GVWR: 26,000 lbs
- Empty weight of the truck with body, liftgate, fuel and driver: 16,500 lbs

Maximum cargo: 26,000 - 16,500 = **9,500 lbs**.

That may be less than you expect. Pallets of dense freight can hit that limit long before the box is full, so always ask the broker for the exact weight and compare it against your payload, not against the box size. Axle ratings also apply, so heavy freight loaded at the rear can overload an axle even when total weight is legal.

## Non-CDL hotshots

Hotshot setups are trickier because two vehicles are involved. There are two common ways operators stay non-CDL.

### Option 1: keep the whole combination at 26,000 lbs or less

If the truck and trailer together are rated and loaded at 26,000 lbs or less, the combination is under the Class A threshold regardless of trailer size.

Assumptions, for illustration only:

- Truck GVWR: 14,000 lbs; empty truck with driver and fuel: 8,500 lbs
- Trailer GVWR: 12,000 lbs; empty trailer: 4,500 lbs
- Combined rating: 14,000 + 12,000 = 26,000 lbs

Maximum cargo: 26,000 - (8,500 + 4,500) = **13,000 lbs**, and still limited by each vehicle's own GVWR and axle ratings.

Be careful with the GCWR definition. If the manufacturer's GCWR appears on the certification label and is higher than 26,000 lbs, it may count. Check your specific truck.

### Option 2: trailer rated 10,000 lbs or less

The Class A definition only applies when the towed unit is rated or weighs **more than 10,000 lbs**. So a truck under 26,001 lbs pulling a trailer rated and loaded at 10,000 lbs or less generally does not require a Class A, even if the combined total is above 26,000.

Assumptions, for illustration only:

- Trailer GVWR: 10,000 lbs; empty trailer: 3,000 lbs

Maximum cargo on the trailer: 10,000 - 3,000 = **7,000 lbs**, plus whatever the truck's own payload allows.

Either way, a non-CDL hotshot carries far less than a CDL setup with a heavy-duty 40 ft gooseneck. That narrows the loads you can take and often the rate you can earn.

## What still applies without a CDL

Skipping the CDL does not skip the rest of the rules. For interstate commercial vehicles over 10,000 lbs, you should expect:

- A **USDOT number**.
- **Operating authority** (MC number) if you haul regulated freight for hire across state lines. See [how to get an MC number](/blog/how-to-get-mc-number-authority-owner-operator.html).
- A **DOT medical card**.
- **Hours-of-service** rules and, in many cases, an ELD. See [hours of service rules explained](/blog/hours-of-service-rules-explained-11-14-70-hour.html).
- Vehicle inspections and maintenance records.
- Commercial insurance that meets FMCSA minimums and broker requirements.

Placarded hazmat requires a CDL with the right endorsement at any vehicle size, so non-CDL operators should pass on those loads.

## How to find non-CDL box truck loads and hotshot loads

The freight is out there; it just has to fit your weight limit.

- **Lead with your real payload.** When you call a broker, state your maximum cargo weight up front. It saves time on both sides.
- **Filter load boards by weight.** Set the maximum weight to your payload, not your GVWR. See the [best load boards for box trucks](/blog/best-load-boards-for-box-trucks.html) and the [best load boards for hotshot](/blog/best-load-boards-for-hotshot.html).
- **Look for light, bulky freight.** Furniture, appliances, retail goods, displays and packaging often fill space before weight.
- **Partial and expedited loads** often suit smaller trucks.
- **Ask about weight on every load.** Never accept "it should be light". Get the number on the rate confirmation.

## Run the numbers

Lower payload usually means lower revenue per load, so cost control matters even more. Use the [cost per mile calculator](/cost-per-mile-calculator.html) to find your break-even and the [load profitability calculator](/load-profitability-calculator.html) to check each offer, including empty miles.

## Dispatch for non-CDL box trucks and hotshots

Texas Solutions is a dispatch service, not a broker or carrier. We dispatch box trucks, straight trucks and hotshots for owner-operators nationwide. Your dispatcher books only loads that fit the payload you give us, and you approve every load before it is booked. We also offer DOT compliance help through our [back office services](/trucking-back-office-services.html).

Box truck and straight truck dispatch is **8% of weekly gross** and hotshot dispatch is **7%**, for OTR, with no setup fee and no long-term contract. The first load is dispatched free. See [box truck dispatch](/box-truck-dispatch.html), [hotshot dispatch](/hotshot-dispatch.html) or [get a free estimate](/estimate.html).

### How to Start a Hotshot Business: Truck, Trailer, Authority and Dispatch
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/how-to-start-a-hotshot-business/
Published: 2026-10-13

Hotshot trucking uses a heavy-duty pickup and a flatbed trailer to move loads that are too small, too urgent or too oddly shaped for a full semi load. Think equipment, machinery parts, building materials, pipe and other freight that needs to move now.

It costs less to start than a semi operation, but it is not cheap, and the weight rules are easy to get wrong. Here is how to set one up step by step.

## Step 1: Understand what hotshot freight looks like

Hotshot loads are usually:

- **Partial or less-than-truckload** in size, often well under what a 48 ft flatbed carries.
- **Time-sensitive.** A broken-down machine or a jobsite waiting on material pays for speed.
- **Open-deck.** Loaded by forklift or crane from the side or top, so securement skills matter.

Rates often run about **$4 to $5 a mile**, depending on lane, urgency and season. See our post on [hotshot rates per mile and fuel](/blog/hotshot-trucking-rates-per-mile-fuel-and-dispatch.html) for more on what moves the number. Rates are never guaranteed.

## Step 2: Choose your truck and trailer

The common setup is a **1-ton diesel dually pulling a 40 ft gooseneck**. When you shop, focus on weight ratings first and price second.

**Truck checklist:**

- GVWR and GCWR (gross combination weight rating) from the manufacturer's label and specs.
- Towing capacity for a gooseneck or fifth-wheel hitch.
- Diesel engine condition and service records.

**Trailer checklist:**

- Deck length (30, 35 and 40 ft are common).
- Trailer GVWR and axle ratings.
- Ramps, winches, stake pockets and tie-down points.
- Empty weight, since every pound of trailer is a pound you cannot haul.

## Step 3: Decide CDL or non-CDL

This decision shapes the whole business.

Under federal rules, a combination generally requires a **Class A CDL** when its gross combination weight rating or actual combination weight (whichever is greater) is **26,001 lbs or more** and the towed unit is rated over **10,000 lbs**. Many 1-ton trucks paired with a heavy-duty gooseneck land in Class A territory.

Some operators run a lighter, "non-CDL" setup by keeping the combination at 26,000 lbs or less. That avoids the CDL but sharply limits payload. Our guide to [non-CDL box truck and hotshot loads](/blog/non-cdl-box-truck-and-hotshot-loads.html) explains how to check this carefully. Always confirm with FMCSA and your state licensing agency before you buy equipment.

If you hold a CDL, drug and alcohol testing rules, including the FMCSA Clearinghouse, apply to you.

## Step 4: Set up the company and authority

The paperwork is similar to any for-hire trucking company:

- Form a business entity, get an EIN and open a business bank account.
- Get a **USDOT number** and **interstate operating authority** (MC number) from FMCSA.
- File a **BOC-3** for process agents.
- Register for **UCR** each year.
- Check whether **IRP** apportioned plates and **IFTA** apply. Combinations over 26,000 lbs commonly qualify, but confirm with your base state.

Our guides on [getting an MC number](/blog/how-to-get-mc-number-authority-owner-operator.html) and [filing IFTA](/blog/ifta-for-owner-operators-how-to-file.html) go deeper. If you want help with the filings, Texas Solutions offers MC authority setup, IFTA filing and DOT compliance help through our [back office services](/trucking-back-office-services.html).

## Step 5: Get insured

FMCSA sets the minimum liability you must have on file. Brokers then set their own requirements, and many want higher auto liability and cargo coverage. Hotshot insurance can be expensive for new authorities, so get several quotes before you commit to equipment.

## Step 6: Gear up for securement

Open-deck freight means you are responsible for securing it properly. Plan for:

- Ratchet straps, chains and binders rated for the loads you will carry.
- Edge protectors and corner guards.
- Tarps if you plan to haul freight that must stay dry.
- Know the cargo securement rules, including how many tie-downs a load needs.

A shifted load can cost you a claim, a ticket and a broker relationship in one trip.

## Step 7: Run the numbers on a sample week

Here is a rough example using assumed figures. Your numbers will differ.

**Assumptions:**

- Weekly gross: $7,500
- Total miles (loaded plus empty): 2,000
- Average fuel economy across loaded and empty miles: 11 mpg
- Diesel price: $4.50 a gallon
- Dispatch at 7% of gross
- Insurance: $400 a week
- Truck and trailer payments: $600 a week
- Maintenance and tire reserve: $0.20 a mile

**Math:**

- Fuel: 2,000 / 11 = 181.8 gallons x $4.50 = **$818**
- Dispatch: $7,500 x 0.07 = **$525**
- Maintenance reserve: 2,000 x $0.20 = **$400**
- Fixed costs: $400 + $600 = **$1,000**
- Total costs: $818 + $525 + $400 + $1,000 = **$2,743**
- Left before taxes, factoring, permits and other expenses: $7,500 - $2,743 = **$4,757**

Slow weeks, repairs and time off will pull the average down, so plan around a range, not one good week. For more detail see [how much hotshot drivers make](/blog/how-much-do-hotshot-drivers-make.html), and check your own fuel with the [truck fuel cost calculator](/truck-fuel-cost-calculator.html).

## Step 8: Find loads and decide on a dispatcher

You can find hotshot freight on load boards, through direct broker relationships, or with a hotshot dispatch company. Our guide to the [best load boards for hotshot](/blog/best-load-boards-for-hotshot.html) covers the first option.

A dispatcher for hotshot trucks is useful when:

- You are new and do not have broker contacts yet.
- You lose hours each day searching boards and making calls.
- You want someone to handle broker packets, rate confirmations and invoicing.
- You want help planning reloads so you are not stuck empty after a delivery.

Before you sign with anyone, read [how to choose a truck dispatcher and avoid scams](/blog/how-to-choose-a-truck-dispatcher-avoid-scams.html).

## Hotshot truck dispatch with Texas Solutions

Texas Solutions is a dispatch service, not a broker or carrier. We dispatch hotshots for owner-operators and small fleets nationwide, with 24/7 remote dispatchers who work with brand-new MC authority from day one. You approve every load before it is booked.

Hotshot dispatch is **7% of weekly gross** for OTR, with no flat rate, no setup fee and no long-term contract, and your first load is dispatched free. Learn more about our [hotshot dispatch service](/hotshot-dispatch.html) or [get a free estimate](/estimate.html?truck=hotshot).

### How to Start a Box Truck Business: Authority, Equipment and First Loads
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/how-to-start-a-box-truck-business/
Published: 2026-10-13

A box truck business is one of the lower-cost ways to own a trucking company. The truck costs less than a tractor and trailer, many box trucks do not require a CDL, and there is steady demand for freight that is too small or too awkward for a 53 ft trailer. The trade-off is that margins are thinner, so the planning you do before the first load matters.

This guide walks through the steps in order. If you are still deciding between a box truck and a semi, our general guide on [how to start a trucking company](/blog/how-to-start-a-trucking-company.html) covers the bigger picture.

## Step 1: Decide what kind of freight you want to haul

Before you shop for a truck, decide how you plan to earn money with it. Box truck freight usually falls into a few groups:

- **OTR and regional spot freight** booked through load boards and brokers.
- **Expedited and partial loads** that need to move faster than a full truckload.
- **Local delivery and final-mile work** for retailers, furniture and appliance sellers, and distributors.
- **Repeat lanes and contracts** that grow out of good service with the same brokers or shippers.

The type of freight you chase decides the truck you need, the insurance you buy and whether a dispatcher makes sense for you.

## Step 2: Choose the right box truck

Most box truck owner-operators settle on a **26 ft box truck with a liftgate**. That size typically holds around 12 standard pallets depending on how they are loaded, works for most brokers' "straight truck" postings, and many models stay at a GVWR of 26,000 lbs or less.

When you compare trucks, look at:

- **GVWR.** At 26,000 lbs or less, a single truck generally does not require a CDL. At 26,001 lbs or more, it generally needs a Class B CDL. Our guide to [non-CDL box truck and hotshot loads](/blog/non-cdl-box-truck-and-hotshot-loads.html) explains the thresholds in detail.
- **Payload.** GVWR minus the truck's empty weight is what you can legally haul. A heavy body and liftgate reduce it.
- **Liftgate.** Many shippers and receivers without docks require one. Without it you will pass on a lot of freight.
- **Door type and interior.** Roll-up versus swing doors, E-track and logistics posts for strapping, and interior height.
- **Fuel and maintenance history.** A cheap truck that spends weeks in the shop is not cheap.

## Step 3: Set up the business

Treat it as a real company from day one:

- Form a business entity (many owner-operators use an LLC) and get an EIN from the IRS.
- Open a separate business bank account.
- Pick a simple bookkeeping method so you can track fuel, repairs and income per load.

Talk with an accountant about the entity and tax setup that fits your situation.

## Step 4: Get your USDOT number and operating authority

For interstate for-hire work, you will generally need:

- **A USDOT number** from FMCSA.
- **Interstate operating authority** (commonly called an MC number) for hauling regulated freight for hire.
- **A BOC-3 filing** naming process agents in each state.
- **Unified Carrier Registration (UCR)**, renewed each year.

FMCSA updates its registration system from time to time, so follow the current instructions on its website. Our post on [how to get an MC number](/blog/how-to-get-mc-number-authority-owner-operator.html) covers the process, and Texas Solutions offers [MC authority setup](/trucking-back-office-services.html) as part of its back office services if you would rather not do the filings yourself.

Drivers of commercial vehicles over 10,000 lbs in interstate commerce generally need a DOT medical card even without a CDL, and hours-of-service rules apply. Check what applies to your operation.

## Step 5: Buy the right insurance

Your authority will not activate until the required liability coverage is on file with FMCSA. Beyond the federal minimum, brokers set their own requirements, and many ask for higher auto liability limits plus cargo coverage. Get quotes from agents who write commercial trucking policies, and ask each one what limits brokers in your target freight usually require.

Insurance is often a new carrier's largest fixed cost, so get quotes before you buy the truck.

## Step 6: Get loads with new authority

This is where many new box truck businesses stall. Some brokers will not work with an MC that has only been active for a short time. You can still get loaded, but it takes more calls and more paperwork.

Ways to find your first loads:

- **Load boards.** Filter for straight trucks or box trucks. See our guide to the [best load boards for box trucks](/blog/best-load-boards-for-box-trucks.html).
- **Brokers who accept new authority.** Build a list and keep your setup packet ready to send.
- **A box truck dispatcher with new authority experience.** A dispatcher already knows which brokers take new carriers and can fill out the setup packets for you.

Texas Solutions works with brand-new MC authority from day one, and the first load is dispatched free.

## A simple startup cost check

Every business is different, so build your own numbers. Here is a sample way to lay them out, using assumed figures only:

- Truck down payment (assumption): $10,000
- First insurance down payment (assumption): $3,000
- Authority, BOC-3, UCR and registrations (assumption): $1,000
- ELD, phone, basic equipment like straps and blankets (assumption): $1,000
- Cash reserve for fuel and repairs while waiting on first payments (assumption): $5,000

Total in this example: $10,000 + $3,000 + $1,000 + $1,000 + $5,000 = **$20,000**.

The reserve matters more than most people expect. Brokers often pay on 30-day terms or longer unless you use [factoring](/blog/freight-factoring-for-owner-operators-explained.html), so you need cash to cover fuel before the first payments arrive.

## Step 7: Know your cost per mile before you book

Box truck rates often run about **$1.80 to $3.20 per mile**, depending on lane and season. That range is wide, and the low end may not cover your costs. Work out your own number with the [cost per mile calculator](/cost-per-mile-calculator.html), then check each offer with the [load profitability calculator](/load-profitability-calculator.html).

If your all-in cost is $1.50 a mile and a load pays $1.90 a loaded mile with 80 empty miles to the pickup on a 300-mile trip, the math looks like this:

- Revenue: 300 x $1.90 = $570
- Cost: (300 + 80) x $1.50 = $570
- Profit: **$0**, before dispatch or factoring fees

That load only looks good if you ignore the empty miles.

## Step 8: Turn spot loads into repeat work

Most box truck contracts do not come on day one. They come from showing up on time, communicating well and making it easy for brokers and shippers to work with you. We cover that in more detail in [box truck contracts and how to get them](/blog/box-truck-contracts-how-to-get-them.html).

## Getting help with 26 ft box truck dispatch

You can run every step yourself, or bring in help for the parts that take you away from driving. Texas Solutions is a dispatch service, not a broker or carrier. Our remote dispatchers work 24/7, find and negotiate loads, and send you each one for approval before it is booked. Box truck and straight truck dispatch is **8% of weekly gross** for OTR, with no setup fee and no long-term contract.

Read more about our [box truck dispatch service](/box-truck-dispatch.html) and [dispatch for new authority](/dispatch-for-new-authority.html), or [get a free estimate](/estimate.html?truck=box-truck).

### How to Get Loads Without a Broker: Direct Freight Explained
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/how-to-get-loads-without-a-broker/
Published: 2026-10-13

Brokers move a large share of the freight small carriers haul. That is not a bad thing, but many owner-operators wonder whether they could keep more of the rate by cutting out the middle. This guide explains **how to get loads without a broker**, what it really takes, and where it makes sense.

## Why carriers look for direct freight

The reasons are usually the same:

- **No broker margin.** The shipper's full rate goes to the carrier.
- **Steadier freight.** A shipper that likes your service may give you the same lanes every week.
- **Better planning.** Knowing your loads in advance makes home time and maintenance easier to schedule.

Those benefits are real, but direct freight is not free money. It comes with its own work and risk.

## Option 1: Direct shippers

A direct shipper is the company that owns the freight: a manufacturer, distributor, farm, food plant or building supply yard.

### How to approach shippers

1. **Start local and in your lanes.** Look for businesses near your home base or along routes you already run.
2. **Find the right person.** Ask for the shipping manager, logistics coordinator or traffic department.
3. **Bring your paperwork.** Authority, insurance certificate, W-9 and a short summary of your equipment and service area.
4. **Offer a specific lane.** "I can run your freight from here to that city twice a week" is easier to say yes to than "do you have anything?"
5. **Follow up.** Shippers often say no the first time. A carrier who checks in politely and shows up when needed is remembered.

### What shippers expect

- On-time pickups and deliveries, every time
- Clean equipment that fits their freight
- Clear communication about delays
- Proper insurance, sometimes above the levels brokers ask for
- A safety record they can check on FMCSA's public data

New carriers often find this hard at first. Many build a track record with brokers before shippers take them seriously.

## Option 2: Contracts and dedicated lanes

A contract or dedicated lane is a standing agreement to haul freight on a lane at an agreed rate for a period of time.

- **Pros:** predictable volume and rate, easier planning
- **Cons:** the rate is fixed even when the spot market rises, and you may be expected to cover loads even when it is inconvenient

Contracts come from shippers directly, and sometimes from brokers who manage a shipper's freight. For the difference between contract and spot pricing, see [spot vs contract rates](/blog/broker-setup-rate-confirmation-spot-vs-contract.html).

## Option 3: Amazon Relay and similar platforms

Amazon Relay is Amazon's platform for booking its own freight with carriers who hold their own authority. Loads are booked through the platform rather than through a broker, and some freight uses Amazon trailers, which suits power only operators.

Keep it in perspective:

- Requirements, rates and rules are set by Amazon and can change
- Some loads pay well and others do not, so judge each load on its own numbers
- Depending on a single customer for all your freight is a risk

## The honest pros and cons of direct freight

| | Direct freight | Broker freight |
|---|---|---|
| Rate | Often higher, no middle margin | Includes broker margin |
| Speed to start | Slow, takes relationship building | Fast, available on day one |
| Payment terms | Can be 30 to 60 days or longer | Varies, many offer quick pay |
| Paperwork and billing | You invoice and chase payment | Broker handles shipper side |
| Flexibility | Less, you are committed | More, you pick load by load |
| Backhauls | Shipper may not have any | Easy to find on boards |

## What high paying freight loads really look like

The best paying loads for owner-operators are the ones that pay well **per total mile**, including deadhead, and do not tie your truck up for days. A high rate from a shipper that pays in 60 days may be worse for your cash flow than a slightly lower broker rate paid in two days.

**Worked example: direct vs broker load (assumptions labelled)**

- Direct shipper load: 600 loaded miles at $3.50 a mile = 600 x $3.50 = **$2,100**, paid in 45 days
- Broker load: 600 loaded miles at $3.20 a mile = 600 x $3.20 = **$1,920**, paid quickly through factoring
- Assumed factoring fee on the broker load: 3% of $1,920 = $57.60, leaving **$1,862.40**
- Difference: $2,100 - $1,862.40 = **$237.60** more for the direct load

The direct load pays more, but you wait about six weeks for it. If you need that cash to buy fuel next week, you might factor the direct invoice too, which narrows the gap. Run your own numbers with the [load profitability calculator](/load-profitability-calculator.html).

## How to keep trucks full while you build direct freight

Direct customers rarely fill every mile. Most owner-operators keep a mix:

- **Direct freight** for the main lane
- **Broker freight** for backhauls and gaps
- **Load boards** to check market rates and fill last-minute openings

Our guide to [finding loads for your truck](/blog/how-to-find-loads-for-your-truck.html) covers how to blend these sources. Keeping deadhead low between them matters just as much. The [deadhead miles calculator](/deadhead-miles-calculator.html) shows what empty miles do to your real rate.

## Where a dispatcher fits

A truck dispatch service is not a broker. Texas Solutions works for the carrier, searching load boards and broker networks and negotiating rates for your truck under your own authority. If you win direct freight, a dispatcher can fill the gaps around it with broker loads so the truck is not sitting while you wait for the next shipper order.

Our back office team can also help with the paperwork that comes with direct work: invoicing, detention and lumper collection, and factoring setup. See [trucking back office services](/trucking-back-office-services.html).

## Getting started

Getting loads without a broker is possible, but it is a long game built on service and reliability. In the meantime, the truck still has to earn. Texas Solutions dispatches owner-operators and small fleets nationwide, with fees of 5% for semi trucks, 7% for hotshots and 8% for box trucks and straight trucks running OTR, no setup fee, no long-term contract, and you approve every load.

See our [owner-operator dispatch service](/owner-operator-dispatch.html) or [get a free estimate](/estimate.html).

### How to Choose a Fuel Card for Truckers: What to Compare
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/how-to-choose-a-fuel-card-for-truckers/
Published: 2026-10-13

Fuel is usually the biggest bill an owner-operator pays that changes every week. A fuel card will not change the price of diesel, but the right one can trim what you pay per gallon, cut down on paperwork and make tax time less painful.

There is no single best fuel card for truckers. Truck stop chains, fleet card companies and factoring companies all offer cards, and each is built around a different kind of customer. This guide explains how to compare them so you can pick one that fits the way you run.

You will find plenty of lists of the best fuel cards for truckers online. We do not rank brands here. Discounts, fees and terms change often, and you should verify them directly with any provider before signing up.

## Step 1: Know where you fuel today

Before you look at any offer, pull your last two or three months of fuel receipts. Note:

- Which truck stop chains and independent stations you use most
- The states you fuel in, and which lanes you run regularly
- About how many gallons you buy each month
- Whether you ever fuel at cardlock or unattended sites

A card with a strong discount at stations you never pass is worth very little. A card that works where you already stop is worth a lot more. If you are not sure what fuel costs on your lanes, check our [diesel prices by state](/diesel-prices/texas.html) pages, which exist for each state.

## Step 2: Understand how the discount works

This is the part that confuses most drivers. Fuel card discounts usually come in two forms.

### Retail-minus

You pay the posted pump price minus a set amount per gallon. It is easy to understand and easy to check against the sign. The discount may be different from one chain or location to another.

### Cost-plus

The price starts from what the station pays for fuel, then a markup is added. On some days and at some stations, this can come in well below the pump price. On others the gap is small. Cost-plus is harder to check because you cannot see the station's cost.

### Other forms

Some cards offer rebates paid later, points or rewards at certain chains, or discounts only at an in-network list of locations. Ask exactly when and how any rebate is paid.

The only reliable way to compare is to look at what you would have paid on real fuel stops along your lanes, not at the headline number.

## Step 3: Check network coverage

The best trucking fuel cards for one driver may be useless for another, mostly because of coverage. Ask:

- Which truck stop chains accept the card, and is the discount the same at each?
- Does it work at independent stations, and is there any discount there?
- Can you buy DEF, reefer fuel or other items on it?
- Does it work in every state you run?

If you run regional lanes, a card tied to one chain might be fine. If your lanes change week to week, broad acceptance matters more.

## Step 4: Add up every fee

A discount can disappear fast once fees are counted. Look for:

- Monthly or annual card fees
- Per-transaction fees
- Fees for using out-of-network stations
- Late payment charges and interest on credit cards
- Fees for adding cards or for paper statements

Ask the provider for a full fee schedule in writing. If they cannot give you one, keep looking.

## Step 5: Credit or prepaid

**Credit cards** give you a line to fuel on now and pay later. That helps cash flow between loads, but usually requires a credit check or business history, and carrying a balance can cost you.

**Prepaid or debit-style cards** use money you load ahead of time. They can be easier to get for a new authority and help prevent overspending, but you need to keep the balance funded.

**Cards through factoring companies** are another option. Some factoring companies let you fuel against your advances. That can be convenient, but read how fuel purchases are deducted and whether the card ties you more tightly to that factor. Our guide to [freight factoring](/blog/freight-factoring-for-owner-operators-explained.html) explains how factoring works.

## Step 6: IFTA reporting and fuel tax data

For an interstate carrier, a good fuel card for truckers is also a record-keeping tool. Look for:

- Transaction reports that show gallons, price and state for every purchase
- Downloadable reports by quarter
- Easy matching between fuel records and your miles by state

Clean fuel data makes filing much smoother. See our guide to [IFTA for owner-operators](/blog/ifta-for-owner-operators-how-to-file.html), or use the [IFTA mileage calculator](/ifta-mileage-calculator.html) to work out miles by state.

## Step 7: Controls and security

Even a one-truck operation benefits from basic controls, and small fleets need them more. Useful features include:

- Purchase limits per day or per transaction
- Restricting purchases to fuel only
- Driver ID or PIN at the pump
- Alerts for unusual transactions
- A simple way to freeze a lost card

## Worked example: how a per-gallon discount adds up

Here is how a discount adds up over time. These are **assumptions for illustration only**, not a quote from any card:

- Fuel economy: 6.3 miles per gallon
- Miles driven: 10,000 per month
- Hypothetical discount: 20 cents per gallon

**Math:**

1. Gallons per month: 10,000 / 6.3 = about **1,587 gallons**
2. Monthly discount: 1,587 x $0.20 = about **$317**
3. Yearly discount: $317 x 12 = about **$3,810**

Now subtract any card fees. If the card cost, say, $15 a month in fees, the yearly benefit drops by $180. Also remember that a discount only helps if you actually fuel in network. Driving out of route to reach a discount station can cost more in fuel and time than it saves.

Your numbers will differ with mpg, miles, discount and fees. Plug your own figures into the [truck fuel cost calculator](/truck-fuel-cost-calculator.html), and see how fuel fits into your total costs with the [cost per mile calculator](/cost-per-mile-calculator.html).

## A short checklist before you apply

- Does it work where I fuel today?
- Is the discount retail-minus, cost-plus or a rebate, and how will I verify it?
- What is the full fee schedule?
- Credit, prepaid or factoring-linked, and what are the approval terms?
- Does it give clean state-by-state data for IFTA?
- Can I set limits and freeze a card quickly?
- Can I cancel without a penalty?

## Fuel savings start with the right loads

A fuel card helps at the pump, but how you plan loads matters even more. Fewer empty miles means fewer gallons bought. Our post on [cutting fuel cost per mile](/blog/diesel-prices-by-state-cut-fuel-cost-per-mile.html) covers that side, and the [fuel surcharge calculator](/fuel-surcharge-calculator.html) helps you check whether a rate covers current diesel prices.

Texas Solutions is a nationwide truck dispatch service, not a fuel card provider, and we have no fuel card partnerships. Our 24/7 remote dispatchers plan loads to keep deadhead down, and you approve every load. Our [back office services](/trucking-back-office-services.html) include IFTA filing, factoring setup and invoicing. OTR fees are 5% of weekly gross for semis, 7% for hotshots and 8% for box trucks and straight trucks, with no setup fee and no long-term contract, and your first load is free.

We cannot promise any set savings, but we can help you run smarter lanes. See our [owner-operator dispatch](/owner-operator-dispatch.html) service or [get a free estimate](/estimate.html).

### How to Become an Owner-Operator: Lease-On or Your Own MC
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/how-to-become-an-owner-operator/
Published: 2026-10-13

Plenty of company drivers think about running their own truck. Some make the jump and never look back. Others find out the hard way that owning a truck is a business, not just a better-paying driving job. This guide explains **how to become an owner-operator** step by step, with the decisions that matter most.

## Owner-operator vs company driver

A company driver is paid by the mile, by the load or by the hour, and the company pays for the truck, fuel, insurance and repairs.

An owner-operator owns or leases the truck and pays those costs. In return, the truck's revenue is yours. The upside is control and earning potential. The downside is that a bad month, a blown engine or a slow freight market comes out of your pocket.

Before you go further, read [how much owner-operators make](/blog/how-much-do-owner-operators-make.html) for an honest look at gross vs net.

## Step 1: Get the license and experience

For a semi truck you need a **Class A CDL**. Many people drive for a company for a year or more first. That time teaches you how freight moves, how to manage hours of service and how to deal with shippers and receivers, while someone else pays for the mistakes.

Smaller equipment is different:

- **Box trucks and straight trucks** under 26,001 lbs GVWR can often be driven without a CDL
- **Hotshot** setups may or may not require a CDL, depending on the combined weight rating of the truck and trailer

Check the weight ratings and your state's rules before you buy anything.

## Step 2: Choose your path: lease-on or your own authority

This is the biggest decision you will make.

### Leasing on to a carrier

You own or lease the truck, but you haul under another carrier's authority.

- **Pros:** the carrier provides authority and often insurance, freight and fuel discounts. Easier to start.
- **Cons:** you usually keep a smaller share of the revenue, you may have limited choice of loads, and you depend on one company.

### Running your own MC authority

You become your own motor carrier.

- **Pros:** you choose your loads, lanes and brokers, and the full rate goes to your business.
- **Cons:** you pay for insurance, compliance and filings, and you have to find your own freight or pay someone to find it.

Many people start leased on, learn the business, then get their own authority.

## Step 3: Get your USDOT number and MC authority

If you choose your own authority, you register with FMCSA for a USDOT number and apply for MC operating authority. You also need a BOC-3 process agent filing and proof of insurance on file before the authority goes active.

We cover each filing in detail in [how to get your MC number and trucking authority](/blog/how-to-get-mc-number-authority-owner-operator.html), and the full business setup (UCR, IRP plates, IFTA, ELD, drug and alcohol consortium) in [how to start a trucking company](/blog/how-to-start-a-trucking-company.html). Texas Solutions also offers MC authority setup help as part of its [back office services](/trucking-back-office-services.html).

Keep in mind that a new carrier enters FMCSA's new entrant program, which includes a safety audit, usually within the first 12 months. Keep your logs, maintenance records and driver files in order from day one.

## Step 4: Pick the truck and trailer

Your equipment decides which freight you can haul and what it pays. Rough planning ranges from our desk (not market data, available loads or quotes), which vary by lane and season:

| Equipment | Rough rate per mile |
|---|---|
| Flatbed / step deck | $5 - $7 |
| Reefer | $4 - $6 |
| Hotshot | $4 - $5 |
| Dry van / power only | $3 - $5 |
| Box truck | $1.80 - $3.20 |

Higher rates usually come with higher costs or more work: tarping and securement for flatbed, fuel for the reefer unit, or more expensive equipment. Compare the trade-offs in [dry van vs reefer vs flatbed](/blog/dry-van-vs-reefer-vs-flatbed-which-trailer.html).

When you look at a used truck, budget for a pre-purchase inspection. A cheap truck that spends weeks in the shop is not cheap.

## Step 5: Build a cash reserve

New owner-operators often underestimate how long it takes for money to come in. Brokers commonly pay on 30-day terms or longer unless you use factoring, and the first insurance down payment can be large.

**Worked example: a startup reserve plan (all figures are assumptions for illustration)**

- Insurance down payment: $4,000
- Filings, registration and plates: $1,500
- First month of truck payment: $2,500
- Fuel for the first two weeks: $3,000
- Repair cushion: $5,000
- Total reserve: $4,000 + $1,500 + $2,500 + $3,000 + $5,000 = **$16,000**

Your own numbers could be higher or lower. The point is to price each item before you start, not after. The [cost per mile calculator](/cost-per-mile-calculator.html) helps you work out what you need to earn per mile to cover it all.

## Step 6: Set up how you get paid

Decide early whether you will wait for brokers to pay or use factoring to get paid within a day or two of delivery. Read [freight factoring explained](/blog/freight-factoring-for-owner-operators-explained.html) before you sign anything, and check the fee, recourse terms and contract length.

## Step 7: Find your first loads

With a new MC number, the first weeks are the hardest. Some brokers want an authority that has been active for a set period. Others will work with new carriers if your paperwork is clean.

Options for getting loads:

- Search load boards and call brokers yourself
- Build relationships with brokers who accept new authority
- Use a dispatch service that books loads under your MC

Our guide on [how to find loads for your truck](/blog/how-to-find-loads-for-your-truck.html) covers each option.

## A quick checklist

- CDL or the right license for your equipment
- Lease-on or own authority decided
- USDOT, MC, BOC-3 and insurance filings complete
- UCR, plates, IFTA and ELD set up
- Truck inspected and cost per mile calculated
- Cash reserve set aside
- Factoring or banking arranged
- Broker setup started

## Dispatch for a new MC number

If you get your own authority, you do not have to figure out the load side alone. Texas Solutions is a truck dispatch service that works with brand-new MC authority from day one. We help with broker packets and setup, search and negotiate loads, and you approve every one. Fees for OTR are 5% of weekly gross for semi trucks, 7% for hotshots and 8% for box trucks and straight trucks, with no setup fee and no long-term contract, and your first load is dispatched free.

Learn more about [dispatch for new authority](/dispatch-for-new-authority.html) or [get a free estimate](/estimate.html).

### How Much Do Hotshot Drivers Make? A Realistic Look at Gross and Net
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/how-much-do-hotshot-drivers-make/
Published: 2026-10-13

Hotshot trucking has a reputation for strong pay per mile, and it can earn well. But a high rate per mile does not automatically mean high take-home pay. What you keep depends on how many paid miles you run, how many empty miles you burn and what your setup costs to own and insure.

This post focuses on hotshot **owner-operators** who run under their own authority or lease to a carrier. Company drivers are paid differently, usually a wage or a percentage, and do not carry the truck's costs.

## What hotshot loads pay

As a rough guide, hotshot loads often pay about **$4 to $5 a mile**. Factors that push the rate up or down:

- **Urgency.** Same-day or next-morning delivery pays a premium.
- **Weight and size.** Heavier or longer pieces that need a 40 ft deck or more securement often pay more.
- **Lane.** Loads into areas with little return freight need to pay for the trip home.
- **Season and industry.** Construction, agriculture and energy activity swing demand.

For a deeper look see [hotshot trucking rates per mile and fuel](/blog/hotshot-trucking-rates-per-mile-fuel-and-dispatch.html), and compare with other equipment on our [rate per mile guide](/truck-dispatch-rates.html). Rates are never guaranteed.

## Example weekly gross (hypothetical)

As a hypothetical example, OTR hotshots might gross about **$7,000 to $9,000 a week**. That figure is not a guarantee. Weeks with repairs, weather, home time or slow freight come in lower.

## Worked example: a good week

These are assumptions for illustration. Use your own numbers.

**Assumptions:**

- Weekly gross: **$8,000**
- Loaded miles: 1,800, empty miles: 450, total 2,250
- Average fuel economy across loaded and empty miles: 11 mpg
- Diesel price: $4.50 a gallon
- Dispatch: 7% of gross
- Factoring: 3% of gross
- Insurance: $400 a week
- Truck and trailer payments: $600 a week
- Maintenance and tire reserve: $0.20 a mile
- ELD, phone, permits, tolls and other: $120 a week

**Costs:**

- Fuel: 2,250 / 11 = 204.5 gallons x $4.50 = **$920**
- Dispatch: $8,000 x 0.07 = **$560**
- Factoring: $8,000 x 0.03 = **$240**
- Insurance: **$400**
- Payments: **$600**
- Maintenance reserve: 2,250 x $0.20 = **$450**
- Other: **$120**
- **Total: $3,290**

**Net before taxes:** $8,000 - $3,290 = **$4,710**, or about 59% of gross.

## Worked example: a slow week

**Assumptions:** weekly gross **$5,000**, total miles 1,400, everything else unchanged.

- Fuel: 1,400 / 11 = 127.3 gallons x $4.50 = **$573**
- Dispatch: **$350**
- Factoring: **$150**
- Insurance: **$400**
- Payments: **$600**
- Maintenance reserve: 1,400 x $0.20 = **$280**
- Other: **$120**
- **Total: $2,473**

**Net before taxes:** $5,000 - $2,473 = **$2,527**, or about 51% of gross.

Fixed costs stayed at $1,000 a week in both examples. In a slow week they take a bigger bite, which is why a cash reserve is part of running a hotshot business.

## From weekly numbers to a yearly estimate

Avoid multiplying a great week by 52. Instead:

1. Pick a realistic average week, somewhere between your good and slow weeks.
2. Count only the weeks you expect to work.
3. Set aside money for income and self-employment taxes.

For example, if your average net is **$3,500 a week** (an assumption) and you work **46 weeks**, that is 3,500 x 46 = **$161,000 before taxes**. Change either number and the result moves a lot, so run your own scenario.

## Own authority vs leased on

How you run also changes what you keep:

- **Own authority.** You book loads under your own MC, keep the full rate and pay all costs, including insurance and compliance. Income has the most upside and the most risk.
- **Leased to a carrier.** You run under another company's authority and usually receive a percentage of the load. The carrier may cover some costs, such as liability insurance, but takes a share of every load.

Neither is right for everyone. Compare the two with your own numbers before deciding, and if you plan to get your own authority, see [how to get an MC number](/blog/how-to-get-mc-number-authority-owner-operator.html).

## What separates higher-earning hotshot operators

There is no secret, but some habits make a clear difference:

### They know their cost per mile

If you do not know your break-even, you cannot tell a good load from a bad one. Use the [cost per mile calculator](/cost-per-mile-calculator.html) and check each offer with the [load profitability calculator](/load-profitability-calculator.html).

### They plan the reload

A $1,500 load into a dead area that leaves you 250 miles empty may pay less than a $1,200 load into a busy market. See [how to reduce deadhead](/blog/what-is-deadhead-in-trucking-how-to-reduce-it.html).

### They watch weight and fuel

Hotshot fuel economy drops as weight goes up. Track your real mpg loaded and empty, then check your cost by state with the [truck fuel cost calculator](/truck-fuel-cost-calculator.html).

### They get paid for their time

Detention and layovers should be documented and billed. If you do not ask, you usually do not get paid.

### They negotiate

Brokers expect a counteroffer. Our guide on [how to negotiate freight rates](/blog/how-to-negotiate-freight-rates.html) explains how to approach it.

## Finding hotshot loads that pay

Most hotshot freight is found through load boards, broker relationships and dispatchers. Our guide to the [best load boards for hotshot](/blog/best-load-boards-for-hotshot.html) covers the boards, and [how to start a hotshot business](/blog/how-to-start-a-hotshot-business.html) covers setup if you are just beginning.

## Hotshot dispatch with Texas Solutions

Texas Solutions is a dispatch service, not a broker or carrier. Our 24/7 remote dispatchers find, negotiate and book hotshot loads for owner-operators and small fleets nationwide, and you approve every load before it is booked. Hotshot dispatch is **7% of weekly gross** for OTR, with no flat rate, no setup fee and no long-term contract. We work with new authority from day one, and the first load is dispatched free.

See our [hotshot dispatch service](/hotshot-dispatch.html) or [get a free estimate](/estimate.html?truck=hotshot).

### How Much Do Box Truck Owner-Operators Make? Gross, Costs and Net
URL: https://dispatch.texassolutions.co/guides/how-much-do-box-truck-owner-operators-make/
Published: 2026-10-13

"How much can I make with a box truck?" is usually the first question people ask, and the honest answer is that it depends on three things: how many miles you run, what those miles pay, and what it costs you to run them. Gross revenue gets the attention, but net income is what you live on.

This post breaks down box truck income with a worked example. For the semi side of the same question, see [how much owner-operators make](/blog/how-much-do-owner-operators-make.html).

## Gross vs net: the difference that matters

- **Gross** is what the loads pay before any expenses.
- **Net** is what is left after fuel, insurance, payments, repairs, fees and other costs.
- **Take-home** is net minus income and self-employment taxes.

Two drivers with the same weekly gross can take home very different amounts if one has a paid-off truck and low insurance and the other has a big payment and runs a lot of empty miles.

## What box truck loads pay

As a rough guide, box truck loads often pay about **$1.80 to $3.20 per mile**. Rates move with:

- **Lane.** Loads into areas with little outbound freight need to pay more to cover the trip out.
- **Season.** Retail peaks and holiday volume can push rates up; slow months push them down.
- **Urgency and service.** Expedited, team or liftgate-required freight often pays more.
- **Distance.** Short loads often pay more per mile but take more time per dollar.

Compare equipment types on our [rate per mile guide](/truck-dispatch-rates.html). Rates are market-driven and not guaranteed.

## Example weekly gross for box trucks (hypothetical)

As a hypothetical example, OTR box trucks might gross about **$7,000 to $9,000 a week**. That is not a promise. Weeks with breakdowns, home time, weather or soft freight markets will come in lower, and some weeks may come in higher.

## Worked example: a good week

Here is a sample week with clearly labelled assumptions. Replace them with your own figures.

**Assumptions:**

- Weekly gross: **$8,000**
- Loaded miles: 3,000, empty (deadhead) miles: 400, total 3,400
- Average fuel economy: 9.5 mpg (26 ft diesel, mix of loaded and empty)
- Diesel price: $4.50 a gallon
- Dispatch: 8% of gross
- Factoring: 3% of gross
- Insurance: $350 a week
- Truck payment: $450 a week
- Maintenance and tire reserve: $0.15 a mile
- ELD, phone, tolls and other: $100 a week

**Costs:**

- Fuel: 3,400 / 9.5 = 357.9 gallons x $4.50 = **$1,611**
- Dispatch: $8,000 x 0.08 = **$640**
- Factoring: $8,000 x 0.03 = **$240**
- Insurance: **$350**
- Truck payment: **$450**
- Maintenance reserve: 3,400 x $0.15 = **$510**
- Other: **$100**
- **Total: $3,901**

**Net before taxes:** $8,000 - $3,901 = **$4,099**, or about 51% of gross.

## Worked example: a slow week

Same truck, same fixed costs, fewer miles and lower rates.

**Assumptions:** weekly gross **$5,000**, total miles 2,200, other assumptions unchanged.

- Fuel: 2,200 / 9.5 = 231.6 gallons x $4.50 = **$1,042**
- Dispatch: **$400**
- Factoring: **$150**
- Insurance: **$350**
- Truck payment: **$450**
- Maintenance reserve: 2,200 x $0.15 = **$330**
- Other: **$100**
- **Total: $2,822**

**Net before taxes:** $5,000 - $2,822 = **$2,178**, or about 44% of gross.

Notice that fixed costs did not shrink when revenue dropped. That is why slow weeks hurt more than the drop in gross suggests, and why a cash reserve matters.

## Turning weekly numbers into a yearly estimate

Do not multiply your best week by 52. A more realistic method:

1. Estimate how many weeks you will actually work. Home time, repairs and holidays count against you.
2. Use an average week, not your best week.
3. Subtract taxes. Set aside money each week for quarterly estimated payments and talk with a tax professional.

For example, if you average **$3,000 net a week** (an assumption between the two examples above) and work **46 weeks**, that is 3,000 x 46 = **$138,000 before taxes**. If your average is lower, or you work fewer weeks, the annual figure drops quickly.

## The costs that decide box truck income

### Fuel

A 26 ft diesel box truck commonly gets somewhere around 8.5 to 11 mpg, lower when heavy. At box truck rates, fuel can take a large share of every dollar. Check your fuel cost by state with the [truck fuel cost calculator](/truck-fuel-cost-calculator.html?truck=box-truck#fuelCalc).

### Empty miles

Every empty mile costs fuel and wear and pays nothing. Planning the next load before you deliver is one of the simplest ways to raise net income. See [what deadhead is and how to reduce it](/blog/what-is-deadhead-in-trucking-how-to-reduce-it.html).

### Insurance and payments

These do not change with how much you run. The more miles you spread them over, the lower your cost per mile.

### Unpaid extras

Detention, layovers and lumper charges add up. If you do not document and invoice them, you are working for free. Texas Solutions handles detention and lumper collection as part of its [back office services](/trucking-back-office-services.html).

## How to find box truck loads that pay

- Know your cost per mile and refuse loads below it. Use the [cost per mile calculator](/cost-per-mile-calculator.html).
- Check each offer, including empty miles, with the [load profitability calculator](/load-profitability-calculator.html).
- Negotiate. Our guide on [how to negotiate freight rates](/blog/how-to-negotiate-freight-rates.html) explains how.
- Use load boards well. See the [best load boards for box trucks](/blog/best-load-boards-for-box-trucks.html).
- Build repeat business with good brokers, covered in [box truck contracts and how to get them](/blog/box-truck-contracts-how-to-get-them.html).

Box truck and straight truck dispatch is **8% of weekly gross** for OTR, with no setup fee and no long-term contract, and the first load is dispatched free.
